questions.why: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with weight loss, hoarseness, chest pain or breathlessness in an older adult needs a chest X-ray. A suspicious film needs an urgent CT and specialist referral, with the patient seen within 2 weeks.
notes: The X-ray shows a discrete apical mass with no pleural effusion, plaques or pleural thickening.
No fevers, night sweats, travel or TB contact, and the lesion is a solid mass without cavitation.
No clubbing, no fine crackles, no reticular change on the X-ray, and it does not explain the mass.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman in general practice. Two spontaneous attacks of spinning vertigo lasting about 8 hours, fluctuating right hearing loss with tinnitus and fullness, a documented right low-frequency sensorineural loss, and a normal examination between attacks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Vestibular schwannoma
Posterior circulation TIA or stroke
Vestibular migraine
Ménière's disease of the right ear
questions.why: Clarify what “dizzy” means first. True vertigo is vestibular, and its timing and triggers (seconds and positional, hours and spontaneous, or days and continuous) narrow the cause.
notes: The symptoms are episodic and the loss is low-frequency, with good word recognition, present acoustic reflexes and normal cranial nerves V and VII.
The attacks lasted 8 hours each with full recovery, there are no neurological symptoms, the examination is normal and the ear symptoms point to the inner ear.
No headache, aura or light or noise sensitivity, and she has a documented one-sided low-frequency sensorineural loss.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman in general practice. Diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, exophthalmos and lid retraction, weight loss, tremor, warm moist hands, AF, suppressed TSH with high free T4 and T3, and positive TRAb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Graves' disease
Impending thyroid storm
Toxic multinodular goitre
Toxic adenoma
questions.why: Examine thyroid status as well as the gland: hands, tremor, reflexes, eyes from the front, side and above, the neck with a swallow and tongue protrusion, palpation from behind, percussion of the manubrium, a bruit, and the legs.
notes: Afebrile (37.0 °C), alert and oriented, no vomiting, only mildly increased bowel frequency, no heart failure, haemodynamically stable. A Burch–Wartofsky score may reach the mid-20s to 30s from the AF and restlessness alone, but clinically she is compensated. Admit if fever, confusion, vomiting, worsening tachycardia or heart failure develop.
She is 32, the gland is smooth and diffuse with no nodules, she has eye signs, and TRAb is positive.
There is no solitary nodule, both lobes are enlarged, and TRAb is positive.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman in the emergency department. Colicky periumbilical pain, faeculent vomiting, no stool or flatus, distension, tinkling bowel sounds, previous laparoscopy, and a CT transition point under the right iliac fossa port site with no mass or hernia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute mesenteric ischaemia
Adhesive small bowel obstruction
Clostridioides difficile colitis
Large bowel obstruction
questions.why: Colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation (no stool or flatus) are the cardinal features of bowel obstruction. Always ask specifically about flatus and previous surgery.
notes: Lactate is normal, bowel wall enhancement is normal, the SMA and SMV are patent, she has no AF and the pain is colicky, not constant.
She had only one episode of diarrhoea and nothing since, she is afebrile, and the colon is collapsed on CT with no wall thickening.
Vomiting began within hours of the pain, and CT shows a collapsed colon with the transition point in the small bowel.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman in the emergency department. Sharp retrosternal pleuritic pain that is worse lying down and better sitting forward, a friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, a febrile son 10 days ago, temperature 37.8 °C and CRP 46. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute pericarditis
ST-elevation myocardial infarction or other acute coronary syndrome
Acute aortic dissection
Pulmonary embolism
questions.why: Pericarditis pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional: worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward. Acute pericarditis needs 2 of 4 criteria: typical pain, a friction rub, typical ECG changes and a pericardial effusion.
notes: She is 34 with no cardiovascular risk factors, the pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional, the ST elevation spans limb and chest leads without fitting one coronary territory, with PR depression and no Q waves, and hs-troponin is normal at 0 and 2 hours.
The pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the mediastinum is not widened on the chest X-ray.
She has no breathlessness, haemoptysis, calf symptoms, previous clot, immobility or oestrogen, SpO2 is 99%, Wells is 1.5 and the D-dimer is normal.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in general practice. Six-week progressive productive cough with 5 days of haemoptysis, low-grade fever, fatigue, breathlessness and 5 kg weight loss; born in and travels annually to Cambodia; right upper zone crackles and right upper lobe opacification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Lung cancer
Pulmonary embolism
Melioidosis
Pulmonary tuberculosis
questions.why: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with haemoptysis, fever and weight loss in someone born in or travelling to a country with high TB rates is pulmonary TB until proven otherwise.
notes: Aged 26 with only 1.5 pack-years and a 6-week history, no clubbing or lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar enlargement on the X-ray.
Gradual productive cough with fever, no pleuritic pain, no immobility or calf signs, SpO2 97% and a normal heart rate.
No diabetes, heavy alcohol use or kidney disease; sputum culture with the lab alerted to Burkholderia will help exclude it.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man in general practice. Constant dull periumbilical pain for 12 hours with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever, pain on coughing and movement, and right iliac fossa tenderness with rebound and a positive Rovsing's sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute appendicitis
Acute pancreatitis
Small bowel obstruction
Crohn's disease
questions.why: Early appendicitis causes vague, constant periumbilical pain (visceral afferents) that later localises to the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
notes: Lower abdominal and periumbilical rather than epigastric pain, no back radiation, and no gallstones.
No distension, bowel sounds present, and no previous abdominal surgery.
No weight loss, fatigue, diarrhoea or blood in the stool, and only a 12-hour history.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman in general practice. Two months of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, perianal inflammation with skin tags, clubbing, a smoker, calprotectin 820, and cobblestoning with skip lesions and granulomas at colonoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Intestinal tuberculosis
Ulcerative colitis
Infective colitis or gastroenteritis
Crohn's disease
questions.why: Chronic diarrhoea with blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss or fever is organic until proven otherwise; ask about each directly, along with NSAIDs, smoking and a family history of IBD.
notes: The granulomas are non-caseating, the acid-fast bacilli stain is negative, and she has no TB risk factors.
Right iliac fossa pain, perianal skin tags, terminal ileal disease, skip lesions with rectal sparing, and granulomas on biopsy.
Symptoms for 2 months with no travel, antibiotics or sick contacts, and negative stool PCR, culture and C. difficile toxin.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man in the emergency department. About 4 beers a night with 12 last night, constant epigastric pain through to the back eased by leaning forward, lipase 1850 U/L, a bulky pancreas with peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound, no gallstones and an isolated raised GGT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Perforated peptic ulcer
Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm
Acute alcohol-related pancreatitis
Inferior myocardial infarction
questions.why: Acute pancreatitis needs 2 of 3 criteria: typical epigastric pain through to the back, lipase more than 3 times the upper limit, and characteristic imaging. The height of the lipase does not reflect severity.
notes: No NSAIDs or previous indigestion, no rigidity or rebound, and the lipase is more than 30 times the upper limit.
The pain is not tearing, BP is normal and equal in both arms, there is no pulsatile mass, the aorta measures 2.0 cm on ultrasound, and (partly) at 56 he is below the usual risk age.
No chest pain or breathlessness, the pain is positional, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST or T wave changes.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman in the emergency department. Constant right upper quadrant pain for about 20 hours after a rich meal, radiating to the shoulder tip, with fever, chills, vomiting, earlier postprandial episodes, a positive Murphy's sign, WCC 15.8, CRP 142 and an ultrasound showing a 6 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and an impacted neck stone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ascending cholangitis
Acute calculous cholecystitis
Perforated peptic ulcer
Ectopic pregnancy
questions.why: Biliary colic settles within a few hours. Constant RUQ pain lasting longer, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP, is acute cholecystitis.
notes: No jaundice or confusion, bilirubin 16, common bile duct 4 mm with no duct stone, normal BP and lactate.
Pain maximal in the RUQ with only mild epigastric tenderness, no reflux or melaena, no rigidity or generalised peritonism, and the ultrasound shows a clear biliary cause.
She takes the pill daily, had a normal period 2 weeks ago, has no bleeding or faintness, a normal BP and a serum beta-hCG below 2 IU/L.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman in the emergency department. She has 4 weeks of burning retrosternal pain that is worse lying down and after meals, with acid regurgitation, no exertional features, a normal ECG and negative serial troponin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
Acute coronary syndrome or unstable angina
Oesophageal or gastric cancer
Peptic ulcer disease
questions.why: In ED chest pain, rule out ACS before settling on reflux: a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, then serial high-sensitivity troponin on a validated assay-specific 0/1 h or 0/2 h pathway. A normal ECG alone does not exclude ACS.
notes: The pain is burning, positional and related to meals, never exertional and has no associated features, and her ECG during pain and her troponin at 0 and 2 hours are normal.
She has no anaemia, haematemesis, hoarseness or palpable lymph nodes, and she is 45 and a non-smoker.
The pain is retrosternal rather than epigastric, with no bloating, early satiety, NSAID use or bleeding, and her Hb is normal.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man in general practice. Twelve weeks of pale floating loose stools with weight loss, fatigue and bloating, an itchy blistering rash on both knees, family type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease, iron and folate deficiency, and strongly positive tTG-IgA and EMA with normal total IgA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Crohn's disease of the small bowel
Hyperthyroidism
Giardiasis
Coeliac disease
questions.why: In chronic diarrhoea, ask what the stool looks like: pale, floating stools suggest fat malabsorption, and weight loss, steatorrhoea or anaemia are red flags that rule out a label of IBS until they are explained.
notes: No blood, abdominal pain, mouth ulcers or perianal disease, a normal CRP, and serology and a rash that point to coeliac disease.
No heat intolerance, palpitations or tremor, no goitre, and a normal TSH and free T4.
No travel, untreated water, sick contacts or fever.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman in general practice. Jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension with known gallstones, a cholestatic LFT pattern and a dilated duct with a distal stone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pancreatic head carcinoma causing malignant biliary obstruction
Severe acute cholangitis
Acute gallstone pancreatitis
Acute calculous cholecystitis
questions.why: Charcot's triad (jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever) suggests acute cholangitis. Adding confusion and hypotension makes Reynolds' pentad, which marks sepsis with organ dysfunction and hypoperfusion and needs urgent drainage of the bile duct.
notes: No weight loss or steatorrhoea, acute febrile onset, a stone seen in the duct, and no distal duct stricture or mass effect on the ERCP cholangiogram.
Normal lipase and no peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound.
Murphy's sign negative, no gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, and conjugated jaundice with a dilated common bile duct.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man in general practice. Four months of daily burning retrosternal pain after dinner, worse lying down and with spicy food, with an acid taste in the throat, a night cough and a normal ECG and bloods. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Barrett's oesophagus or oesophageal adenocarcinoma
Stable angina
Peptic ulcer disease
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
questions.why: Burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying down, with an acid taste and a night cough, is typical of GORD, which is a clinical diagnosis.
notes: No dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting or anaemia, and a short 4-month history.
Burning pain that lasts about 30 minutes whatever he does and is not relieved by rest, is not brought on by tennis, is worse lying down with an acid taste, and a normal ECG.
No epigastric tenderness, no NSAID or aspirin use, and a normal haemoglobin and ferritin.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman in the emergency department. Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after 3 days of a swollen, tender right calf, a long-haul flight 4 days ago, oestrogen HRT, limited mobility and smoking, with sinus tachycardia and bilateral filling defects on CTPA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute pulmonary embolism
Acute coronary syndrome
Acute aortic dissection
Spontaneous pneumothorax
questions.why: Ask every patient with pleuritic chest pain or breathlessness about VTE risk factors (travel, oestrogen, immobility, surgery, cancer, previous VTE, smoking), and examine both legs.
notes: The pain is sharp and pleuritic with no radiation, nausea or sweating, and the ECG and hs-troponin are normal.
No tearing pain or radiation to the back, no syncope or hypertension, equal arm BPs, and a normal-calibre aorta with no flap on CT.
No chest trauma or lung disease, the trachea is central, percussion and breath sounds are normal, and CT shows no pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man in the emergency department. A 64-year-old with a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, worsening right visual loss with RAPD and a pale swollen disc, a tender pulseless right temporal artery, ESR 86 and CRP 78. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Giant cell arteritis
Intracranial mass lesion
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
questions.why: A new headache in anyone over 50 is giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise. Always ask about scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms and polymyalgia rheumatica.
notes: The onset was gradual, not thunderclap, and he has no meningism, vomiting or focal signs.

The headache is not worse in the morning or on lying or straining, he has no weight loss or behaviour change, and the disc swelling is in one eye with a field defect and RAPD rather than bilateral papilloedema.
The disc is pale (chalky) rather than hyperaemic, and he has headache, jaw claudication, an abnormal temporal artery and ESR 86 with CRP 78.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man in general practice. Sudden single hot, swollen knee with an effusion, pain on any movement, unable to bear weight, fever with rigors and tachycardia, a dirty nail puncture 2 days earlier, diabetes and pre-existing OA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute crystal arthritis
Septic prepatellar or superficial infrapatellar bursitis
Disseminated gonococcal arthritis
Septic arthritis of the left knee
questions.why: An acute, single hot, swollen joint with fever is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. The knee is involved in about half of cases.
notes: Against gout: no previous attacks, no tophi, no diuretics, normal first MTPs. Pseudogout (CPPD) is common in an OA knee at 70 and cannot be excluded clinically; only crystals on aspiration distinguish it, and crystals do not exclude coexisting infection. The nail puncture and rigors favour infection.
A true joint effusion with tenderness all around the joint, pain on any movement and no separate swelling in front of the patella.
Married and monogamous for 45 years, with no discharge, dysuria, rash or tenosynovitis.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man in general practice. Sharp pain with every bowel motion lasting hours since a hard stool, small bright red bleeding, constipation, a posterior midline tear with clean edges and no sentinel tag, and too tender for a DRE. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute primary anal fissure
Perianal abscess or fistula-in-ano
Secondary anal fissure
Anorectal or colorectal cancer
questions.why: Anal fissure pain is sharp during a bowel motion and lasts minutes to hours afterwards, often with a small amount of bright red blood on the paper, after a hard stool.
notes: Pain is episodic rather than constant and throbbing, he is afebrile, and there is no swelling, fluctuance, discharge or external opening.
Single posterior midline fissure; one long-term partner, no anal sex or STI symptoms; no diarrhoea, weight loss, abdominal pain or extraintestinal features.
Short history with bleeding on the paper explained by the fissure, no change in bowel habit, weight loss or family history.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman in clinic. Three months of symmetrical synovitis of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs with DIP sparing, tender MTPs, 90 minutes of morning stiffness, raised CRP and ESR, positive RF and anti-CCP, and marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Psoriatic arthritis
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Early seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis
Viral polyarthritis
questions.why: Examine the hands in order: prepare (consent, exposure above the elbows, pillow, ask about pain), general inspection, look at the backs and palms, elbows, feel each joint group, move with special tests and function, then the feet and the systemic features.
notes: No psoriasis, nail pitting, onycholysis or dactylitis, the DIPs are spared, there is no periostitis or pencil-in-cup change, and anti-CCP is strongly positive.
No rash, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, alopecia or Raynaud's, ANA is negative, and the X-ray shows erosions, which SLE arthritis does not cause.
It has lasted 3 months rather than a few weeks, there is no rash in her or her contacts, and she has erosions and a strongly positive anti-CCP.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man in general practice. Prodrome of nausea, chills, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort then jaundice, 4 to 7 weeks after eating street food in Thailand and Vietnam with no travel vaccines, with hepatocellular LFTs and a positive hepatitis A IgM. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute hepatitis A infection
Acute hepatitis B infection
Paracetamol or other drug-induced liver injury
Acute hepatitis E infection
questions.why: Classify jaundice as pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic using the urine and stool colour, itch, and the LFT pattern (transaminases versus ALP and GGT, conjugated versus unconjugated bilirubin).
notes: HBsAg and anti-HBc are both negative.
Only occasional doses within the recommended amount, a normal INR, and a positive hepatitis A IgM.
Hepatitis E IgM not detected, and hepatitis A IgM is positive.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man in general practice. Right neck pain radiating to the thumb with paraesthesia, weakness of shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and wrist extension, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, pain reproduced by neck extension, and concordant right C4-5 and C5-6 foraminal stenosis on MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
Right C5 and C6 radiculopathy
Transient ischaemic attack
Motor neurone disease
questions.why: Examine the upper limbs in a fixed order, comparing sides at every step: inspection, tone, pronator drift, power, reflexes, coordination, then sensation. Isolate each movement and use reinforcement before calling a reflex absent.
notes: No hand clumsiness, gait change or bladder symptoms, normal tone, no Hoffmann's sign or inverted supinator reflex, normal lower limbs and a normal cord on MRI.

The weakness is never sudden in onset; it comes only when he loads the arm and settles with rest, with no face, speech or leg involvement, and there is a fixed lower motor neuron deficit with radicular pain.

Pain and sensory symptoms, no fasciculations, no upper motor neuron signs anywhere (normal tone, no Hoffmann's sign, normal lower limbs), a deficit confined to two roots and concordant root compression on MRI.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman in general practice. Five to six months of new constipation at 62 with straining, tenesmus, blood mixed with the stool, fatigue, iron deficiency anaemia, a brother diagnosed at 48 and smoking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Upper gastrointestinal source of iron deficiency
Recurrent haemorrhoids
Colorectal cancer
Diverticular disease
questions.why: A new, persistent change in bowel habit at an older age, especially with rectal bleeding, tenesmus or anaemia, is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise, even when there is a benign explanation such as previous haemorrhoids.
notes: No dyspepsia, weight loss or melaena, and the visible blood and change in bowel habit point to the colon.
Blood is mixed through the stool rather than on the paper, there are no haemorrhoids on rectal examination or proctoscopy, and haemorrhoids do not explain the change in habit.

Diverticulosis is usually silent and does not cause a progressive change in habit or chronic iron deficiency; no LIF pain or fever to suggest diverticulitis; diverticular bleeding is usually sudden, painless and large.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man in general practice. Strictly left orbital pain at 10/10, lasting 2 to 3 hours, at the same time almost daily for 2 months and waking him, with same-sided tearing, red eye, rhinorrhoea and partial Horner's, restlessness, an earlier bout a year ago with 8 pain-free months, a father with similar headaches, and a normal examination and MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Cluster headache
Space-occupying lesion or raised intracranial pressure
Carotid artery dissection
questions.why: Strictly one-sided orbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, at the same time each day, with tearing, a red eye, a runny or blocked nose on the same side and restlessness, is cluster headache. Patients with migraine lie still, while patients with cluster headache pace.
notes: Daily recurrent attacks that build over minutes and resolve completely, with no thunderclap onset, meningism or neurological deficit, and a normal MRI with no blood on SWI.
Fixed-time attacks with complete resolution, no vomiting, positional or Valsalva features or progression, no papilloedema or focal signs, and a normal MRI with contrast.
Recurrent stereotyped attacks over months with full resolution; Horner's resolves between attacks; no neck pain, trauma or focal deficit.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl in the emergency department. Three weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and weight loss, then vomiting, Kussmaul breathing and ketotic breath, an autoimmune family history, glucose 38.2, pH 7.05 and blood ketones 6.0. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sepsis
Adrenal crisis
Severe diabetic ketoacidosis as the first presentation
Viral gastroenteritis
questions.why: Vomiting with polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and weight loss in a young person is DKA until proven otherwise; check a bedside glucose and ketones early.
notes: Afebrile, no rigors, dysuria or loin pain, CRP 3, and no leucocytes, nitrites or bacteria in the urine.
Glucose is high not low, the corrected sodium is normal, K is only 5.3, no pigmentation, and the ketoacidosis explains the picture.
No diarrhoea or sick contacts, 3 weeks of osmotic symptoms and weight loss, and a severe ketoacidosis with a glucose of 38.2.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in general practice. Pale foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating, 3 kg weight loss, grouped vesicles on both extensor knees, a mother with Graves' and a twin with type 1 diabetes, and tTG-IgA 128 U/mL with normal total IgA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Crohn's disease
Coeliac disease
Iron deficiency anaemia
Chronic pancreatitis
questions.why: Do not accept 'stress' for new fatigue with diarrhoea and weight loss: screen every system, and ask specifically about the stool, the skin and the periods.
notes: No blood or mucus, no mouth ulcers, normal CRP and ESR, and serology strongly positive for coeliac; faecal calprotectin, or ileocolonoscopy (with terminal ileal biopsy), with MR enterography or capsule endoscopy if needed, if duodenal histology is not typical.
Heavy periods do not explain the steatorrhoea, weight loss, low folate and vitamin D, or the strongly positive coeliac serology.
Her faecal elastase is normal at 410 and her pain does not radiate to the back.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in the emergency department. Sudden maximal tearing central pain through to the back with syncope in a hypertensive smoker, a weak right radial with a 32 mmHg arm BP difference, an aortic regurgitation murmur, very raised D-dimer and a CT flap from the ascending aorta. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute myocardial infarction
Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection
Pulmonary embolism
Pneumothorax
questions.why: Sudden, maximal, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, especially with syncope, is aortic dissection until proven otherwise; descending dissection may give interscapular pain and some patients present with syncope alone.
notes: The pain is tearing and goes to the back rather than crushing to the jaw or arm, the ECG shows no ST elevation and is unchanged from 2024, and the small troponin rise can be explained by demand or coronary involvement by the dissection.
He has no calf symptoms, travel, immobility, previous clot or cancer, and the arm BP difference, murmur and CT findings explain everything.
There was no trauma, the pain is not pleuritic, the chest is resonant with equal breath sounds, and CT shows no pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in general practice. Gradual, constant left calf pain with 3.5 cm calf swelling, pitting oedema and deep vein tenderness while on the combined pill after months of sitting, and a non-compressible popliteal vein on ultrasound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pulmonary embolism
Acute proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left leg
Cellulitis of the left leg
Gastrocnemius or soleus tear or contusion
questions.why: In unilateral calf pain, ask specifically about immobility, oestrogen-containing contraception, pregnancy, previous or family VTE, cancer and PE symptoms.
notes: No breathlessness, chest pain, cough or haemoptysis, and HR 84 with SpO2 99% on room air.
No fever, redness, streaking or skin break, and a normal white cell count.
No injury or sudden tearing pain, she weight bears, there is no palpable defect, and the ultrasound shows no tear or haematoma.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in general practice. Worsening left calf claudication, night rest pain eased by hanging the foot down, a punched-out pale ulcer on a bony prominence, absent left popliteal and pedal pulses, Buerger's angle 20 degrees, ABI 0.56 and toe pressure 24 mmHg in a smoker with diabetes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Infected diabetes-related foot ulcer or osteomyelitis
Acute limb ischaemia
Neuropathic diabetes-related foot ulcer
Arterial ulcer
questions.why: Ask about rest pain: night pain in the forefoot eased by hanging the foot down, with an ulcer, means chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and needs urgent vascular referral.
notes: No cellulitis, pus or odour, afebrile, probe to bone negative, and normal WCC and CRP.
Gradual worsening over a year, no sudden pain, coldness, numbness or weakness, and sensation and movement are normal.
The ulcer is painful, not on the sole, has no callus, and monofilament and vibration sensation are intact.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in the emergency department. A 75-year-old with lifelong constipation and a low-fibre diet who suddenly passed a large volume of painless dark red blood with clots, has a normal anorectal examination and CRP, and whose colonoscopy shows extensive sigmoid and descending diverticula with no other source. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Colorectal cancer
Angiodysplasia of the colon
Diverticular bleeding
Haemorrhoids
questions.why: Diverticular bleeding is sudden, painless and often large-volume, bright red or maroon with clots, in an older patient with constipation or a low-fibre diet. It usually stops by itself but can recur.
notes: No change in bowel habit, weight loss or tiredness, no rectal mass, normal MCV and ferritin, and no tumour or polyp on a complete colonoscopy (a negative screening FOBT 2 years ago gives little reassurance in a symptomatic patient).
No vascular lesions were seen on a complete colonoscopy and diverticula explain the bleed.
No lump, itch or prolapse, the blood was dark with clots and mixed with stool rather than on the paper, and no haemorrhoids on inspection or retroflexion.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman in the emergency department. One day of fever with worsening confusion, personality change and right arm weakness in an immunosuppressed woman with past cold sores, left temporal hypodensity on CT and HSV-1 PCR detected in a lymphocytic CSF. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bacterial meningitis
Brain abscess
Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis
Left hemisphere ischaemic stroke
questions.why: Fever with an altered mental state, personality change or focal signs is encephalitis until proven otherwise. Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly at once, without waiting for CT, LP or PCR.
notes: She has no headache, neck stiffness, photophobia or rash, and her CSF has a normal glucose, no organisms and a lymphocytic pattern.
She has no swinging fevers, seizures or ear, sinus or dental source, and CT shows no mass or collection.
She has fever and a progressive course over a day, no facial droop or dysarthria, an inflammatory CSF and a CT change outside a single arterial territory.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man in the emergency department. A thunderclap worst-ever headache while jogging, a sentinel headache 2 weeks ago, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, GCS 13 and subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages in a man with ADPKD and hypertension, with basal cistern blood and a 7 mm ACom aneurysm on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Intracerebral haemorrhage
Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage
Bacterial meningitis
Extradural or subdural haematoma
questions.why: A thunderclap headache, maximal within seconds to a minute, is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Always ask about an earlier 'warning' headache, which is often mistaken for migraine.
notes: He has no focal deficit, and the CT shows no parenchymal haematoma.
The onset was sudden rather than over hours, he is afebrile at 37.3 °C, and he has no rash or infective symptoms.
He had no head injury or fall, and the CT shows no extra-axial collection.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man in the emergency department. Two hours of central pressure to the left arm and jaw on exertion with breathlessness, sweating and nausea, multiple risk factors, new ST depression in V4 to V6, I and aVL and hs-troponin T rising from 62 to 148 ng/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute aortic dissection
Pulmonary embolism
Pneumothorax
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
questions.why: Central pressure radiating to the arm and jaw, brought on by exertion and not relieved by rest, with breathlessness, sweating and nausea in a man with many risk factors is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise; get an ECG within 10 minutes.
notes: The pain built over minutes as a pressure, is not tearing and does not go to the back, the arm BPs are equal and the mediastinum is not widened.
No pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, immobility, surgery, travel or previous clot, and the ECG and troponin pattern fit coronary ischaemia.
The pain was not sudden or one-sided, breath sounds and percussion are equal, and the chest X-ray shows no pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man in general practice. A daily bilateral pressing headache of 5 to 6/10 that builds through the day, not worse with cycling, with neck and shoulder stiffness, tender pericranial muscles, thesis stress and long desk hours, and a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Meningitis
Raised intracranial pressure / space-occupying lesion
Tension-type headache
Migraine without aura
questions.why: Separate primary from secondary headache by grouping your red flag questions by diagnosis: SAH (thunderclap onset), meningitis (fever, rash, neck stiffness), raised pressure or tumour (progressive, worst on waking, worse with coughing or straining, vomiting), stroke or TIA, and head injury.
notes: Six weeks of daily headache in someone who is well, afebrile, with no rash, photophobia or meningism and full passive neck flexion.
Never on waking, not worse with coughing, straining or lying down, no vomiting, sharp discs with venous pulsations and a normal neurological examination.
The pain is bilateral, pressing and moderate, not throbbing, with no nausea, light or noise sensitivity or aura, and it is not worsened by activity.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in general practice. Sudden-onset, self-terminating, fast irregular palpitations now daily, an irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit, an ECG with no P waves, a regular pulse after the episode stopped, and heavy alcohol, smoking, hypertension, OSA and obesity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ventricular tachycardia
Atrial or ventricular ectopic beats
Atrial flutter
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
questions.why: Ask the patient to tap out the palpitations: fast and irregular points to AF, fast and regular to SVT or VT, and a missed beat to ectopics.
notes: Narrow QRS complexes, no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting, and no ischaemic change on the ECG.
Sustained fast episodes lasting minutes to hours, and the ECG shows a continuous irregular rhythm without P waves rather than isolated early beats.
The rhythm he taps and the ECG are irregularly irregular, with no regular flutter waves.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman in general practice. 50 pack-years, progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic white productive cough, wheeze, flare-ups with colds, hyperinflation with wheeze, and post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50 with FEV1 58% predicted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Lung cancer
Chronic stable angina
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
questions.why: COPD is confirmed on spirometry by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7; by COPD-X, an FEV1 of 40 to 59% predicted is moderate disease. A chest X-ray supports it and excludes other causes but cannot diagnose it.
notes: No weight loss, appetite change, night sweats, haemoptysis, hoarseness or lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar enlargement on the chest X-ray.
The tightness comes with wheeze and breathlessness, is not crushing, does not radiate and has no sweating or nausea.
Productive rather than dry cough, no fine crackles or clubbing, no interstitial change on X-ray, and obstructive rather than restrictive spirometry.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in general practice. Lower abdominal pain before bowel motions with urgency, alternating loose and hard stools, bloating, triggers of stress and dairy, gastroenteritis 6 months ago, and normal bloods, coeliac serology, calprotectin and stool tests. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Inflammatory bowel disease
Irritable bowel syndrome
Colorectal cancer
Coeliac disease
questions.why: In chronic lower GI symptoms, screen every patient for red flags: rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, fever, a mass, and a family history of colorectal cancer, IBD or coeliac disease. Rectal bleeding with a change in bowel habit warrants colonoscopy even in a young adult.
notes: No blood, weight loss, night symptoms or extraintestinal features, no right iliac fossa mass, and a normal CRP and calprotectin of 28.
Aged 26 with no rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia or family history, a normal examination and a normal calprotectin.
Negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA while eating gluten, and normal ferritin and folate.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman in general practice. Months of daytime sleepiness with unrefreshing sleep, chronic heavy snoring, poor concentration, BMI 36 with a 42 cm neck and crowded oropharynx, hypertension, T2DM, smoking, evening alcohol, ESS 15, STOP-Bang 5 and OSA50 6. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Obstructive sleep apnoea
Underlying malignancy
Hypothyroidism
Perimenopause
questions.why: Separate sleepiness (dozing off) from fatigue (lack of energy) early. Sleepiness points to a sleep disorder such as OSA.
notes: No weight loss, night sweats, fevers, lumps or bleeding, and a normal blood count.
No cold intolerance, constipation or skin changes, normal reflexes and a normal TSH.
Regular periods and no hot flushes or night sweats.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man in the emergency department. A minor fall hitting the right side of his head 5 days ago, then 3 days of progressive right-sided headache on apixaban, now drowsier; crescentic mixed-density right collection crossing sutures with 8 mm midline shift. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Right subdural haematoma
Extradural haematoma
Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Intracranial tumour
questions.why: In every older person with a new or progressive headache, ask directly about falls or head injury and about anticoagulants. A trivial knock days earlier, with no loss of consciousness, is the typical story for a subdural haematoma.
notes: No loss of consciousness or lucid interval, no skull fracture, and the collection is crescentic and crosses the suture lines.
Gradual onset over days with no thunderclap, no neck stiffness or photophobia, and no subarachnoid blood on CT.
Clear history of head trauma, no morning or postural features or weight loss, and no mass on CT.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man in the emergency department. A sudden 30-second blackout with no warning, palpitations minutes before, quick full recovery, on metoprolol, HR 34 with cannon a waves, and an ECG showing AV dissociation with a broad infranodal escape. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ventricular tachyarrhythmia
Cardiac syncope
Acute myocardial infarction causing AV block
Vasovagal syncope
questions.why: In transient loss of consciousness, first establish that consciousness was truly lost. Then take the history before, during and after the event, including the witness account and a question about head strike and injuries.
notes: The monitor and ECG show a slow escape rhythm with no ventricular tachycardia, and he has no family history of sudden cardiac death.
He had no chest pain or breathlessness, the ECG has no ST elevation or Q waves, and the first troponin is not raised (repeat pending).
He had no prodrome (no light-headedness, sweating, pallor or visual greying), no emotional or situational trigger, and his ECG shows complete heart block.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man in the emergency department. Fever, chills and constant diffuse abdominal pain since yesterday with ascites growing over 2 weeks, in untreated alcohol-related cirrhosis with ongoing drinking, and an ascitic neutrophil count of 1295 x10^6/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Secondary bacterial peritonitis
Decompensated cirrhosis
Acute alcohol-related pancreatitis
questions.why: Fever, abdominal pain, worsening ascites, encephalopathy, AKI or a GI bleed in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites call for a diagnostic ascitic tap. SBP can be painless.
notes: Gradual onset, no guarding or rigidity, no previous surgery, ascitic protein 9 g/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L and LDH below the serum limit, and no organisms on Gram stain.
It does not explain the fever, rigors, WCC 13.8 or the ascitic neutrophil count.
The pain is generalised, not epigastric through to the back, there is no vomiting, and lipase is 40 U/L.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman in the emergency department. Four months of exertional dyspnoea, 2-pillow orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling a year after an anterior STEMI, with a raised JVP, S3, bibasal crackles, oedema, cardiomegaly and congestion on CXR and an NT-proBNP of 4850. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome precipitating heart failure
Decompensated biventricular heart failure
Lung cancer
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
questions.why: Quantify breathlessness against the patient's baseline (distance, stairs or activities) and ask specifically about orthopnoea (number of pillows), PND and ankle swelling.
notes: No chest pain, a gradual 4-month course, a flat troponin (24 then 25) and an ECG unchanged from 12 months ago.
No weight loss, haemoptysis or hoarseness, and no mass or nodule on CXR.
No cough, sputum or wheeze, orthopnoea and PND with oedema, and no hyperinflation on CXR.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man in general practice. Eight years of type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% from metformin non-adherence, gradual symmetrical stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg and loss of protective sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spinal cord or cauda equina compression
Vitamin B12 deficiency neuropathy
Alcohol-related peripheral neuropathy
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
questions.why: Glove-and-stocking sensory loss points to a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy, a dermatomal pattern to a root or cord lesion, and a single nerve territory to a nerve compression or injury.
notes: Against cord compression: no upper motor neuron signs (flexor plantars, no clonus, normal tone, knee reflexes not brisk) and no sensory level; against cauda equina: no back pain, no sphincter or saddle symptoms, and a gradual symmetrical stocking pattern rather than a saddle or radicular one.
He rarely takes the metformin, he is not vegetarian or vegan, and his B12, folate and MCV are normal.
He drinks only an occasional can of beer on weekends, and his GGT, LFTs and MCV are normal.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man in the emergency department. Five months of progressive breathlessness with 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, a hoarse voice, clubbing, a hard right supraclavicular node and 50 pack-years, with a large unilateral right effusion on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Malignant right pleural effusion
Parapneumonic effusion or empyema
Malignant pleural mesothelioma
Tuberculous pleural effusion
questions.why: In a smoker with progressive breathlessness, ask directly about weight loss, haemoptysis, hoarseness and night sweats, and quantify smoking in pack-years (20 a day for 50 years is 50 pack-years).
notes: The 5-month gradual course, no pleuritic pain or sick contacts, and a normal white cell count.
Haemoptysis, a hoarse voice and a supraclavicular node point more to a primary lung cancer.
Born in Australia with no TB travel, contacts or past TB, and the smoking history and node make cancer more likely.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman in the emergency department. Three weeks of constant burning forefoot pain that is worse lying flat and eased by hanging the leg, after years of claudication, with gangrene of three toes, absent right popliteal and pedal pulses, right ABI 0.28 and heavy cardiovascular risk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute-on-chronic limb ischaemia or atheroembolism
Deep vein thrombosis
Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of the right leg
Intermittent claudication
questions.why: Ischaemic rest pain is constant forefoot and toe pain, worse lying flat or at night and eased by hanging the leg down. Present for more than 2 weeks, or with gangrene or an ulcer, it defines chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
notes: She has no new numbness or weakness, power is 5/5 and her rhythm is regular, with a stable 3-week course.
Her calves are soft, non-tender and equal with no warmth or swelling, and the pain is in the toes and eased by dependency.
The current pain is constant at rest and there is tissue loss, so she has moved beyond claudication.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man on the ward. Day 5 after major orthopaedic surgery with little mobilisation, sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, HR 124, SpO2 92%, a swollen red right calf, Wells 9, and bilateral lower lobe emboli on CTPA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome
Acute aortic dissection
Hospital-acquired pneumonia
Acute pulmonary embolism
questions.why: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after major orthopaedic surgery is PE until proven otherwise: always examine both legs for a DVT.
notes: Sharp right-sided pleuritic pain without radiation, sweating or nausea, no ischaemic change on the ECG, and two normal troponins.
Pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the aorta is normal on CT.
No cough or sputum, a clear chest on examination and no consolidation on CT.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man in the emergency department. Breathlessness and sharp left pleuritic pain straight after a fall onto the left side, with tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, and complete left lung collapse with mediastinal shift on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Left tension pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
Traumatic haemothorax or haemopneumothorax
Pulmonary embolism
questions.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: breathlessness, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and hyper-resonance with reduced or absent breath sounds. Decompress before imaging.
notes: Heart sounds are not muffled, the trachea is deviated, and the left chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds on one side; a normal cardiac silhouette does not exclude acute tamponade, so eFAST is still needed.
The left chest is hyper-resonant rather than dull, the X-ray shows no effusion or fluid level, the neck veins are distended rather than flat, and the Hb is normal.
No leg swelling, immobility, travel or previous clots, and the trauma and one-sided signs explain the picture.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy in the emergency department. Acute expiratory wheeze with recession over a few hours after a 2-day cold, a partial response to salbutamol, rhinovirus on PCR, smoke exposure, day-care, preterm birth and atopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Inhaled foreign body
Anaphylaxis
Acute asthma
Viral-induced wheeze
questions.why: In a wheezy preschool child, always ask about anaphylaxis (skin signs with another system involved, new foods, stings) and an inhaled foreign body (sudden choking), because both need different, urgent treatment.
notes: There was no choking episode, the wheeze is bilateral and symmetrical, and it followed a coryzal illness.
No urticaria, angioedema, vomiting or floppiness, no new food or sting, and the onset was gradual after a cold.
He has no wheeze or night cough between colds and no other triggers, and at 3 years episodic viral wheeze is more likely.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man in the emergency department. Two weeks of worsening breathlessness with orthopnoea, PND and pink frothy sputum a month after an MI, 2 weeks of regular ibuprofen, a raised JVP, S3 and crackles, NT-proBNP 8400 and a chest X-ray showing alveolar oedema, upper lobe diversion and effusions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Recurrent myocardial infarction
Pulmonary embolism
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Community-acquired pneumonia
questions.why: Ask every breathless patient about orthopnoea (how many pillows), PND, frothy pink sputum and exercise tolerance, and examine the JVP, heart sounds for an S3, lung bases and ankles.
notes: No chest pain, nausea or radiation, and the ECG is unchanged from his discharge ECG.
No pleuritic pain, calf swelling or immobility, and orthopnoea, PND, an S3 and oedema on X-ray explain the picture.
No fever or purulent sputum, normal WCC, only a small CRP rise, and the change is bilateral with upper lobe diversion and effusions.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman in the emergency department. Constant right upper quadrant pain for over 24 hours after a fatty meal, with right shoulder radiation, fever to 38.9, a positive Murphy's sign, WCC 14.2, CRP 96, and an ultrasound showing a 5 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Choledocholithiasis or ascending cholangitis
Acute calculous cholecystitis
Acute coronary syndrome or right lower lobe pneumonia
Biliary colic
questions.why: Biliary colic is postprandial pain that settles within about 6 hours. Constant RUQ pain for hours, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP, is acute cholecystitis.
notes: No clinical jaundice, bilirubin only 26, common bile duct 5 mm with no intrahepatic dilatation, and normal BP and lactate.
No chest pain, breathlessness or cough, chest clear including the right base, SpO2 97% on room air, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST or T wave changes.
This pain has been constant and worsening for over a day, with fever, raised WCC and CRP, and a thickened gallbladder wall.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man in the emergency department. He shared needles 2 months ago, had a prodrome of fever, arthralgia, urticaria and malaise, now has jaundice with dark urine and pale stools and a tender smooth liver, with ALT 1635 and HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc and HBeAg positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute ascending cholangitis
Paracetamol or other drug-induced liver injury
Acute hepatitis C infection
Acute hepatitis B infection
questions.why: Viral hepatitis has a prodrome (anorexia, malaise, fever, RUQ pain; urticaria and arthralgia especially in hepatitis B), then an icteric phase with dark urine, pale stools, itch and jaundice.
notes: No rigors, haemodynamically stable, normal WCC with only a mild CRP rise, transaminase rise far greater than the ALP rise, a viral prodrome, and no duct dilatation or stones on ultrasound.
He denies any paracetamol, overdose, other medicines or supplements, and the paracetamol level is undetectable.
The HCV antibody is negative, although this can be falsely reassuring in the window period, and the hepatitis B serology already explains the illness.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman in general practice. Returned from Thailand a month ago after eating street food without pre-travel vaccination, with a 2-week prodrome, then jaundice, a hepatocellular picture and a positive HAV IgM. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ascending cholangitis
Acute hepatitis A infection
Malaria
Choledocholithiasis
questions.why: Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Always ask the 4 Ps (pee, poo, pruritus, pain) in jaundice.
notes: No gallstones or bile duct dilatation on ultrasound, ALT far higher than ALP, and a normal white cell count.
Normal haemoglobin and platelets, and a positive HAV IgM explains the picture.
Constant pain not related to food, no history of gallstones, and no stones or duct dilatation on ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in the emergency department. RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad), pale stools, dark urine and itch, cholestatic LFTs with WCC 17.8 and CRP 186, and an 11 mm common bile duct with a distal stone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute ascending cholangitis
Acute gallstone pancreatitis
Acute calculous cholecystitis
Acute viral hepatitis
questions.why: RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad) is acute cholangitis until proven otherwise. Confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) mean severe disease.
notes: Lipase 42 is normal, the pain does not go through to the back, and the visualised pancreas is normal.
She is jaundiced with obstructive features, Murphy's sign is negative, and the gallbladder wall is thin with no pericholecystic fluid.
No IV drugs, travel or unsafe sex, the LFTs are cholestatic with ALP and GGT raised more than ALT, and the bile ducts are dilated.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man in the emergency department. Two days of worsening headache with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and positive Kernig's sign in a man on prednisolone, with turbid neutrophilic CSF, high protein and a low glucose ratio. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bacterial meningitis
Viral encephalitis
Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Viral meningitis
questions.why: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean meningitis until proven otherwise. Always ask about and look for a non-blanching rash.
notes: He is oriented with GCS 15, intact attention, no drowsiness, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs.
It was not a thunderclap or worst-ever, with no collapse, and has built over 2 days with fever; the CT is normal and the CSF has minimal red cells.
His CSF is turbid with neutrophils, a high protein and a low glucose, and he has a CRP of 214 with a raised lactate.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman in general practice. Fever of 39 °C, a worsening generalised headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign in an 18-year-old after a crowded festival with a shared tent and uncertain meningococcal vaccination; the CSF is neutrophilic with a low glucose, Gram-negative diplococci and a positive N. meningitidis PCR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Viral encephalitis
Bacterial meningitis
Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Viral meningitis
questions.why: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. Ask about and look for a rash, but its absence does not exclude meningococcal disease.
notes: She is alert and oriented (GCS 15) with no seizures, behaviour change or focal signs, and the CSF is neutrophilic with organisms seen.
The headache built up over hours, she has a fever and a coryzal prodrome, and the CSF has no xanthochromia and only 5 red cells.
The CSF has 8500 neutrophils, a protein of 1.1 g/L, a glucose ratio of 0.24 and Gram-negative diplococci.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman in general practice. Five stereotyped attacks of severe, one-sided throbbing headache lasting 6 to 7 hours, with light and noise sensitivity and nausea, each preceded by about 20 minutes of fully reversible visual aura, with a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Bacterial meningitis
Migraine
Transient ischaemic attack
questions.why: Ask how fast the headache started and whether it matches previous attacks. A gradual, stereotyped headache with a normal examination and no red flags (SNOOP) needs no imaging.
notes: The onset was gradual, it is the same as four previous attacks, and the neurological examination and fundi are normal.
She is afebrile, with no neck stiffness, negative Kernig's sign and no rash.
The visual symptoms are positive (dots, jumbled lines), spread gradually, resolve fully and are followed by headache, with no weakness, numbness or speech change and a normal examination.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man in general practice. Two months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with LIF pain, weight loss, fatigue and erythema nodosum, and continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 25 cm with crypt distortion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ulcerative colitis
Colorectal cancer
Crohn's colitis
Infective colitis
questions.why: Chronic bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with weight loss in a young adult is inflammatory bowel disease until proven otherwise; IBS cannot be diagnosed with blood, weight loss, nocturnal stools or a raised calprotectin.
notes: Age 25, and colonoscopy found no mass, with no dysplasia on biopsy.
Continuous inflammation from the rectum, normal terminal ileum, inflammation confined to the mucosa, no granulomas and no perianal disease.
No travel, sick contacts or antibiotics, a 2-month course, and negative stool PCR, culture, C. difficile and parasite tests.

questions.stem: Dorothy, 71, is in ED resus with 2 mm ST elevation in V2 to V5, sepsis from a right lower lobe pneumonia, and a husband who died 4 days ago. She asks: "My daughter says people die of a broken heart. Is that what this is?" Which reply is best?
options: Yes, grief can cause broken heart syndrome, and it usually recovers fully with rest.
Likely a heart attack and chest infection; an urgent angiogram will check the arteries
No, that's a myth; this is your chest infection, and antibiotics should settle it.
We can't tell until a heart scan tomorrow, so tonight we'll treat the chest infection.
notes: Takotsubo can't be diagnosed until angiography shows no culprit lesion, so telling her it is broken heart syndrome is wrong and may lead her to refuse urgent reperfusion.
This dismisses her concern and ignores the anterior STEMI, which needs emergency angiography, not just antibiotics.
An echo can't exclude ACS, and putting reperfusion off until tomorrow misses the 90-minute target from first medical contact.
questions.why: Give an honest answer in plain words: this looks like a heart attack plus a serious chest infection. Stress can affect the heart, but Takotsubo can only be diagnosed after an urgent angiogram shows no blocked artery, so that comes first.

questions.stem: Dorothy, 71, has 6 hours of central chest pressure, 2 mm ST elevation in V2 to V5, BP 86/52, lactate 3.4 and right lower lobe pneumonia. She has no bleeding history, no ulcers, no anticoagulants and no allergies. The cath lab is being activated. Which antithrombotic step is best now in ED?
options: Withhold aspirin until systolic BP is above 90 mmHg and sepsis is controlled
Withhold antiplatelets until angiography has excluded Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Aspirin 100 mg orally with enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily for VTE prophylaxis
Aspirin 300 mg orally now; second antiplatelet and anticoagulant per cardiologist
notes: Sepsis and hypotension are not contraindications to aspirin, and delaying it takes away a treatment that lowers mortality.
Takotsubo is only a differential, so she should be treated as STEMI until angiography; withholding antiplatelets until then is unsafe.
100 mg is a maintenance dose, not the 300 mg loading dose, and VTE prophylaxis is deferred until the angiography and antithrombotic plan is set.
questions.why: In suspected STEMI, give aspirin 300 mg (chewed or dispersed) unless there is a true contraindication such as allergy or active major bleeding. The interventional cardiologist chooses the second antiplatelet and the anticoagulant.

questions.stem: Dorothy, 71, with an anterior STEMI and septic shock from pneumonia, has BP 86/52, HR 112, a CRT of 4 seconds and cool, clammy peripheries. The nurse asks whether she can have sublingual GTN for her ongoing chest pain. What is the main reason GTN is withheld here?
options: Venodilation cuts preload, so stroke volume and BP fall further in shock
Arteriolar dilation diverts flow away from the ischaemic anterior wall
It raises systemic vascular resistance, increasing afterload on the injured LV
It causes methaemoglobinaemia, worsening her hypoxia from the pneumonia
notes: Coronary steal is a theoretical effect of some vasodilators. It is not why GTN is withheld here; the reason is hypotension from reduced preload.
Nitrates lower systemic vascular resistance and afterload rather than raising them, so this has the mechanism backwards.
Methaemoglobinaemia is rare at therapeutic GTN doses and is not why it is contraindicated in a hypotensive patient.
questions.why: GTN mainly dilates veins. This lowers venous return and preload, so by the Frank-Starling mechanism stroke volume and BP drop. That is why it is avoided when systolic BP is below 90 mmHg; give titrated IV opioid for the pain instead.

questions.stem: Dorothy, 71, has 2 mm ST elevation in V2 to V5, isoelectric inferior leads, no change in I, aVL or V6, and no ST elevation in aVR. If angiography finds a culprit coronary occlusion, which artery is it most likely to be in?
options: Right coronary artery
Left circumflex artery
Left anterior descending artery
Left main coronary artery
notes: RCA occlusion usually gives inferior ST elevation (II, III, aVF), often with reciprocal depression in aVL, and her inferior leads are isoelectric.
Circumflex occlusion affects the lateral or posterior wall (I, aVL, V5 to V6, or ST depression in V1 to V3), not isolated V2 to V5 elevation.
Left main occlusion typically gives ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression and severe shock, and her aVR is normal.
questions.why: Leads V2 to V5 face the anterior wall and septum, which are supplied by the left anterior descending artery. Contiguous ST elevation in these leads localises the occlusion to the LAD.

questions.stem: You are seeing Noah, 18 days old, in general practice. He has been jaundiced since day 3, and now has pale putty-coloured stools and dark urine that stains the nappy. His parent Alex asks, "Do we just need more sunshine?" Which response is best?
options: "A little sun is fine, but it won't fix the pale stools, so we'll test him as well."
"No: sun won't treat this jaundice and can burn him; his pale stools need checking today."
"Yes, a few minutes behind a window each morning safely lowers his bilirubin."
"Sun helps breastmilk jaundice, so try it for a week and come back if he's still yellow."
notes: Calling sun exposure fine is wrong: it is unsafe for newborns and does nothing for conjugated jaundice, and Alex has already said she will take him to the park.
Window sunlight is not a safe or reliable treatment, and phototherapy only lowers unconjugated bilirubin, which is not Noah's problem.
Pale stools and dark urine rule out breastmilk jaundice, and waiting a week delays the diagnosis of biliary atresia, where early Kasai surgery gives better outcomes.
questions.why: Sunlight is not a treatment for newborn jaundice and is unsafe because of sunburn and overheating. Pale stools with dark urine point to conjugated (cholestatic) jaundice, which even phototherapy does not treat, so the answer is a clear no plus same-day assessment.

questions.stem: Noah, 18 days old, arrives in the paediatric ED from his GP. He has acholic stools, dark urine and a firm liver. He had no vitamin K at birth, and on day 9 his cord stump bled for 10 to 15 minutes. Nothing is bleeding now, and coagulation studies have been sent. What is the most appropriate vitamin K treatment?
options: Phytomenadione 1 mg by slow IV injection now, before the INR result returns
Phytomenadione 2 mg orally now, repeated at 4 weeks of age
Phytomenadione 1 mg IM, given only once the INR comes back prolonged
Fresh frozen plasma 10–15 mL/kg now, then vitamin K if bleeding starts
notes: The oral regimen is prophylaxis for a well baby. Absorption is unreliable in cholestasis, and it does not treat a deficiency that may already be there.
Waiting for the INR delays treatment in a baby at risk of intracranial haemorrhage, and IM injection risks a haematoma if he is coagulopathic.
FFP is kept for active, life-threatening bleeding alongside vitamin K. It is not first-line here, and vitamin K should not be held back until bleeding starts.
questions.why: In suspected late VKDB, give vitamin K 1 mg by injection straight away without waiting for results. Slow IV in hospital works quickly and avoids an IM haematoma if clotting is already deranged.

questions.stem: Noah, 18 days old, has conjugated jaundice with pale putty stools and probably has biliary atresia. He is exclusively breastfed and had no vitamin K prophylaxis. His liver is firm, 2 cm below the costal margin, and he is thriving. Which mechanism best explains why his cholestasis raises his risk of bleeding?
options: Hepatocyte failure reduces the liver's synthesis of fibrinogen and factor V
Conjugated bilirubin in plasma directly inhibits platelet aggregation
Portal hypertension causes hypersplenism, which consumes circulating platelets
Absent bile salts impair vitamin K uptake, so II, VII, IX and X are not carboxylated
notes: Factor V and fibrinogen do not depend on vitamin K. Their synthesis falls only in advanced liver failure, which a thriving 18-day-old does not have.
Bilirubin does not meaningfully impair platelet function. The bleeding risk in cholestasis comes from deficiency of the vitamin K-dependent factors.
Portal hypertension and hypersplenism develop months into untreated biliary atresia, not at 18 days of age.
questions.why: Bile salts form the micelles needed to absorb fat-soluble vitamins. Without bile in the gut, vitamin K is not absorbed, so the liver cannot gamma-carboxylate factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S) into working form.

questions.stem: Noah, 18 days old, is confirmed to have biliary atresia, and the surgeons plan a Kasai portoenterostomy. They will excise the fibrosed extrahepatic bile ducts and bring up a Roux-en-Y loop of jejunum. Where is the jejunal loop anastomosed?
options: The common bile duct, as for excision of a choledochal cyst
The porta hepatis, over the transected fibrous ductal remnant
The gallbladder fundus, as a cholecystojejunostomy
The common hepatic duct, at the confluence of the hepatic ducts
notes: Joining a dilated common bile duct (hepaticojejunostomy) is the repair for a choledochal cyst. In biliary atresia this duct is fibrosed and has no lumen.
The gallbladder is usually atretic or fibrosed in biliary atresia, and it does not connect to the obliterated proximal ducts, so bile would not drain.
The common hepatic duct and the confluence are part of the obliterated extrahepatic tree, so there is no patent lumen to anastomose to.
questions.why: In biliary atresia the extrahepatic ducts are obliterated, so there is no patent duct to join. The jejunal limb is sewn onto the porta hepatis, where tiny residual ductules can drain bile. Outcomes are best when this is done early, ideally before about 8 weeks.

questions.stem: You are examining Helen Marchetti, 46, in general practice. She has a firm, tender left retroareolar lump and nipple retraction. With a chaperone present you have already inspected her with her arms by her sides and then raised. Which manoeuvre best tests whether the mass is fixed to pectoralis major?
options: Ask her to lean forward with her arms hanging so that the breasts fall away from the chest
Ask her to raise both arms above her head while you look for skin dimpling
Ask her to press her hands firmly on her hips, then check how freely the mass moves
Lie her back at 45° with her hand behind her head, then palpate the mass
notes: Leaning forward helps show asymmetry or skin tethering, especially in large breasts, but it does not tense pectoralis to test for deep fixation.
Raising the arms brings out skin dimpling and nipple changes from tethering to the skin, not fixation to the underlying muscle.
This is the position for systematic palpation, because it spreads the breast tissue over the chest wall. It does not contract pectoralis to test for deep fixation.
questions.why: Pressing the hands into the hips makes pectoralis major contract. If the mass moves less once the muscle is tensed, it is fixed to the deep fascia or muscle, which is a feature of malignancy.

questions.stem: Mrs Marchetti, 46, has a 5 mL left retroareolar abscess. Deep to it is an irregular, vascular solid mass (category 4), with 6 mm skin thickening and an axillary node with a 5 mm cortex. You phone the breast clinic. What is the most appropriate way to get a tissue diagnosis of the mass?
options: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy now, in the same visit as aspiration of the abscess
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the solid mass
Repeat the ultrasound after 2 weeks of antibiotics, then biopsy if the mass persists
Send the aspirated pus for cytology, and biopsy only if malignant cells are seen
notes: FNA gives cytology only, with no tissue architecture or receptor status, and is less reliable than core biopsy for a solid lesion.
Waiting delays the diagnosis of a possible cancer. Biopsy should happen now, not after the infection settles.
Pus cytology is insensitive and does not sample the solid mass, so a negative result would give false reassurance.
questions.why: A suspicious solid mass needs a core biopsy at presentation, not after the infection settles. Core biopsy gives tissue architecture and receptor status, and is preferred to FNA. Triple-test concordance is needed before the lump can be called benign.

questions.stem: On examination Mrs Marchetti, 46, has early peau d'orange over the inner left breast. Her ultrasound shows 6 mm skin thickening. Inflammatory breast cancer is in the differential. Which mechanism best explains the peau d'orange appearance?
options: Tumour shortening Cooper's ligaments and pulling focal areas of skin inwards
Dermal lymphatic obstruction causing oedema, with the skin tethered at hair follicles
Cytokine-driven dermal vasodilation and hyperaemia caused by the bacterial infection
Compression of superficial veins by the mass, causing venous congestion of the skin
notes: Shortening of Cooper's ligaments causes focal skin dimpling or tethering, not the diffuse pitted oedema of peau d'orange.
Vasodilation explains the redness and warmth, but not the pitted, thickened skin of lymphoedema.
Venous obstruction causes dilated superficial veins, not pitted dermal oedema; lymphatic blockage is the key mechanism.
questions.why: Peau d'orange is dermal oedema from blocked lymphatics, classically from tumour emboli in the dermal lymphatics in inflammatory cancer. The skin swells around hair follicles and sweat ducts, which stay tethered, giving the pitted orange-peel look.

questions.stem: Mrs Marchetti, 46, has a suspicious left retroareolar mass that extends into the upper inner quadrant. Ultrasound shows a left axillary node with a 5 mm cortex, and the breast surgeon plans to sample it. Which group of nodes receives most of the lymph drained from the breast?
options: Internal thoracic (parasternal) nodes, which lie alongside the sternum
Supraclavicular nodes, reached through the deep cervical chain
Contralateral breast, reached directly from the subareolar plexus
Axillary nodes, with the anterior (pectoral) group usually first
notes: The internal thoracic nodes take a smaller share of lymph, mainly from the medial breast. They are not the main drainage route, even for medial tumours.
Supraclavicular nodes are usually reached only after the axillary or apical nodes, so they are a later site of spread, not the main drainage.
Lymph only crosses to the opposite breast in a small amount, usually when the normal channels are obstructed. It is not the main route.
questions.why: About 75% of the breast's lymph, including lymph from the subareolar plexus, drains to the ipsilateral axillary nodes, usually reaching the anterior (pectoral) group first. This is why the axilla is examined and imaged in every breast lump assessment.

questions.stem: Rachel, 34, is 36+2 weeks with a previous term stillbirth. Her CTG and ultrasound are normal and she is going home from the maternity day assessment unit. She asks what she should do if the baby seems quieter again. Which safety-netting advice is best?
options: Do a kick count and call if you feel fewer than 10 movements in 2 hours
Contact the maternity unit and come in straight away, at any time of day or night
Lie on your left side with a cold drink for an hour, then call if it's no better
Check the heartbeat with a home Doppler first, then decide whether to come in
notes: There is no validated fixed kick count. Women should know their own baby's pattern and report any change, without waiting to reach a number.
Trying a cold drink or a position change delays assessment. Rachel already waited 18 hours doing this, and delay is linked to stillbirth.
Home Dopplers give false reassurance, because a heartbeat can be found even when a baby is compromised. Their use is discouraged.
questions.why: Any reduction or change in her baby's usual pattern of movements should prompt immediate contact and assessment, day or night. She is never wasting anyone's time. This is the core message of the Safer Baby Bundle and RANZCOG guidance.

questions.stem: Rachel, 34, at 36+2 weeks, has had reduced movements for about 18 hours. Her 40-minute CTG is normal, BP is 116/72 and the dipstick is clear. Her last growth scan was at 32 weeks. She had a previous term stillbirth with a small placenta. What is the most appropriate next investigation today?
options: Kleihauer test to look for fetomaternal haemorrhage
Repeat CTG in one week at her routine antenatal visit
Ultrasound for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler
Serum sFlt-1/PlGF ratio to assess for placental dysfunction
notes: A Kleihauer test looks for fetomaternal haemorrhage after trauma or bleeding. Rachel has had neither, and the test does not assess growth.
Waiting a week leaves possible growth restriction unassessed in a high-risk pregnancy where movements have already reduced.
The sFlt-1/PlGF ratio helps rule out pre-eclampsia when it is suspected. Rachel has no features of it, and the ratio does not measure fetal growth or liquor.
questions.why: A normal CTG is only a snapshot. With risk factors for placental insufficiency, reduced fetal movements need an ultrasound the same day to assess fetal growth, amniotic fluid volume and umbilical artery Doppler before she is discharged.

questions.stem: Rachel, 34, at 36+2 weeks, says she often falls asleep or wakes on her back. You advise her to go to sleep on her side. In the third trimester, what is the main mechanism by which going to sleep on the back raises the risk of stillbirth?
options: The uterus compresses the IVC and aorta, reducing venous return and uterine blood flow
The uterus presses the umbilical cord against the maternal lumbar spine
Splinting of the diaphragm causes maternal hypoxaemia and so fetal hypoxia
Lying supine triggers uterine contractions that cut placental perfusion
notes: The cord lies inside the amniotic sac, cushioned by liquor. Supine risk comes from compression of the maternal great vessels, not the cord.
Lung volumes fall slightly when supine, but maternal oxygen saturation stays normal. Reduced uterine blood flow is the key mechanism.
Lying supine does not provoke contractions. The harm comes from lower maternal cardiac output and less flow to the uterus.
questions.why: Lying supine lets the gravid uterus compress the inferior vena cava and aorta. This lowers maternal cardiac output and uteroplacental perfusion, which reduces fetal oxygenation. That is why side sleeping from 28 weeks is advised.

questions.stem: You palpate Rachel's abdomen at 36+2 weeks. The baby is in a longitudinal lie and cephalic presentation, with the fetal back on her left side. Where should you place the hand-held Doppler to find the fetal heart most easily?
options: Midline at the uterine fundus, just below the xiphisternum
Above the umbilicus on the mother's right side
Midline just above the pubic symphysis, over the fetal head
Below the umbilicus on the mother's left, over the fetal anterior shoulder
notes: In a cephalic presentation the breech occupies the fundus, so the heart is too far away to hear well from here. This spot suits a breech presentation.
This is the side of the fetal limbs, and the area above the umbilicus is where the heart is heard in a breech presentation, not a cephalic one.
The head lies over the pelvic brim. The fetal heart is in the thorax, higher up and towards the side of the fetal back.
questions.why: The fetal heart is heard best through the fetal back, over the anterior shoulder. In a cephalic presentation this lies below the umbilicus, on the side of the fetal back.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl at the GP has short stature, a low posterior hairline and widely spaced nipples. Her mother recalls a doctor once heard a soft heart murmur that was never followed up. You are examining her cardiovascular system with a chaperone present. Which bedside step best screens her for coarctation of the aorta?
options: Measure blood pressure lying and then standing after three minutes
Feel right radial and femoral pulses together for delay, and compare arm and leg BP
Listen at the apex with the bell, with her rolled into the left lateral position
Palpate the carotid pulse for a slow-rising, low-volume character
notes: A postural BP drop screens for volume depletion or autonomic dysfunction, not for an obstruction between the arm and leg circulations.
The left lateral position with the bell brings out mitral stenosis and low-pitched sounds, not the delay in leg perfusion that coarctation causes.
A slow-rising carotid pulse suggests significant aortic stenosis. It does not detect coarctation, which spares the carotid and right arm pulses.
questions.why: Coarctation narrows the aorta, usually just past the left subclavian artery. This delays and weakens the femoral pulse compared with the right radial and makes leg BP lower than arm BP. Coarctation is a key cardiac lesion in Turner syndrome, so check radio-femoral delay and four-limb BP.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl has 45,X Turner syndrome. FSH is 58 IU/L, LH 24 IU/L and oestradiol is below 40 pmol/L. She has no breast development, and her bone age is 11 years with open growth plates. She is to start growth hormone. Her mother asks how puberty will be brought on. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Wait until she is 15 years old in case puberty starts on its own before treating
Start the combined oral contraceptive pill now to bring on breasts and periods
Endocrinology-led low-dose transdermal oestradiol, increased gradually over 2 to 3 years
Start full adult-dose oestradiol now, with a cyclical progestogen from the start
notes: Her raised gonadotrophins show ovarian failure, so puberty is very unlikely to start on its own. Waiting delays bone and breast development and adds to her distress.
The pill's ethinylestradiol dose is too high to begin with. It closes the growth plates early and gives poorer breast and uterine development than gradual oestradiol.
