Venous valves do not amplify the waveform. A competent valve would block transmission of pressure, which is one reason the external jugular vein is less reliable.
questions.why: The right IJV runs in an almost straight line via the right brachiocephalic vein and the SVC into the right atrium, so its pulsation reflects right atrial pressure faithfully. It lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, so you usually see its pulsation transmitted through the muscle rather than the vein itself.

questions.stem: Chris, 23, is ready to go home from the ED after successful needle aspiration of a left primary spontaneous pneumothorax. While you are giving safety-netting advice, he says he has booked a scuba diving course in Bali in three months. What is the most appropriate advice to give him?
options: He can dive once a repeat chest X-ray shows the lung has fully re-expanded
He should avoid diving for life unless he has definitive surgery to prevent recurrence
He can dive after 6 weeks if he has stopped smoking and has no symptoms
He can dive if he stays shallower than 10 m and ascends slowly on every dive
notes: Waiting for X-ray resolution is the rule for flying. It does not make diving safe, because the risk of recurrence stays high.
Stopping smoking lowers his recurrence risk, but not enough to make diving safe without definitive surgery.
Gas expands most in the shallowest 10 m, so a depth limit and slow ascents do not remove the risk of a pneumothorax.
questions.why: Diving after a pneumothorax is avoided for life unless definitive surgery (such as VATS pleurectomy) has been done. Pressure changes on ascent can expand any trapped air into a tension pneumothorax underwater.

questions.stem: Chris, 23, has a first left primary spontaneous pneumothorax measuring 3 cm at the hilum on an erect X-ray. He is breathless at rest, RR 26, SpO2 93% on room air, HR 110, BP 124/76, trachea central. He has no lung disease. What is the most appropriate next step in the emergency department?
options: Observe on high-flow oxygen and repeat the chest X-ray in 4 hours
Immediate needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space
Needle aspiration with a 16–18 G cannula, then a repeat chest X-ray
Insert a large-bore (28 Fr) chest drain by blunt dissection
notes: Conservative management suits patients with few symptoms; Chris is breathless at rest and hypoxic, so he needs the air removed.
Needle decompression is for tension, which is a clinical diagnosis; his BP is normal, the trachea is central and there is no mediastinal shift.
Large-bore drains are not first line for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax; if aspiration fails, a small-bore drain to an underwater seal is used.
questions.why: A symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax needs intervention. First line is needle aspiration (or an ambulatory device), stopping once more than 2.5 L has been aspirated, followed by a repeat X-ray. If it fails, insert a small-bore drain.

questions.stem: Chris, 23, has a large left primary spontaneous pneumothorax with the left lung partly collapsed towards the hilum. His SpO2 is 93% on room air and he is breathing at 26/min. What is the main mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
options: Blood still perfusing the collapsed, poorly ventilated left lung (shunt)
Impaired diffusion across a thickened alveolar–capillary membrane
Global alveolar hypoventilation from splinting due to pleuritic pain
Increased dead space from ventilated lung that is no longer perfused
notes: Diffusion impairment is seen in interstitial lung disease or oedema; his alveolar membrane is normal.
Global hypoventilation would raise the PaCO2; he is tachypnoeic, and the problem lies in one lung, not in total ventilation.
Ventilated but unperfused lung (high V/Q, dead space) is the pattern of pulmonary embolism, not of a collapsed lung.
questions.why: Collapsed lung is still perfused but barely ventilated, so a low V/Q and shunt send deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts some of this blood away, which is why hypoxaemia is often only mild.

questions.stem: Chris's needle aspiration fails, and a small-bore chest drain is inserted in the left triangle of safety, 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line. The clinician enters the space just above the upper border of the lower rib. Which anatomical fact explains this technique?
options: Internal thoracic artery runs along the upper border of each rib
Long thoracic nerve runs deep within each intercostal space
Main intercostal vessels run mid-space between adjacent ribs
Intercostal vein, artery and nerve lie in the groove under the rib above
notes: The internal thoracic artery runs vertically about 1 cm lateral to the sternal edge; it matters for anterior approaches, not along each rib.
The long thoracic nerve runs on the surface of serratus anterior in the mid-axillary line, not inside the intercostal spaces.
The main bundle sits in the costal groove under the rib above, not mid-space; only small collateral branches run lower in the space.
questions.why: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve, from top to bottom) runs in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib. Going in just above the rib below avoids it.

questions.stem: In ED, Terry, 20, has severe acute asthma. He can say only 3 to 5 words at a time, so you are keeping the history short. You have started treatment and now want the single question that best tells you whether he is at risk of a fatal attack. Which question should you ask?
options: "Does anyone in your family have asthma, eczema or hayfever?"
"How old were you when you were first told you had asthma?"
"Have you ever needed intensive care or a breathing tube for asthma?"
"Do dust, cats or pollen ever set off your wheeze?"
notes: A family history of atopy supports the diagnosis of asthma, but it does not tell you whether this patient is at risk of a fatal attack.
Age at diagnosis does not mark risk of a fatal attack, and it wastes his limited breath.
Knowing his allergen triggers helps prevention later, but it does not grade how dangerous his asthma is.
questions.why: A previous ICU admission or intubation is the strongest single marker of risk for a fatal asthma attack. Other markers are hospital admission, systemic steroids, reliever-only use, no preventer and no action plan.

questions.stem: Terry, 20, arrives in ED with severe acute asthma: he speaks in phrases, uses his accessory muscles, has RR 28 and SpO2 93% on room air. He has no life-threatening features and no cannula yet. He has had 8 puffs of his own salbutamol without a spacer. What is the most appropriate initial bronchodilator regimen?
options: Salbutamol 100 microgram pMDI via spacer, 4 puffs every 4 hours
Salbutamol 100 microgram pMDI via spacer, 12 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour
Salbutamol IV infusion, started before any further inhaled doses
Salbutamol 2.5 mg nebulised once, then reassess in 4 hours
notes: 4 puffs every 4 hours is a maintenance or mild dose. It is far too little and too infrequent for a severe attack.
IV salbutamol is reserved for life-threatening asthma that is not responding to inhaled treatment, under senior care. It is not first-line.
A single 2.5 mg nebule followed by a 4-hour gap underdoses him. Severe asthma needs 5 mg repeated every 20 minutes.
questions.why: For severe acute asthma in an adult, give salbutamol 12 puffs (100 microgram each) via spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, or 5 mg nebulised every 20 minutes. Add ipratropium, and reassess after each dose.

questions.stem: Terry, 20, has severe acute asthma with widespread wheeze. His SpO2 is 93% on room air and he is breathing at 28 per minute. His spirometry from a few months ago, taken when well, showed a normal TLCO (93% predicted). What is the main mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
options: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch from uneven narrowing of the airways
Impaired diffusion across a thickened alveolar-capillary membrane
Alveolar hypoventilation from reduced central respiratory drive
Right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale
notes: Asthma affects the airways, not the alveolar membrane. His normal TLCO shows that gas transfer is preserved.
He is tachypnoeic with a high respiratory drive. Hypoventilation only appears late, with exhaustion, as a rising PaCO2.
Nothing suggests an intracardiac shunt, and a true shunt would barely respond to oxygen, whereas his sats improve with it.
questions.why: In acute asthma, uneven bronchoconstriction, mucus and oedema under-ventilate alveoli that are still perfused, so the blood leaving them is poorly oxygenated. This V/Q mismatch usually responds to modest supplemental oxygen.

questions.stem: Terry, 20, with severe acute asthma, is given ipratropium 8 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes alongside his salbutamol. Ipratropium is a muscarinic antagonist that reduces the cholinergic bronchoconstrictor tone of airway smooth muscle. Which nerve carries the parasympathetic supply to the bronchi?
options: Phrenic nerve
Sympathetic trunk (T1 to T4)
Intercostal nerves
Vagus nerve
notes: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) is the motor supply to the diaphragm. It does not supply bronchial smooth muscle.
The sympathetic trunk is the autonomic supply that opposes the parasympathetic one. Bronchodilation is mainly driven by circulating adrenaline acting on beta-2 receptors, not by vagal tone.
Intercostal nerves supply the intercostal muscles and the chest wall, not the airway smooth muscle.
questions.why: Parasympathetic fibres in the vagus nerve reach the bronchi through the pulmonary plexus. Their acetylcholine acts on M3 receptors to constrict the bronchi and increase mucus secretion, and ipratropium blocks these receptors.

questions.stem: Angela Green, 60, has a 10-day cough with rusty sputum and left pleuritic pain. You are examining her in general practice. Percussion is dull at the left base, so either consolidation or an effusion could explain it. Which finding at that spot best points to consolidation rather than fluid?
options: Reduced chest expansion on the left side
Tracheal deviation towards the left side
Bronchial breath sounds with increased vocal resonance
Stony dullness extending up into the left axilla
notes: Reduced expansion on the affected side happens with both consolidation and effusion, so it cannot tell them apart.
Simple consolidation does not shift the trachea; it moves towards collapse and away from a large effusion, and this effusion is small.
Stony dullness that rises into the axilla is the sign of pleural fluid, not consolidation.
questions.why: Consolidated lung is solid but its airways stay open, so it carries sound from the large airways well, giving bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance. Fluid in the pleural space damps sound, so breath sounds and vocal resonance are reduced over an effusion.

questions.stem: Angela, 60, 68 kg, has left lower lobe pneumonia confirmed on X-ray. She is alert, RR 22, BP 126/74, SpO2 95% on room air, urea 6.1 mmol/L, so CURB-65 is 0. She has no drug allergies and you and the GP agree to treat her at home. Which antibiotic regimen does eTG recommend?
options: Amoxicillin 1 g orally 8-hourly for 5 days
Amoxicillin–clavulanate 875/125 mg orally 12-hourly for 5 days
Roxithromycin 300 mg orally once daily for 5 days
Cefuroxime 500 mg orally 12-hourly for 5 days
notes: Adding clavulanate gives broader cover than low-severity CAP needs and causes more side effects; eTG does not use it first line here.
A macrolide on its own gives unreliable cover for pneumococcus because resistance is common, so eTG does not use it as first-line monotherapy.
An oral cephalosporin is not first line for low-severity CAP when there is no penicillin allergy; amoxicillin is preferred.
questions.why: For low-severity community-acquired pneumonia, eTG recommends high-dose oral amoxicillin, 1 g 8-hourly for 5 days, which treats Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most likely cause. Doxycycline is the alternative if she is allergic to penicillin.

questions.stem: Angela, 60, a lifelong non-smoker, had a cold 10 days ago. For the past 4 days she has been coughing up sticky, rust-coloured sputum, and her X-ray shows lobar consolidation with air bronchograms. Her GP thinks pneumococcus is the likely cause. What best explains the rust colour of her sputum?
options: Haemosiderin-laden macrophages from chronic pulmonary venous congestion
Red cells and fibrin leaking into the alveolar exudate as the lobe consolidates
Bleeding from a tumour that has eroded a branch of a bronchial artery
Haemorrhagic infarction beyond an occluded branch of the pulmonary artery
notes: Heart-failure cells come from long-standing venous congestion, but she has no features of heart failure and this is an acute febrile illness.
She has never smoked, has not lost weight and her X-ray shows no mass, so a tumour does not explain an acute infective consolidation.
She has no risk factors for PE, and her purulent sputum, neutrophilia and air bronchograms point to infection rather than infarction.
questions.why: In pneumococcal lobar pneumonia, inflamed capillaries leak neutrophils, fibrin and red cells into the alveoli (red hepatisation). Breakdown of haemoglobin from those red cells gives the classic rusty sputum.

questions.stem: Angela's PA chest X-ray shows an opacity with air bronchograms behind the heart. The outline of the medial left hemidiaphragm is lost but the left heart border is clearly seen. There is also a small meniscus at the left costophrenic angle. Where does the consolidation lie?
options: Lingular segments of the left upper lobe
Anterior segment of the left upper lobe
Apicoposterior segment of the left upper lobe
Basal segments of the left lower lobe
notes: The lingula touches the left heart border, so consolidation there would blur the heart border rather than the hemidiaphragm.
The anterior segment of the upper lobe is in the upper zone, well away from the diaphragm, so it would not blur the hemidiaphragm.
The apicoposterior segment is at the lung apex, so consolidation there would show in the upper zone and not near the diaphragm.
questions.why: The left lower lobe sits behind the heart and rests on the diaphragm. Consolidation there blurs the outline of the left hemidiaphragm but leaves the left heart border visible (silhouette sign). If the left heart border were lost, think of the lingula.

questions.stem: Jenny, 26, is at her GP with 6 weeks of productive cough, streaks of blood in her sputum, weight loss and right upper lobe opacification on X-ray. Pulmonary TB is suspected. You give her three sputum jars to fill at home. Which instruction is best?
options: Spit saliva into the jar after rinsing your mouth with antiseptic mouthwash
On waking, breathe deeply and cough phlegm up from the chest, outdoors or by a window
Collect all three samples within one hour this afternoon so results come back sooner
Cough into the jar in the small bathroom with the door closed to protect your family
notes: Saliva does not reliably contain bacilli, so the sample is poor, and antiseptic mouthwash can reduce the chance of the culture growing; she should rinse with plain water only.
The specimens should be collected on separate occasions, at least 8 hours apart and including at least one early morning sample, because spreading them out improves the diagnostic yield.
A small closed room concentrates infectious droplet nuclei, which puts the next family member to go in at risk; she should collect outdoors or in a well-ventilated area.
questions.why: A good AFB sample is sputum coughed up from deep in the chest, best collected early in the morning when overnight secretions have built up. She should collect it outdoors or in a well-ventilated space, away from other people, because coughing spreads infectious aerosols.

questions.stem: Jenny, 26, born in Cambodia, has 6 weeks of productive cough, 5 days of blood-streaked sputum, a temperature of 37.8 °C and 5 kg weight loss. Her X-ray shows right upper lobe opacification. SpO2 is 97% on room air. She is wearing a surgical mask in a separate room. What is the most appropriate next step in general practice?
options: Prescribe moxifloxacin 400 mg orally daily for 5 days and review in a week
Start isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol today at weight-based doses
Arrange 3 sputum samples for AFB microscopy, culture and NAAT; phone the TB service today
Request an interferon-gamma release assay and refer if it comes back positive
notes: A fluoroquinolone partly treats TB, which can delay the diagnosis, make sputum cultures falsely negative and select for fluoroquinolone resistance, so avoid it whenever TB is suspected.
Treatment is started by the TB service after specimens have been taken, so that culture and drug-susceptibility testing are not compromised; empirical TB treatment is not started in general practice.
An IGRA cannot tell latent from active TB and can be negative in active disease, so it does not confirm or exclude TB, and waiting for it delays urgent referral.
questions.why: With suspected pulmonary TB, the GP collects three sputum specimens for AFB microscopy, culture and NAAT and refers urgently, by phone the same day, to the state TB service. That service confirms the diagnosis, starts treatment and organises contact tracing.

questions.stem: Jenny, 26, has suspected reactivation (post-primary) pulmonary TB. Her chest X-ray shows multifocal opacification in the right upper lobe and clear lower zones. Which mechanism best explains why reactivation TB favours the lung apices?
options: A high apical V/Q ratio raises alveolar PO2, which favours the aerobic Mycobacterium
Apical perfusion is the highest in the lung, so it delivers the most bacilli to the apex
Upright breathing sends most inhaled droplets to the apices rather than the bases
Low apical alveolar PO2 suppresses macrophage killing and lets the bacilli multiply
notes: Because of gravity, perfusion is lowest at the apex and highest at the bases, so this gets the gradient the wrong way round.
Ventilation per unit volume is greater at the bases, which is why inhaled primary infection often lands in the mid and lower zones, not the apices.
Apical alveolar PO2 is higher, not lower, than at the bases, and the high oxygen tension favours the bacillus rather than impairing host defence.
questions.why: In the upright lung, perfusion falls off toward the apex more than ventilation does, so the apical V/Q ratio is high and the alveolar PO2 is the highest in the lung. M. tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe and thrives there. Poorer apical lymphatic clearance also contributes.

questions.stem: Examining Jenny, 26, with suspected right upper lobe TB, you hear crackles over the upper right anterior chest. To map the right upper lobe on the front of the chest, you need its lower boundary. Which surface marking forms the inferior limit of the right upper lobe anteriorly?
options: Sternal angle, level with the 2nd costal cartilage, across to the midclavicular line
Oblique fissure, from the T3 spinous process round to the 6th costal cartilage
Lower border of the lung, along the 6th rib in the midclavicular line
Horizontal fissure, along the right 4th costal cartilage to the midaxillary line
notes: The sternal angle marks the 2nd costal cartilage and the tracheal bifurcation, which is well above the lower edge of the upper lobe; most of the anterior upper lobe lies below it.
The oblique fissure separates the upper lobe from the lower lobe posteriorly, but on the anterior chest it separates the middle lobe from the lower lobe.
The 6th rib in the midclavicular line is the inferior border of the whole lung, which lies below the middle lobe, not the upper lobe.
questions.why: The horizontal fissure runs from the sternum along the right 4th costal cartilage and rib to meet the oblique fissure at the midaxillary line. It separates the right upper lobe from the middle lobe, so the anterior chest above it overlies the upper lobe.

questions.stem: Daniel, 32, is on the couch at his GP with 12 hours of periumbilical pain, fever and vomiting. You have found tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa. You now want to test for Rovsing's sign and tell the examiner what you are doing. How do you elicit it, and what is a positive result?
options: Extend his right hip while he lies on his left side; right iliac fossa pain increases
Press deeply in the left iliac fossa; he feels the pain in the right iliac fossa
Flex his right hip and knee, then rotate internally; he feels pain in the hypogastrium
Press slowly in the right iliac fossa, then let go suddenly; the pain is worse on release
notes: This is the psoas sign. It suggests a retrocaecal appendix lying on the iliopsoas, not Rovsing's sign.
This is the obturator sign. It suggests a pelvic appendix lying against obturator internus.
This is rebound tenderness, a sign of peritonism. It is not Rovsing's sign, and many examiners prefer gentle percussion because it hurts less.
questions.why: Rovsing's sign is right iliac fossa pain when you press on the left iliac fossa. Pressing there shifts gas and bowel and moves the inflamed peritoneum on the right, so pain referred to the RIF points to appendicitis.

questions.stem: Daniel, 32, has been transferred to ED and the surgeons plan a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He weighs 78 kg. As a child he got an itchy rash a few days into a course of amoxicillin, with no swelling or breathing trouble. What is the most appropriate pre-incision antibiotic prophylaxis?
options: Vancomycin IV plus metronidazole IV, because all beta-lactams must be avoided
Ciprofloxacin IV plus metronidazole IV, because cephalosporins cross-react
Cefazolin 2 g IV plus metronidazole 500 mg IV, as his allergy history is low risk
Amoxicillin–clavulanate IV after premedication with an oral antihistamine
notes: Avoiding every beta-lactam is only needed after a severe reaction (such as anaphylaxis or a severe skin reaction). Using vancomycin without reason gives worse cover and drives resistance.
Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cefazolin is very low. Ciprofloxacin is not the standard prophylaxis and adds no benefit here.
Premedicating with an antihistamine does not make re-exposure safe. Restarting a penicillin is done by a formal oral challenge, not around emergency surgery.
questions.why: eTG prophylaxis for appendicectomy is cefazolin 2 g IV plus metronidazole 500 mg IV. A non-severe delayed rash to a penicillin is low risk, and cefazolin, whose side chain is unlike amoxicillin's, can be given safely.

questions.stem: Daniel, 32, says his pain started 12 hours ago as a dull, vague ache around the umbilicus. On examination he now has peritonism in the right iliac fossa. What best explains why early appendicitis is felt around the umbilicus?
options: Irritation of the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic innervation from T12 and L1
Referred pain via the phrenic nerve from irritated peritoneum under the diaphragm
Direct spread of inflammation to the muscles of the periumbilical abdominal wall
Stretching of the appendix wall, sensed by visceral afferents entering the cord at T10
notes: Parietal peritoneal irritation causes the later, well-localised pain in the right iliac fossa, not the early vague periumbilical ache.
Phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) irritation is referred to the shoulder tip, not the umbilicus.
The abdominal wall is not involved early. If it were, the pain would be sharp and well localised, not vague.
questions.why: The appendix is a midgut structure. When it swells, visceral afferents enter the spinal cord at about T10 and the pain is referred, poorly localised, to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus. It localises to the right iliac fossa later, once the somatic parietal peritoneum is inflamed.

questions.stem: Examining Daniel, 32, you find tenderness that is maximal at McBurney's point, with guarding and rebound. The examiner asks you to show exactly where this point is on the surface of his abdomen. Where is McBurney's point?
options: One-third of the way along a line from the right ASIS to the umbilicus
Midpoint of a line joining the right ASIS to the umbilicus
Midpoint of the right inguinal ligament, just above the femoral pulse
Where the right lateral rectus border meets the costal margin (9th costal cartilage)
notes: The midpoint is too far medial. McBurney's point is closer to the ASIS, one-third of the way along the line.
The midpoint of the inguinal ligament overlies the femoral vessels, deep ring and hernial region, not the appendix base.
This is the surface marking of the gallbladder fundus, where Murphy's sign is tested.
questions.why: McBurney's point lies one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. It marks the usual position of the base of the appendix, where the taeniae coli meet on the caecum.

questions.stem: In a GP clinic, Beth, 20, has had 2 months of right iliac fossa pain and loose stools 3 to 4 times a day. She wonders if it is exam stress. You want to ask the history question that best separates an organic bowel cause from irritable bowel syndrome. Which question should you ask?
options: "Does opening your bowels ease the pain?"
"Do you ever wake at night needing to open your bowels?"
"Does the pain get worse when you are stressed?"
"Do you feel bloated after you eat?"
notes: Pain relieved by defecation is one of the Rome IV criteria for IBS, so it points towards a functional cause rather than ruling out an organic one.
Stress makes both IBS and IBD symptoms worse, so this answer cannot separate the two.
Bloating is common in both IBS and organic disease and is not a red flag, so it does little to tell them apart.
questions.why: Waking at night to open the bowels is a red flag for organic disease such as IBD. Functional symptoms rarely wake patients. Chronic diarrhoea with nocturnal symptoms, blood, weight loss or fever is organic until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: Beth, 20, has ileocolonic Crohn's disease confirmed on colonoscopy. Her gastroenterologist plans to start azathioprine for maintenance and asks you, her GP, to arrange the bloods before treatment starts. Which test identifies her risk of severe early bone marrow suppression on this drug?
options: HLA-B*5801 genotyping
G6PD enzyme activity
Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) enzyme activity
Interferon-gamma release assay
notes: HLA-B*5801 predicts severe skin reactions to allopurinol, not toxicity from azathioprine.
G6PD deficiency predicts haemolysis with drugs such as primaquine, dapsone and rasburicase, not myelosuppression from thiopurines.
An IGRA screens for latent TB before immunosuppression, especially before anti-TNF biologics, but it does not predict marrow toxicity.
questions.why: TPMT breaks down thiopurines. People with low or absent TPMT activity build up toxic thioguanine nucleotides and can develop severe myelosuppression. TPMT is checked before azathioprine to choose the dose or avoid the drug, and FBC and LFTs are then monitored.

questions.stem: Beth, 20, has active ileocolonic Crohn's disease. Her bloods show Hb 108 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 9 µg/L, raised transferrin and CRP 36 mg/L. The gastroenterologist warns that oral iron may be poorly absorbed while her disease is active. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Ileal inflammation destroys the main site of dietary non-haem iron absorption
Low serum albumin reduces carriage of absorbed iron from enterocyte to plasma
Inflammation stops transferrin being made, so absorbed iron cannot be carried
IL-6 raises hepatic hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin and blocks iron export
notes: Non-haem iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not the terminal ileum (where B12 and bile salts are absorbed).
Absorbed iron travels in plasma bound to transferrin, not albumin. Her low albumin reflects inflammation and protein loss.
Her transferrin is high, as expected in iron deficiency, so a lack of carrier protein is not the problem.
questions.why: Inflammatory cytokines, mainly IL-6, make the liver produce more hepcidin. Hepcidin binds ferroportin and causes it to be broken down, so iron stays trapped in enterocytes and macrophages and less is absorbed. This is also why IV iron is often preferred in active IBD.

questions.stem: Beth, 20, has Crohn's disease that is most severe in the terminal ileum, with cobblestoning and deep linear ulcers. Her gastroenterologist mentions that if the ileal disease extends, or she needs an ileal resection, absorption of one nutrient is particularly at risk because it is absorbed mainly at this site. Which nutrient is this?
options: Iron
Folate
Calcium
Vitamin B12
notes: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Beth's iron deficiency comes from blood loss and hepcidin, not from ileal malabsorption.
Folate is absorbed mainly in the proximal jejunum, so it is at more risk from proximal small bowel disease.
Calcium is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, so it does not depend on an intact terminal ileum.
questions.why: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed by receptors in the terminal ileum, which also reabsorbs bile acids. Extensive ileal Crohn's disease or resection can cause B12 deficiency and bile acid diarrhoea, so B12 should be monitored.

questions.stem: Gary, a 56-year-old builder in ED with severe epigastric pain going through to his back, tells you he drinks 4 full-strength stubbies a night and had about 12 at a party last night. He is likely to be admitted for several days. Which history question best assesses his immediate risk of alcohol withdrawal on the ward?
options: "How many standard drinks do you have on a typical day, and what do you drink?"
"Have you ever felt annoyed when people criticise your drinking?"
"When was your last drink, and have you had shakes, fits or hallucinations off it?"
"Has anyone in your family ever had a problem with alcohol or other drugs?"
notes: Daily intake helps judge dependence, but it does not tell you when withdrawal will start or whether he has had severe withdrawal before.
This is a CAGE screening item for problem drinking. It does not tell you when withdrawal will happen or how severe it might be.
Family history of alcohol problems adds to long-term risk but tells you nothing about withdrawal over the next few days.
questions.why: The time of the last drink tells you when withdrawal is likely (usually 6 to 24 hours after it), and past shakes, seizures or hallucinations are the strongest predictors of severe withdrawal. Record both, then monitor with a withdrawal scale.

questions.stem: Gary, 56, has acute alcohol-related pancreatitis. In ED his HR has risen from 109 to 114, he has vomited again and has passed no urine since arrival. Haematocrit is 0.52, and creatinine, BP, SpO2 and lactate are normal. What is the most appropriate IV fluid plan?
options: Hartmann's bolus, reassess, then titrate the rate to urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h
Hartmann's 20 mL/kg bolus, then a fixed 3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours regardless
5% glucose at 125 mL/h as maintenance until he can drink again
Hold IV fluids and give oral fluids until his creatinine starts to rise
notes: An aggressive fixed regimen like this caused more fluid overload with no benefit in the WATERFALL trial, so it is no longer recommended.
5% glucose is hypotonic maintenance fluid, not resuscitation fluid, and in a heavy drinker glucose should not be given before thiamine.
He is already tachycardic, haemoconcentrated and not passing urine. Waiting for the creatinine to rise means waiting for organ failure.
questions.why: Use goal-directed balanced crystalloid in pancreatitis: give a moderate bolus, reassess, then titrate to haemodynamics and a urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/h. Aggressive fixed high-volume regimens cause fluid overload and do not improve outcomes.

questions.stem: Gary, 56, has a lipase of 1850 U/L after a heavy binge on top of daily drinking. Ultrasound shows a bulky, oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid and no gallstones. What is the central initiating event in the pathogenesis of acute pancreatitis?
options: Ascending bacterial infection of the pancreatic duct from the duodenum
Ischaemia of the pancreas from atherosclerosis of the coeliac trunk
Autoimmune destruction of acinar cells by circulating autoantibodies
Premature activation of trypsinogen to trypsin within the acinar cells
notes: Pancreatitis starts as sterile inflammation. Infection, if it happens at all, is a late complication of necrosis, which is why prophylactic antibiotics are not given.
Ischaemia is a rare cause (for example after cardiac bypass) and does not explain pancreatitis after a binge in someone with a normal lactate.
Autoimmune pancreatitis is an uncommon IgG4-related condition with a subacute course. It does not cause sudden pancreatitis after drinking.
questions.why: Trypsinogen activated too early inside acinar cells (alcohol makes acinar cells more prone to this) activates other enzymes and causes autodigestion. The cytokine release that follows explains SIRS and capillary leak.

questions.stem: Gary, 56, describes constant epigastric pain going straight through to his back, eased a little by leaning forward. On ultrasound, bowel gas partly obscured the view of his pancreas. Which description of the pancreas's position best explains why the pain radiates to the back?
options: Intraperitoneal, in the greater omentum in front of the transverse colon
Retroperitoneal, on the posterior abdominal wall at L1–L2 behind the stomach
Retroperitoneal, at T10–T11 directly behind the oesophageal hiatus
Intraperitoneal, within the lesser omentum between the stomach and liver
notes: The pancreas is not in the greater omentum. An organ hanging in front of the colon would not cause pain through to the back.
This level is too high. The pancreas lies at about L1–L2, below the oesophageal hiatus (T10), and its body crosses in front of the aorta and the origin of the SMA.
The lesser omentum carries the hepatic portal triad, not the pancreas, which lies behind the lesser sac on the posterior abdominal wall.
questions.why: The pancreas (except the tail) is retroperitoneal. It lies across L1–L2 behind the stomach and lesser sac, close to the coeliac plexus, so inflammation is felt in the back. The stomach and colon in front of it are also why bowel gas limits ultrasound views.

questions.stem: Gabby, 41, lies still in the ED with constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting. Examining her abdomen, you tell the examiner you will now check for Murphy's sign. Which manoeuvre correctly elicits it?
options: Ask her to lift her head off the trolley while you press on the tender area
Flex and internally rotate her right hip while watching her face for pain
Rest fingers under the right costal margin, midclavicular line, and ask her to breathe in
Press deeply over the tender point, then release suddenly and watch her face
notes: This is Carnett's sign. It helps tell abdominal wall pain from visceral pain but does not test the gallbladder.
This is the obturator sign, used for a pelvic appendix or a pelvic abscess irritating obturator internus, not the gallbladder.
This tests for rebound tenderness, a sign of peritonism. It is not specific to the gallbladder and is unkind to a patient already in severe pain.
questions.why: On deep inspiration the diaphragm pushes the inflamed gallbladder down onto the examiner's fingers, so she catches her breath and stops inhaling. It is positive only if the same manoeuvre on the left does not hurt.

questions.stem: Gabby, 41, has acute calculous cholecystitis on ultrasound (TG18 grade I). T 38.8 °C, HR 114, BP 122/74, WCC 15.8, normal renal function, no drug allergies. She is vomiting. Blood cultures have just been taken. Which antibiotic plan matches eTG?
options: Amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin IV, single daily dose by weight
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg oral 12-hourly and discharge to surgical clinic
Meropenem 1 g IV 8-hourly until blood culture results are available
Withhold antibiotics until blood cultures identify an organism
notes: She is febrile, tachycardic and vomiting. She needs IV therapy and admission for early cholecystectomy, not oral antibiotics at home.
Meropenem is held back for resistant organisms such as ESBL producers. Using it first line for mild community-acquired biliary sepsis is poor stewardship.
She has fever, tachycardia and a high WCC. Antibiotics start straight after blood cultures and are not delayed for culture results.
questions.why: eTG recommends IV amoxicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin (4 to 7 mg/kg, dosing interval by renal function) for acute cholecystitis, with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily if gentamicin is contraindicated. She is admitted for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

questions.stem: Gabby, 41, says her pain began within an hour of a large creamy pasta dinner, and her earlier shorter episodes also came after rich meals. Which hormone, released when fat reaches the duodenum, makes her gallbladder contract against the stone impacted in its neck?
options: Secretin from duodenal S cells
Gastrin from gastric antral G cells
Somatostatin from pancreatic D cells
Cholecystokinin from duodenal I cells
notes: Secretin is released mainly in response to acid. It drives bicarbonate secretion from the pancreatic ducts and has little effect on gallbladder contraction.
Gastrin drives gastric acid secretion and antral motility. It is not the main hormone that makes the gallbladder contract after a fatty meal.
Somatostatin inhibits gallbladder contraction and the secretion of most GI hormones, so it does the opposite of what is asked.
questions.why: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum release cholecystokinin from I cells. It contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. Contraction against a blocked cystic duct raises the pressure in the gallbladder and causes pain after meals.

questions.stem: Gabby, 41, has acute cholecystitis. Her constant right upper quadrant pain now goes up into the tip of her right shoulder. The inflamed gallbladder is irritating the peritoneum on the central undersurface of the diaphragm. Which nerve carries this pain and explains the referral?
options: Greater splanchnic nerve (T5 to T9)
Phrenic nerve (C3 to C5)
Lower intercostal nerves (T7 to T11)
Right vagus nerve (CN X)
notes: The splanchnic nerves carry visceral pain from the gallbladder itself, felt as poorly localised epigastric or RUQ pain, not shoulder tip pain.
These supply the peripheral diaphragm and the parietal peritoneum of the abdominal wall. They cause local pain at the costal margin and abdominal wall, not shoulder pain.
The vagus carries parasympathetic and visceral reflex fibres, for example for nausea. It does not carry somatic diaphragmatic pain to the C3 to C5 segments.
questions.why: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) carries sensation from the central diaphragm and its peritoneum. The supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4) share these segments and supply the skin over the shoulder tip, so the pain is felt there.

questions.stem: Kelly, 45, is in ED with 4 weeks of burning retrosternal pain after meals. She mentions that solid food sometimes sticks behind her breastbone. Which question best helps you tell a mechanical narrowing (stricture or cancer) from an oesophageal motility disorder?
options: "Does the pain spread to your arm, jaw or neck?"
"Do you get a sour or bitter taste coming up into your mouth?"
"Do drinks stick as well, or only solid foods like bread or meat?"
"Is the pain worse when you lie flat or bend over?"
notes: Radiation to the arm, jaw or neck helps separate cardiac from oesophageal pain, but it says nothing about the cause of her dysphagia.
Acid regurgitation supports a diagnosis of GORD, but it does not tell you whether the food sticking is due to a stricture or a motility disorder.
Worse pain when lying flat or bending over points to reflux, but it does not tell you whether the dysphagia is mechanical or due to a motility disorder.
questions.why: Dysphagia to solids only, especially if it is getting worse, points to a mechanical narrowing such as a peptic stricture or cancer. Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia or oesophageal spasm.

questions.stem: Kelly, 45, has had ACS ruled out in ED (normal ECG during pain, hs-troponin I 3 ng/L at 0 and 2 hours). She has typical reflux symptoms, plus 2 weeks of dysphagia to solids and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss over 3 months. What is the best plan for her GORD on discharge?
options: Urgent gastroscopy referral and start pantoprazole 40 mg daily before breakfast
Pantoprazole 40 mg daily for 8 weeks; gastroscopy only if symptoms persist
Urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori, then eradication therapy if positive
Barium swallow first, then gastroscopy only if a stricture is seen
notes: An empirical PPI trial is suitable only for uncomplicated reflux. With alarm features, waiting for a response could delay the diagnosis of a stricture or cancer.
Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features. It does not investigate dysphagia or weight loss.
Gastroscopy is the first-line test for dysphagia with alarm features because it allows biopsy and treatment. A barium swallow only delays it.
questions.why: Dysphagia and unintentional weight loss are alarm features. She needs a prompt gastroscopy to look for a stricture, Barrett's oesophagus or cancer, and to take biopsies, not just a PPI trial. A standard-dose PPI before breakfast treats the reflux while she waits.

questions.stem: Kelly, 45, gets burning retrosternal pain with acid regurgitation after big meals and when she lies on the couch. It is never brought on by exertion. What is the main mechanism of reflux in GORD that explains this pattern?
options: Excess gastric acid secretion overwhelming a normally competent sphincter
Transient LOS relaxations triggered by gastric distension, worse without gravity
Failure of LOS relaxation with loss of peristalsis in the oesophageal body
Delayed gastric emptying from vagal neuropathy raising intragastric volume
notes: Most people with GORD secrete a normal amount of acid. The problem is acid getting into the oesophagus, not making too much of it.
This describes achalasia, which causes dysphagia to solids and liquids and regurgitation of undigested food, not post-meal acid reflux.
Gastroparesis can make reflux worse, but it is not the main mechanism. Kelly has no early satiety, bloating or vomiting to suggest it.
questions.why: Most reflux happens during transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) that are not caused by swallowing. These are triggered by stretch receptors in the distended gastric fundus after a meal. Lying flat removes the help of gravity, so acid refluxes more easily and clears more slowly.

questions.stem: Kelly, 45, has dysphagia and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss. As part of your examination, you palpate the left supraclavicular fossa for Virchow's node. Why do upper GI cancers typically spread to a node on the left side?
options: The right lymphatic duct drains the abdomen into the left brachiocephalic vein
Gastric lymph drains directly to the left deep cervical nodes along the left vagus
The cervical oesophagus lies left of midline, so its nodes sit in the left neck
The thoracic duct carries abdominal lymph to the left subclavian–jugular junction
notes: The right lymphatic duct drains only the right side of the head, neck, thorax and right upper limb. It enters the venous system on the right, not the left.
Gastric lymph drains to the left gastric and coeliac nodes and then up the thoracic duct. There is no direct path to the cervical nodes along the vagus.
Her lesion is likely in the distal oesophagus or gastro-oesophageal junction, which drains to the left gastric and coeliac nodes, not straight to the neck.
questions.why: Lymph from the abdomen drains through the coeliac nodes to the cisterna chyli and then up the thoracic duct. The thoracic duct empties at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins, so tumour cells can lodge in a node in the left supraclavicular fossa.

questions.stem: In a GP clinic, John, 21, tells you he has had loose stools 3 to 4 times a day for 12 weeks, with no blood. He feels tired and his clothes are looser. You want to find out whether he has fat malabsorption. Which question asks about this most directly?
options: "Do you wake up at night needing to open your bowels?"
"Does any tummy pain ease after you open your bowels?"
"What colour is it, and does it float or is it hard to flush?"
"Have you noticed any mucus or slime in your poo?"
notes: Night-time diarrhoea suggests an organic cause in general, but it doesn't tell you specifically that fat is not being absorbed.
Pain that eases after opening the bowels is one of the Rome IV criteria for IBS. It doesn't screen for malabsorption.
Mucus points to colonic inflammation or IBS, not to fat malabsorption in the small bowel.
questions.why: Pale, bulky, floating, greasy stools that are hard to flush point to steatorrhoea. Patients rarely mention it unless you ask, and it makes IBS unlikely as the explanation.

questions.stem: John, 21, comes back to the GP a week later. His tTG-IgA is 210 U/mL (more than 10 times the upper limit), EMA-IgA is positive at 1:320 and total IgA is normal. He has been eating gluten normally throughout. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Refer for gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies while he keeps eating gluten
Start a strict gluten-free diet and repeat tTG-IgA in 6 months
Order HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 typing to confirm the diagnosis
Arrange a colonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsies
notes: The no-biopsy approach is a paediatric pathway. Starting the diet now in an adult would hide the histology and leave the diagnosis unconfirmed.
About a third of the population carries HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. A negative result helps rule coeliac disease out, but a positive one cannot confirm it.
Coeliac disease affects the proximal small bowel. A colonoscopy looks for Crohn's disease or colitis, which are unlikely here.
questions.why: In Australian adults, coeliac disease is still confirmed on duodenal biopsy, even when serology is strongly positive. He must keep eating gluten until the biopsy, because the diet lets the villi heal and can make the histology falsely normal.

questions.stem: John, 21, has coeliac disease confirmed by serology. For 12 weeks he has had loose stools that are light coloured and float in the toilet, and he has lost 4 kg. Which mechanism best explains what his stools look like?
options: Blocked bile flow stops bilirubin breakdown products from reaching the gut
Autoimmune destruction of the exocrine pancreas stops lipase secretion
Colonic mucosal inflammation causes secretion of chloride and water
Villous atrophy shrinks the absorptive surface, so unabsorbed fat reaches the colon
notes: Biliary obstruction causes pale stools but also jaundice, dark urine and a cholestatic LFT pattern. John has none of these.
Coeliac disease does not destroy the pancreas. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in a young man would suggest cystic fibrosis or chronic pancreatitis.
Colonic inflammation causes watery or bloody diarrhoea with mucus, not pale, fatty, floating stools.
questions.why: Gluten-driven villous atrophy in the proximal small bowel leaves too little absorptive surface, and the damaged duodenum releases less CCK. Unabsorbed fat makes the stool pale, bulky and floating (steatorrhoea).

questions.stem: John, 21, has coeliac disease. His bloods show Hb 116 g/L, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 microg/L, low folate and a normal B12. Damage to which part of the gut best explains why iron and folate are low while B12 is spared?
options: Terminal ileum
Duodenum and proximal jejunum
Gastric body and fundus
Caecum and ascending colon
notes: The terminal ileum absorbs B12 and bile salts. Disease here, such as Crohn's, would lower B12, but John's B12 is normal.
Parietal cells in the gastric body and fundus make intrinsic factor. Losing them, as in pernicious anaemia, would cause B12 deficiency, not this pattern.
The colon absorbs water and electrolytes but plays no real part in absorbing iron or folate.
questions.why: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and folate in the proximal jejunum. Coeliac disease damages this proximal bowel most, while B12 is absorbed further down, in the terminal ileum.

questions.stem: Minh, 63, is in a GP clinic with jaundice, spider naevi and palmar erythema. You suspect portal hypertension and want to examine for an enlarged spleen while he lies supine with his abdomen exposed. How should you palpate for the spleen?
options: Start in the right iliac fossa, advance towards the left costal margin on inspiration
Start at the left costal margin and move down towards the left iliac fossa
Start in the left iliac fossa and move straight up towards the left costal margin
Start in the epigastrium and move laterally along the left costal margin
notes: Starting under the costal margin can put your hand over a massive spleen, so you miss its edge completely.
The spleen grows diagonally towards the right iliac fossa, not straight down, so a vertical line from the left iliac fossa can miss it.
The epigastrium is not where an enlarging spleen extends, and moving along the costal margin does not follow its path of enlargement.
questions.why: The spleen enlarges down and medially towards the right iliac fossa. Starting there and working diagonally towards the left costal margin, with the patient breathing in to bring the tip down, means you will not miss a large spleen.

questions.stem: Minh's HCV RNA is 1.8 x 10^6 IU/mL. He is jaundiced (bilirubin 60 µmol/L), with albumin 29 g/L, INR 1.4 and platelets 120 x 10^9/L. He has no ascites or encephalopathy, which gives Child-Pugh class B. He wants to start treatment as soon as possible. What is the most appropriate next step in treating his hepatitis C?
options: GP prescribes sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks, and checks HCV RNA 12 weeks after
GP prescribes glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks, and checks HCV RNA 12 weeks after
Urgent hepatology referral for specialist-led antiviral therapy, usually with ribavirin
Hold off antiviral therapy until a FibroScan has confirmed and staged the cirrhosis
notes: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir is the right drug, but a GP should not treat decompensated cirrhosis alone. He needs ribavirin, close monitoring and hepatology care.
Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir contains a protease inhibitor, which is contraindicated in decompensated (Child-Pugh B or C) cirrhosis because of the risk of liver injury.
Jaundice, low albumin and a raised INR already show decompensation. Waiting for elastography would delay urgent specialist care and does not change the need to refer.
questions.why: GPs can prescribe direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) on the PBS, but decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B or C) needs a specialist to lead treatment. The usual regimen is sofosbuvir/velpatasvir plus ribavirin for 12 weeks, alongside variceal screening and transplant assessment.

questions.stem: Minh, 63, has untreated chronic hepatitis C. Over the past year he has had about five episodes of a bumpy, non-itchy, painless rash on his lower legs, each settling within a week. It is palpable purpura. Platelets are 120 x 10^9/L and INR is 1.4. Which mechanism best explains the rash?
options: Bleeding into the skin from thrombocytopenia caused by splenic sequestration
Deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors from impaired liver synthesis
IgA immune complex deposition in dermal small vessels, as in IgA vasculitis
Rheumatoid factor–IgG–HCV immune complexes deposit in small vessels and fix complement
notes: Spontaneous skin bleeding usually needs platelets well below 50, and purpura from thrombocytopenia is flat, not palpable.
Coagulopathy causes bruising and ecchymoses, not recurrent palpable purpura, and an INR of 1.4 is only mildly raised.
IgA vasculitis is mainly a disease of children after infection. The small-vessel vasculitis linked to hepatitis C is mixed cryoglobulinaemia.
questions.why: In mixed cryoglobulinaemia, HCV drives B cells to make IgM rheumatoid factor. This binds IgG and HCV antigen to form complexes that precipitate in the cooler, dependent leg vessels and activate complement (low C4), causing a palpable leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

questions.stem: Minh, 63, has decompensated hepatitis C cirrhosis with a palpable spleen and platelets of 120. The hepatologist plans a gastroscopy to screen for oesophageal varices. At the lower oesophagus, varices form at an anastomosis between which veins?
options: Superior rectal vein and middle and inferior rectal veins
Paraumbilical veins and superficial epigastric veins
Left gastric vein and oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
Splenic vein and left renal vein
notes: This is the portosystemic anastomosis in the anorectal region, which forms rectal varices, not oesophageal ones.
This anastomosis at the umbilicus produces caput medusae, not oesophageal varices.
A splenorenal shunt can form on its own in portal hypertension, but it is not the anastomosis that forms oesophageal varices.
questions.why: In portal hypertension, blood is diverted from the left gastric vein (portal system) into the oesophageal veins that drain to the azygos vein (systemic system). The submucosal veins of the lower oesophagus dilate into varices, which can bleed severely.

questions.stem: Michelle, 56, sees you at a GP practice with 5 days of jaundice, right upper quadrant pain and feeling hot. She is slow to answer and loses her train of thought now and then. Which history question best identifies severe disease that needs same-day transfer to hospital?
options: "Do you get pain in your upper tummy after fatty meals?"
"Have your stools been greasy, floating or hard to flush?"
"Have you or anyone else noticed confusion or poor concentration?"
"Have you had any tattoos, injecting drug use or transfusions?"
notes: Pain after fatty meals suggests biliary colic. It doesn't tell you how severe this illness is or how urgently she needs hospital.
Steatorrhoea suggests pancreatic insufficiency or pancreatic cancer. It helps sort out the differential, but it isn't a marker of acute severity.
Viral hepatitis risk factors are part of every jaundice history, but they help with the differential. They don't show sepsis with organ dysfunction.
questions.why: Confusion with Charcot's triad (jaundice, RUQ pain, fever) points towards Reynolds' pentad, which means severe cholangitis with organ dysfunction. Patients often don't mention it themselves, so ask directly. If it's present, she needs an ambulance to hospital.

questions.stem: At ED triage Michelle, 56, has jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Her temperature is 39.1 °C, BP 86/50, HR 126 and lactate 3.6, and she is newly confused. Ultrasound shows a stone in a dilated common bile duct. Blood cultures have been taken. She is allergic to latex but has no drug allergies. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
options: Piperacillin with tazobactam 4 g + 0.5 g IV 6-hourly
Amoxicillin with clavulanate 875 mg + 125 mg orally 12-hourly
Metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly as monotherapy
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV 6-hourly as monotherapy
notes: An oral agent is not appropriate for a hypotensive, septic patient. She needs IV antibiotics within the hour.
Metronidazole covers only anaerobes and misses the enteric Gram-negative bacilli that cause most cholangitis.
Flucloxacillin is aimed at staphylococci and streptococci and gives no useful cover against enteric Gram-negative organisms.
questions.why: For severe biliary sepsis, eTG recommends broad IV cover of enteric Gram-negatives, enterococci and anaerobes, such as piperacillin with tazobactam 4 g + 0.5 g IV 6-hourly, given within 60 minutes. Urgent ERCP to drain the duct follows once she is resuscitated.

questions.stem: Michelle, 56, has had pale, almost clay-coloured stools for several days. Her bilirubin is 98 µmol/L, mostly conjugated, and ultrasound shows a stone obstructing the distal common bile duct. What best explains her pale stools?
options: Hepatocytes cannot conjugate bilirubin, so unconjugated bilirubin builds up in blood
Pancreatic lipase is blocked, so undigested fat makes the stools pale and bulky
Bilirubin is diverted into the urine as urobilinogen instead of entering the stool
Conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut, so bacteria make no stercobilin
notes: Failure of conjugation causes unconjugated jaundice, as in Gilbert's syndrome. Her bilirubin is mostly conjugated, so conjugation is working.
Fat malabsorption gives greasy, floating stools. She denies these and her lipase is normal. The pale colour comes from missing stercobilin.
Urobilinogen is made in the gut, so urinary urobilinogen falls in obstruction. Dark urine comes from water-soluble conjugated bilirubin itself.
questions.why: Normally conjugated bilirubin passes into the gut in bile. Gut bacteria turn it into urobilinogen and then stercobilin, which makes stool brown. When the duct is blocked, little bilirubin reaches the gut, so the stool is pale.

questions.stem: The next morning Michelle has ERCP for her distal common bile duct stones. The endoscopist passes a side-viewing duodenoscope and cannulates the bile duct where it opens into the bowel. Where is this opening?
options: Minor duodenal papilla, in the second part of the duodenum
Major duodenal papilla, in the second part of the duodenum
Major duodenal papilla, in the first part of the duodenum
Major duodenal papilla, in the third part of the duodenum
notes: The minor papilla drains the accessory pancreatic duct, not the bile duct. It sits about 2 cm proximal to the major papilla.
The first part of the duodenum (the duodenal bulb) has no bile duct opening. The common bile duct runs behind it.
The third (horizontal) part crosses in front of the IVC and aorta, below the superior mesenteric artery. It has no bile duct opening.
questions.why: The common bile duct joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla. This opens at the major duodenal papilla on the posteromedial wall of the descending (second) part of the duodenum. The sphincter of Oddi, which is cut at sphincterotomy, controls the opening.

questions.stem: Sarah, 24, is in the ED with a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150/min since 09:35. BP 114/72, alert, well perfused, no chest pain. Pads are on and a rhythm strip is running. You decide to try the modified Valsalva manoeuvre. Which instruction should you give her?
options: Lie flat, blow into a 10 mL syringe for 15 s, then sit up quickly and stay up for 15 s
Sit upright, blow hard into the syringe for 5 s, then stay sitting quietly for a minute
Semi-recumbent, blow into a 10 mL syringe for 15 s, then lie flat with legs raised to 45°
Stand, hold your breath and bear down for 60 s, then sit down slowly on the trolley
notes: This is the wrong way round: the leg raise and lying flat come after the strain. Sitting up afterwards cuts venous return and loses the reflex vagal surge.
A 5 s strain is too short to set off the reflex, and staying upright afterwards leaves out the postural step that makes the modified version work.
A 60 s strain while standing is too long and risks syncope in a patient who is already light-headed. The standard strain is 15 s, done semi-recumbent.
questions.why: Modified Valsalva (REVERT): she strains semi-recumbent for 15 s, hard enough to move the plunger of a 10 mL syringe, then lies flat straight away with her legs raised to 45° for 15 s. The leg raise boosts venous return and vagal tone in the release phase and roughly doubles the reversion rate.

questions.stem: Sarah, 24, stays in a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150/min after two modified Valsalva attempts. BP 114/72, alert, no asthma, not on any rate-slowing drugs. She has an 18G antecubital cannula and a rhythm strip is running. Which adenosine regimen is correct?
options: 6 mg rapid IV push followed by a 20 mL saline flush; if no reversion, 12 mg rapid IV push
3 mg slow IV injection over 2 minutes, repeated every 5 minutes up to 12 mg in total
12 mg IV infusion over 10 minutes through the peripheral line, then reassess the rhythm
6 mg intramuscular injection into the deltoid, then 12 mg IM after 15 minutes if needed
notes: A slow injection lets the drug break down before it reaches the AV node. A 3 mg start is kept for central lines, heart transplant recipients or patients on dipyridamole, and even then it is a rapid push.
An infusion is ineffective: adenosine is cleared by red cells and endothelium within seconds, so it never reaches an effective level at the AV node.
Adenosine is not given intramuscularly. Absorption is far too slow for a drug with a half-life of seconds.
questions.why: Adenosine has a half-life of under 10 seconds, so give it as a rapid IV push through a proximal large vein, straight away followed by a saline flush: 6 mg first, then 12 mg (a further 12 mg can follow), with a rhythm strip recording.

questions.stem: Sarah, 24, has AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia at 150/min. Within seconds of adenosine her monitor shows a brief pause, then sinus rhythm at 105/min. By what mechanism did adenosine end her tachycardia?
options: Blocks fast sodium channels, slowing conduction in an accessory pathway
Blocks beta-1 receptors, lowering cAMP and slowing the sinus node rate
Blocks L-type calcium channels in ventricular myocytes, reducing contractility
Activates A1 receptors, opening K+ channels and transiently blocking the AV node
notes: Sodium channel blockade is how class I drugs work (e.g. flecainide), and AVNRT does not use an accessory pathway; its circuit sits within the AV node.
That is how beta blockers act; adenosine is not a beta blocker, and slowing the sinus node would not break a re-entry circuit in the AV node.
Adenosine does not block calcium channels in ventricular muscle; the problem here is the AV nodal circuit, not ventricular contractility.
questions.why: Adenosine acts on A1 receptors in the AV node. These open acetylcholine/adenosine-sensitive K+ channels and lower cAMP, which hyperpolarises nodal cells and causes a brief AV block. AVNRT needs the AV node as part of its circuit, so blocking the node ends the re-entry.

questions.stem: Sarah, 24, stays in SVT at 150/min after modified Valsalva. Before adenosine, the registrar considers right carotid sinus massage, having confirmed no carotid bruit. Which nerve carries the afferent signal from the carotid sinus baroreceptors to the brainstem?
options: Vagus nerve, through its superior laryngeal branch
Hypoglossal nerve, through its descending branch
Ansa cervicalis, from the C1 to C3 roots
Glossopharyngeal nerve, through the carotid sinus nerve
notes: The vagus is the efferent limb of the reflex and carries aortic arch baroreceptor afferents. The superior laryngeal branch supplies the larynx, not the carotid sinus.
The hypoglossal nerve is motor to the tongue. It crosses the carotid arteries near the bifurcation but carries no baroreceptor fibres.
The ansa cervicalis is a motor loop supplying the infrahyoid strap muscles. It lies on the carotid sheath but plays no part in the baroreflex.
questions.why: Carotid sinus baroreceptors, at the carotid bifurcation (about the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage), send signals through the carotid sinus nerve (a branch of CN IX) to the nucleus tractus solitarius. The vagus is the efferent limb: it slows the SA node and the AV node and can interrupt AV nodal re-entry.

questions.stem: Philip, 69, has had 40 minutes of racing palpitations and has come to a rural ED. He is not yet on a cardiac monitor. You find an irregularly irregular radial pulse of about 110 and want to know whether some heartbeats are not reaching the periphery. The triage nurse is free to help. How do you best show this?
options: Feel both radial pulses at the same time and compare their timing and volume
Listen at the apex and count the rate for 1 min while the nurse counts the radial pulse
Feel the radial and femoral pulses at the same time, checking for a delay
Count the radial pulse for 15 seconds and compare it with the carotid pulse rate
notes: Comparing the two radial pulses looks for a radio-radial delay (for example aortic dissection or subclavian stenosis). It does not compare central beats with peripheral beats.
A radio-femoral delay points to coarctation of the aorta. Both are peripheral pulses, so this cannot show beats that fail to reach the periphery.
A 15-second count multiplied up is inaccurate in an irregular rhythm, and the carotid is also a peripheral pulse rather than the apical heart rate.
questions.why: A pulse deficit is the gap between the apical rate (heard with a stethoscope) and the radial rate, counted at the same time over a full minute. In AF it shows that some beats are too weak to be felt at the wrist.

questions.stem: Philip, 69, has new-onset AF that started under 2 hours ago, and he is haemodynamically stable. He has hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no diabetes, heart failure, stroke, TIA or vascular disease, and no valve disease. His father died of a stroke. Creatinine 92, eGFR 74, Hb 146, INR 1.0. What is the best choice for his long-term stroke prevention?
options: CHA2DS2-VA 2: apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily
CHA2DS2-VA 1: aspirin 100 mg orally once daily
CHA2DS2-VA 3: warfarin, aiming for an INR of 2 to 3
CHA2DS2-VA 1: no antithrombotic, and review the score yearly
notes: He scores 2, not 1, because both age 65 to 74 and hypertension count. Aspirin is not used for stroke prevention in AF: it works poorly and still causes bleeding.
Family history and high cholesterol do not score, so he scores 2. Warfarin is also second line to a DOAC in non-valvular AF.
He scores 2, not 1, so anticoagulation is recommended now. Leaving him without treatment exposes him to a preventable risk of stroke.
questions.why: He scores 1 for age 65 to 74 and 1 for hypertension, so CHA2DS2-VA is 2 and oral anticoagulation is recommended. In non-valvular AF a DOAC is preferred, and he meets none of the dose-reduction criteria for apixaban.

questions.stem: Philip, 69, has atrial fibrillation. His atria are depolarising chaotically at about 400 to 600 times a minute, but his ECG shows a ventricular rate of about 132/min. Which property mainly stops most of these atrial impulses from reaching the ventricles?
options: Slowing conduction and a long refractory period in the AV node, which block many impulses
Overdrive suppression of the sinoatrial node by the rapidly fibrillating atria
Fast conduction in the His–Purkinje system, which limits how often the ventricles capture
The plateau of the ventricular action potential, which makes ventricular muscle refractory
notes: The sinus node is suppressed in AF, but that explains the absent P waves, not why the ventricular rate is held well below the atrial rate.
The His–Purkinje system conducts quickly and does not filter impulses. The rate-limiting gate sits above it, in the AV node.
Ventricular refractoriness would still allow rates above 200/min. The ventricles beat at about 132 because the AV node lets through only that many impulses.
questions.why: Conduction in the AV node slows as impulses arrive faster, and the node has a relatively long refractory period. Many fibrillatory impulses therefore arrive while the node is still refractory and are blocked. Rate-control drugs (beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil) work by lengthening this AV nodal refractoriness further.

questions.stem: Philip, 69, has new-onset non-valvular AF. He asks why the doctors keep mentioning his father's stroke when his problem is his heart rhythm. You explain that blood pools where the atrium no longer contracts properly. In non-valvular AF, where in the heart does the thrombus behind most cardioembolic strokes usually form?
options: The apex of the left ventricle
The right atrial appendage
The openings of the pulmonary veins
The left atrial appendage
notes: Left ventricular apical thrombus is typical after an anterior MI or with an LV aneurysm. It is not the usual source in AF when ventricular function is normal.
Clot from the right side of the heart travels to the lungs, not the brain, and right atrial appendage thrombus is much less common in AF.
The openings of the pulmonary veins are where the ectopic triggers that start AF usually arise, and this is the target of catheter ablation. They are not the usual site of thrombus.
questions.why: About 90% of thrombi in non-valvular AF form in the left atrial appendage. It is a blind-ending, trabeculated pouch where blood stagnates once the atrium stops contracting, and clot from there can travel to the brain. This is why TOE looks at the appendage before cardioversion.

questions.stem: Carl, 54, has type 2 diabetes and 4 months of burning retrosternal pain after dinner. He mentions it is worse if he walks to the shops straight after eating. You are taking the history in general practice. Which follow-up question best separates stable angina from reflux?
options: Does the pain feel burning rather than heavy or tight?
Is the pain worse after a large or heavy meal?
Does it come on with exertion alone and settle within minutes of rest?
Does the pain spread to your arm, jaw or neck?
notes: How patients describe the pain is unreliable: angina can be described as burning, especially in people with diabetes, so this question cannot separate the two.
Angina can also be worse after a heavy meal, so a link with meals does not distinguish it from reflux.
Many patients with angina have no radiation, so a 'no' answer does not exclude it. Duration and response to rest discriminate better.
questions.why: Angina is brought on by exertion and settles within minutes of rest. Carl's pain does not start with tennis on its own and lasts about 30 minutes whatever he does. How the pain relates to exertion and to rest is the key discriminator.

questions.stem: Carl, 54, has daily typical reflux symptoms with no alarm features. His ECG is normal and his Hb and ferritin are normal. Alongside lifestyle advice (smaller, earlier, less spicy meals, raising the head of the bed, weight loss), you start drug treatment in general practice. Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Esomeprazole 20 mg orally once daily, 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, for 4 to 8 weeks
Esomeprazole 40 mg orally twice daily with meals for 12 weeks, then stop
Omeprazole 20 mg orally once daily at bedtime, continued long term
Famotidine 20 mg orally twice daily for 2 weeks, then stop if improved
notes: A high dose twice daily is for when standard-dose treatment fails or for severe oesophagitis. Taking it with meals rather than before them also makes it work less well.
A dose at bedtime on an empty stomach misses the meal-stimulated proton pumps. Starting with indefinite treatment, rather than a trial and then step-down, is not appropriate.
An H2 antagonist is an alternative but works less well than a PPI for daily troublesome reflux, and 2 weeks is too short to judge a response.
questions.why: First-line treatment for troublesome GORD is a standard-dose PPI once daily, 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, for 4 to 8 weeks. The trial is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Then step down to the lowest effective dose.

questions.stem: Carl, 54, gets reflux mainly after a large curry at 8 pm, and it is worse when he lies down at 9.30 pm. He has type 2 diabetes but no early satiety or vomiting. In most patients with GORD like Carl, what is the main mechanism that lets gastric contents reflux into the oesophagus?
options: Persistently low resting pressure of the lower oesophageal sphincter
Transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter triggered by gastric distension
Gastric acid hypersecretion driven by raised serum gastrin
Delayed gastric emptying from diabetic autonomic neuropathy
notes: A low resting sphincter pressure matters mainly in severe or erosive disease and in scleroderma. It is not the main mechanism in most patients.
Most patients with GORD secrete a normal amount of acid. Hypergastrinaemia with hypersecretion suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and nothing here points to it.
Gastroparesis can contribute in some patients with diabetes, but Carl has no early satiety or vomiting, and it is not the main mechanism of GORD.
questions.why: Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations, which are not triggered by swallowing, cause most reflux episodes. Stretch of the proximal stomach after a big meal sets them off through a vagal reflex. This is why large, late meals make reflux worse.

questions.stem: Carl, 54, is centrally obese and has nocturnal reflux. At gastroscopy he is found to have a small sliding hiatus hernia, in which the gastro-oesophageal junction moves up above the diaphragm. Which structure normally forms the external part of the antireflux barrier around the lower oesophagus?
options: Left crus of the diaphragm, at the level of T12
Median arcuate ligament, at the level of T12
Central tendon of the diaphragm, at the level of T8
Right crus of the diaphragm, at the level of T10
notes: The left crus is the smaller crus and does not classically form the oesophageal hiatus. T12 is the level of the aortic hiatus.
The median arcuate ligament joins the two crura in front of the aorta at T12. It forms the aortic hiatus, not the oesophageal one.
The central tendon at T8 contains the opening for the inferior vena cava, not the opening for the oesophagus.
questions.why: Fibres of the right crus of the diaphragm loop around the oesophageal hiatus at T10 and act as an external sphincter that adds to the lower oesophageal sphincter. In a sliding hiatus hernia the junction is pulled away from the crus, which weakens the barrier.

questions.stem: You are examining Bertha, 51, in the ED. She has sudden pleuritic chest pain and 3 days of a painful right calf after a 22-hour flight. Her right calf looks red and swollen. You want to record the swelling the way the Wells criteria define it. How should you do this?
options: Passively dorsiflex the right ankle and note whether this causes calf pain (Homans' sign)
Measure the right calf at its widest point and compare it with a population normal value
Measure both calves 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity and compare; >3 cm is significant
Measure both legs 10 cm above the medial malleolus and compare; >1 cm is significant
notes: Homans' sign is unreliable. It has poor sensitivity and specificity for DVT and is not how swelling is measured or recorded.
Calf size varies a lot between people. Only a comparison with her own other leg, at the same landmark, is meaningful.
The Wells landmark is 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, and the significant difference is more than 3 cm, not 1 cm.
questions.why: The Wells criteria define calf swelling as more than 3 cm larger than the other side, with both calves measured at the same fixed landmark, 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Always examine and compare both legs.

questions.stem: CTPA confirms bilateral PE in Bertha, 51, with no RV strain. BP is 126/80, hs-troponin is normal, eGFR is above 90, and you have found no bleeding risk. She has been admitted under medicine and you plan to start oral anticoagulation tonight. Which regimen is correct?
options: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily from day 1, continued for at least 3 months
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily for at least 3 months
Rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily from day 1, continued for at least 3 months
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily from day 1, continued for at least 3 months
notes: This leaves out the 7-day loading phase of 10 mg twice daily, so she would be undertreated during the period of highest risk.
Rivaroxaban starts at 15 mg twice daily for 21 days. Only after that does it change to 20 mg once daily.
Dabigatran for VTE needs at least 5 days of parenteral anticoagulation, such as enoxaparin, before it is started.
questions.why: For acute VTE, apixaban starts with a higher loading phase of 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then drops to 5 mg twice daily. Treatment of provoked PE lasts at least 3 months.

questions.stem: Bertha, 51, has bilateral PE on CTPA. On room air her RR is 28 and SpO2 is 92%. With supplemental oxygen her SpO2 rises to 96%. Her chest is clear and there is no consolidation on CT. What is the main mechanism of her hypoxaemia?
options: V/Q mismatch: flow diverted from blocked arteries overperfuses other lung units
Alveolar hypoventilation from splinting of the chest due to pleuritic pain
Diffusion limitation from thickening of the alveolar-capillary membrane
Fixed right-to-left shunt of blood through a patent foramen ovale
notes: She is tachypnoeic, and PE usually causes hypocapnia. Hypoventilation would raise CO2 and is not the main mechanism here.
PE does not thicken the alveolar-capillary membrane. Diffusion limitation is a feature of interstitial lung disease.
A shunt through a PFO happens only when right heart pressures are raised, as in massive PE. She has no RV strain, and a true shunt responds poorly to oxygen.
questions.why: In PE, blood is diverted away from the blocked arteries into the remaining lung, which is now relatively underventilated. These low V/Q units cause hypoxaemia. Hypoxaemia from V/Q mismatch improves with supplemental oxygen.

questions.stem: Bertha, 51, describes sharp, well-localised pain low in the right side of her chest, worse on deep breathing and coughing, with no radiation. CTPA shows a small pleural-based right lower lobe infarct with a trace effusion. Which structure, and which nerve supply, explains her pain?
options: Visceral pleura, supplied by the vagus nerve via the pulmonary plexus
Pulmonary artery wall, supplied by sympathetic fibres from T1 to T4
Diaphragmatic pleura centrally, supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5)
Costal parietal pleura, supplied by the intercostal nerves
notes: Visceral pleura has only autonomic supply and is insensitive to pain, so it cannot produce sharp, localised pleuritic pain.
Visceral pain from vessels is dull and poorly localised and does not change with breathing. That does not fit her pain.
Irritation of the central diaphragmatic pleura is referred to the shoulder tip through C3 to C5. Her pain is in the lower chest wall and does not radiate.
questions.why: The pleura-based infarct inflames the overlying costal parietal pleura. This pleura has somatic supply from the intercostal nerves, so the pain is sharp, well localised to the chest wall and worse when the pleura moves on breathing.

questions.stem: Sara, 32, is in your GP clinic. Before her headache she had zigzag lights and then numbness in her right hand and face. She takes the combined pill and smokes. You want to tell a migraine aura apart from a TIA. Which question helps most?
options: "Did your eye water or your nose run on that side during the pain?"
"Is the headache worse when you cough, strain or bend over?"
"Did the lights and numbness spread gradually over minutes, or start all at once?"
"Have you had any pain in your jaw when you chew?"
notes: Tearing and rhinorrhoea point to cluster headache. They do not help separate an aura from a TIA.
Pain worse with coughing or straining is a red flag for raised intracranial pressure, not a way to tell aura from TIA.
Jaw claudication screens for temporal arteritis, which almost never occurs under 50. It does not help separate aura from TIA.
