questions.why: Tempo and quality separate the two. A migraine aura is positive (lights, tingling) and spreads gradually over 5 minutes or more. A TIA is sudden, negative (numbness, visual loss) and at its worst from the start.

questions.stem: Sara, 32, has migraine with aura, a normal neurological examination and a negative urine pregnancy test. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill, smokes up to 5 cigarettes a day and wants reliable contraception. What is the most appropriate advice about her contraception?
options: Stop the combined pill and switch to an implant, IUD or progestogen-only pill
Keep taking the combined pill continuously to avoid the oestrogen-withdrawal week
Change to the combined vaginal ring to give steadier oestrogen levels
Change to a combined pill with 20 microgram ethinylestradiol
notes: Continuous use can help menstrual migraine without aura, but it is still oestrogen. It stays contraindicated with aura.
The ring contains ethinylestradiol, so it carries the same stroke risk and the same contraindication as the combined pill.
Lowering the dose does not remove the contraindication. Any combined hormonal method is category 4 in migraine with aura.
questions.why: Migraine with aura makes any oestrogen-containing contraceptive category 4 (contraindicated) because it raises the risk of ischaemic stroke, and smoking adds to that risk. Progestogen-only and copper methods are safe. She should use condoms until the new method is working.

questions.stem: Sara, 32, says her zigzag lights started near the centre of her vision and spread outwards over 20 minutes. Next, tingling spread from her right hand to her face over 10 to 15 minutes, and everything resolved before the headache. What best explains this slow spread of aura symptoms?
options: Embolic occlusion moving distally along a branch of the posterior cerebral artery
Focal epileptiform discharge spreading through the occipital and parietal cortex
Vasospasm of cerebral arteries cutting perfusion below the ischaemic threshold
A wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation spreading across cortex at about 3 mm/min
notes: An embolus causes a sudden negative deficit that is worst at onset. It does not cause shimmering lights that move over 20 minutes.
Seizure activity spreads within seconds and gives brief stereotyped symptoms, not a march over 20 minutes followed by a migraine headache.
The old vascular theory has been replaced. Blood flow falls modestly after the depolarisation wave, and it does not reach ischaemic levels during a typical aura.
questions.why: Cortical spreading depolarisation is a slow wave of depolarisation followed by suppression. It travels at 2 to 5 mm/min, so symptoms move across the visual and sensory maps over minutes. Positive features at the leading edge are followed by negative ones, and the wave can activate the trigeminovascular system.

questions.stem: During today's aura, Sara, 32, had tingling and then numbness that started in her right hand and crept into the right side of her face and lips over 10 to 15 minutes, with no weakness. Where in the brain did this sensory aura most likely arise?
options: Left precentral gyrus, spreading from the hand area towards the face area
Left postcentral gyrus, spreading from the hand area laterally to the face area
Right postcentral gyrus, spreading from the hand area laterally to the face area
Left ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
notes: The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex. Aura arising there would cause weakness or jerking, which she did not have.
The somatosensory pathways cross, so the right postcentral gyrus would cause symptoms on the left side, as in her one right-sided attack.
The VPL nucleus relays body sensation only. The face relays through VPM, and a thalamic lesion would not spread across the cortical map over minutes.
questions.why: Right-sided sensory symptoms come from the left primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus). On the sensory homunculus the face lies lateral and inferior to the hand, so a wave spreading laterally moves the symptoms from the hand to the face.

questions.stem: In the ED you are examining Fred, 64, who has suspected giant cell arteritis and a blurred right eye (acuity 6/18). You do the swinging light test in a dim room, moving the torch from one eye to the other every 2 to 3 seconds. Which finding confirms a right relative afferent pupillary defect?
options: Both pupils constrict to a near target but react poorly to the torch light
The right pupil stays dilated while the left constricts to light in either eye
Both pupils dilate as the torch swings from the left eye across to the right eye
Both pupils dilate as the torch swings from the right eye across to the left eye
notes: Light-near dissociation (e.g. Argyll Robertson or tectal lesions) is not an RAPD and does not localise to one optic nerve.
A pupil that stays dilated whatever eye is lit is an efferent defect (third nerve or pharmacological), not an afferent one.
Dilation when the light swings onto the left eye would mean a left RAPD, which would point to the left optic nerve, not Fred's affected right eye.
questions.why: With a right optic nerve lesion, less afferent signal comes from the right eye, so both pupils dilate (paradoxically) when the light moves onto it. An RAPD shows the optic nerve or a large area of retina is affected, which is what you expect in arteritic AION.

questions.stem: Fred, 64, in the ED has a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication. His right acuity has fallen from 6/18 to 6/36 over an hour. ESR 86, CRP 78. The earliest temporal artery biopsy is later this week. What is the most appropriate treatment now?
options: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily with an early rheumatology clinic review
Withhold corticosteroids until the temporal artery biopsy has been done
IV methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days, first dose now
Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily, starting after ophthalmology review tomorrow
notes: 15 mg is the starting dose for polymyalgia rheumatica alone. It is far too low to protect the optic nerves in GCA.
Delaying steroids risks permanent loss of the right eye and involvement of the left. The biopsy stays positive for 1 to 2 weeks after treatment starts.
Waiting until tomorrow leaves progressing ischaemic visual loss untreated, and visual involvement calls for IV pulse therapy now.
questions.why: Suspected GCA with visual loss is a sight-threatening emergency. Give pulse IV methylprednisolone (500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days) straight away, then oral prednisolone. Never wait for the biopsy, which stays diagnostic for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start.

questions.stem: Fred, 64, has giant cell arteritis. His right eye has reduced acuity, an RAPD, an inferior altitudinal field defect and a pale, chalky, swollen optic disc. The left eye is normal. What is the mechanism of his right visual loss?
options: Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery, causing inner retinal infarction
Raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath to the disc
Inflammatory demyelination of the retrobulbar segment of the right optic nerve
Granulomatous occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries, infarcting the disc
notes: Central retinal artery occlusion gives a pale retina with a cherry-red spot. The disc is not swollen, and the cause in GCA is arteritic rather than embolic.
Raised intracranial pressure gives bilateral papilloedema with preserved acuity early on. It does not cause a single swollen disc with an RAPD.
Optic neuritis affects younger patients, causes pain on eye movement, and the disc is usually normal (retrobulbar) or hyperaemic rather than chalky white.
questions.why: In GCA, granulomatous inflammation narrows and occludes the short posterior ciliary arteries, which supply the optic nerve head. The result is arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, with a pale, swollen disc that is infarcted and oedematous.

questions.stem: You examine Fred's head for signs of giant cell arteritis. You are looking for a tender, thickened, pulseless right superficial temporal artery, the vessel usually sampled at biopsy. Where do you palpate it, and what is its parent artery?
options: At the anterior border of masseter over the mandible; a branch of the facial artery
Just anterior to the tragus over the zygomatic arch; external carotid terminal branch
Behind the auricle over the mastoid process; a branch of the posterior auricular artery
Above the medial eyebrow at the supraorbital notch; a branch of the ophthalmic artery
notes: This is where you feel the facial artery pulse. The facial artery is a separate branch of the external carotid and is not the vessel examined or biopsied in GCA.
The posterior auricular artery runs behind the ear. It is not the temporal artery you palpate or biopsy.
The supraorbital artery comes from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid). It is not the superficial temporal artery.
questions.why: The superficial temporal artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid. Feel it just in front of the tragus over the root of the zygomatic arch, then follow it up over the temple. In GCA it may be tender, thickened, nodular or pulseless.

questions.stem: Jamie, 18, has had 4 hours of worsening generalised headache, fever, rigors, photophobia and a stiff neck. She is alert and lying flat on an ED trolley. You tell the examiner you will test for Kernig's sign. Which manoeuvre do you perform?
options: Passively flex her neck towards her chest and watch for her hips and knees flexing
Raise her straightened leg off the bed and note pain shooting down the back of the leg
With her hip and knee flexed to 90°, passively extend the knee and note pain or resistance
Turn her head side to side two to three times a second and ask if the headache worsens
notes: This is Brudzinski's neck sign, the other meningeal sign examined in this station, not Kernig's.
This is the straight leg raise (Lasègue's test) for lumbosacral nerve root irritation, done with the knee kept straight.
This is jolt accentuation of headache, a separate bedside test for meningism, not Kernig's sign.
questions.why: Kernig's sign is pain or resistance (hamstring spasm) when the knee is extended with the hip flexed to 90°. It is specific but insensitive, so a negative sign does not rule out meningitis.

questions.stem: Jamie, 18, has had dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV in ED. At 15:10 the CSF Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci, with culture and susceptibilities pending. She has no allergies and is not immunocompromised. What is the most appropriate change to her antimicrobial therapy now?
options: Add IV amoxicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes until the culture returns
Add IV vancomycin to ceftriaxone until pneumococcal susceptibilities are known
Switch ceftriaxone to IV benzylpenicillin because pneumococcus is the likely organism
Switch to IV meropenem alone to cover resistant Gram-positive organisms
notes: Listeria cover is for people over 50, pregnant women, the immunocompromised or people with alcohol dependence, and Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus, not a diplococcus.
Benzylpenicillin is used only as directed therapy once the isolate is shown to be penicillin-susceptible, so it is not safe while susceptibilities are pending.
Meropenem alone is not the recommended empirical regimen and does not reliably cover highly resistant pneumococci, which is the reason vancomycin is added.
questions.why: Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, which can be resistant to penicillin and less often to ceftriaxone. eTG says to add vancomycin to ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly until susceptibilities are known, and to keep dexamethasone going for 4 days.

questions.stem: Jamie, 18, with suspected bacterial meningitis, is given dexamethasone 10 mg IV just before her first dose of IV ceftriaxone. Why is giving dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose important?
options: It increases ceftriaxone penetration across the inflamed blood–brain barrier
It reduces CSF production by the choroid plexus, lowering pressure before the LP
It replaces cortisol lost through adrenal haemorrhage in overwhelming sepsis
It blunts the cytokine surge set off when the first antibiotic dose lyses bacteria
notes: Steroids reduce blood–brain barrier inflammation and permeability, so if anything they reduce antibiotic penetration. This is one reason vancomycin dosing needs care.
Lowering CSF production is not why it is given, and lowering pressure before the LP is not the aim of giving it early.
Adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen) is linked mainly to meningococcal sepsis, and replacing cortisol is not why dexamethasone is timed with antibiotics.
questions.why: Bactericidal antibiotics lyse bacteria and release cell wall components, which trigger a surge of TNF-α and IL-1 in the subarachnoid space. Giving dexamethasone first blunts this inflammation and reduces hearing loss, neurological damage and death in pneumococcal meningitis.

questions.stem: The ED registrar performs Jamie's lumbar puncture with her in the left lateral position. Which landmark and anatomical reason best explain the level chosen for the needle in this 18-year-old?
options: Iliac crests mark L4; L3/4 or L4/5 lies below the conus, which ends near L1–L2
Iliac crests mark L2; L2/3 lies below the conus, which ends near T12–L1
Lowest ribs mark L1; L1/2 lies below the conus, which ends near T11–T12
Posterior superior iliac spines mark L4; L5/S1 is used as the dural sac ends at L5
notes: The line between the iliac crests crosses about L4, not L2, and a needle at L2/3 risks injuring the conus in some adults.
The ribs are not a lumbar puncture landmark, and L1/2 is at the level of the conus, so it risks cord injury.
The PSIS lie at about S2, and the dural sac ends at about S2, not L5, so this landmark and reason are both wrong.
questions.why: In adults the spinal cord (conus medullaris) ends at about L1–L2, but the dural sac and CSF continue to about S2. The line joining the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) crosses about L4, so the L3/4 or L4/5 space reaches CSF below the cord, where the cauda equina roots float aside.

questions.stem: Roger Sinclair, 70, has had a hot, swollen, red left knee for 20 hours, with fevers and rigors overnight. You see him in general practice. When you ask about trauma he says, "I haven't fallen on it or injured my knee at all." Which question should you ask next to find out how bacteria could have got into the joint?
options: Have you ever had a sudden hot, swollen joint or a painful big toe before?
Have you had any diarrhoea, or red or sore eyes, in the past month?
Have you had any cut, scratch or puncture to the skin of that knee lately?
Do you take any fluid tablets, or drink alcohol most days?
notes: This screens for gout, a crystal differential. It doesn't find a way for bacteria to get into the joint.
This screens for reactive arthritis, which follows a gut or genitourinary infection. It doesn't find a way for bacteria to get into the joint.
Diuretics and alcohol are risk factors for gout. This question doesn't find a way for bacteria to get into the joint.
questions.why: Patients often don't count a small puncture as an injury. Asking directly about breaks in the skin is what uncovers direct inoculation, here a dirty nail knelt on 2 days earlier, as the route into the joint.

questions.stem: Mr Sinclair, 70, is in general practice with a hot, swollen left knee and a likely septic arthritis after a nail puncture. His temperature has risen from 38.4 to 38.7 °C with a rigor. Now HR 108, BP 134/80, RR 20, SpO2 97% on room air, and he is alert. He cannot bear weight. What is the most appropriate management now?
options: Give IV flucloxacillin 2 g in the practice now, then send him to hospital
Same-day hospital transfer by ambulance for aspiration; withhold antibiotics
Start oral flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly and review him in the practice tomorrow
Request CRP, urate and knee X-ray today and review results with him tomorrow
notes: Giving antibiotics before aspiration can make the synovial culture negative. Give them first only if there are signs of shock or organ dysfunction, and he has none.
Oral antibiotics and outpatient review undertreat a joint-destroying emergency, and starting them before aspiration hides the organism.
Outpatient tests delay definitive diagnosis. Blood tests and an X-ray cannot rule septic arthritis in or out, and the cartilage can be destroyed within days.
questions.why: Suspected septic arthritis is an emergency that needs same-day hospital care. With no shock or organ dysfunction, hold antibiotics until the joint has been aspirated (with blood cultures) so the organism can be identified. Keep him nil by mouth in case he needs a washout.

questions.stem: Mr Sinclair, 70, has a septic left knee with a large effusion. He sits holding the knee bent at about 20–30°, supported on a pillow, and resists any attempt to straighten or bend it further. What is the main reason this position is the most comfortable?
options: Joint capsule volume is greatest, so intra-articular pressure is lowest
Reflex quadriceps inhibition leaves the hamstrings unopposed in flexion
The collateral ligaments are tightest, so the inflamed joint is stabilised
Synovial blood flow falls in flexion, so less exudate forms in the joint
notes: Muscle inhibition does happen, but it doesn't explain why he holds the knee still at this angle. The main reason is lower capsular pressure.
The collateral ligaments are tight in extension and slack in flexion, so this has it the wrong way round.
Flexion doesn't usefully reduce synovial exudate. The comfort comes from lower pressure inside the joint, not from less fluid being made.
questions.why: The knee capsule holds the most fluid at about 20–30° of flexion. In that position the pressure inside the joint, and so the stretch on the inflamed, richly innervated capsule, is lowest. Full extension or deeper flexion raises the pressure and the pain.

questions.stem: Examining Mr Sinclair's left knee, you find a tense swelling that extends about a hand's breadth above the upper border of the patella. The bulge test and patellar tap are positive. Which structure, continuous with the knee joint cavity, accounts for the swelling above the patella?
options: Prepatellar bursa
Superficial infrapatellar bursa
Pes anserinus bursa
Suprapatellar bursa
notes: The prepatellar bursa lies between the skin and the patella and does not connect with the joint. It swells over the front of the kneecap, not above it.
The superficial infrapatellar bursa lies over the patellar tendon, below the patella. It does not connect with the joint, so it can't explain swelling above the patella.
The pes anserinus bursa is on the upper medial tibia, deep to the sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus tendons. It is separate from the joint.
questions.why: The suprapatellar bursa (pouch) runs up deep to quadriceps and connects with the knee joint, so a joint effusion fills it and bulges above the patella. It is also the space the needle enters in the usual superolateral approach to aspirating the knee.

questions.stem: You are examining Mr Tan, a 36-year-old fisherman in the ED, whose left ring finger DIP joint became hot, swollen and painful overnight. Fishermen are at risk of hand infections, so you check for flexor sheath infection as well as joint disease. Which finding would most suggest flexor tenosynovitis rather than a DIP joint problem?
options: Tenderness localised to the DIP joint line on gentle palpation
Erythema and swelling confined to the dorsum of the DIP joint
Severe pain along the volar finger on passive extension of the finger
Fluctuant swelling and redness along the lateral nail fold
notes: Tenderness that stays at the joint line points to the joint itself, as in gout or septic arthritis, not to the tendon sheath.
Redness and swelling confined to the DIP joint fit a monoarthritis; sheath infection makes the whole finger swell along the volar side.
A fluctuant, red nail fold is a paronychia, a superficial infection of the nail fold, not an infection of the flexor sheath.
questions.why: Pain on passive extension is the most specific of Kanavel's signs for flexor sheath infection. The others are a finger held flexed, swelling of the whole finger and tenderness along the sheath. Flexor sheath infection is a surgical emergency.

questions.stem: Mr Tan, 36, has had his second gout attack, confirmed by urate crystals on aspirate. At GP review after the flare has settled, he agrees to start allopurinol with flare prophylaxis. He has no tophi on examination and his eGFR is above 90. What target should his allopurinol be titrated to?
options: Serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L, starting allopurinol low and titrating up
Serum urate below 0.42 mmol/L, the upper limit of the lab reference range
Serum urate below 0.30 mmol/L, starting allopurinol low and titrating up
Serum urate below 0.48 mmol/L, the level above which gout risk climbs steeply
notes: The lab upper limit is above the urate saturation point (about 0.40 mmol/L), so crystals would keep forming; being 'in range' is not the goal.
A lower target of below 0.30 mmol/L is kept for tophaceous or severe gout, and Mr Tan has no tophi.
At 0.48 mmol/L urate is well above saturation, so this target would not dissolve crystals or prevent attacks.
questions.why: Australian guidance (eTG, RACGP) sets a treat-to-target urate below 0.36 mmol/L for gout without tophi. Allopurinol is started at a low dose and increased every few weeks until the target is reached. Below this level crystals dissolve and attacks stop.

questions.stem: Mr Tan, 36, has acute gout of his left ring finger DIP joint, confirmed by needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals on aspirate. Yet his serum urate taken during the flare is 0.40 mmol/L, within the lab reference range. What best explains a normal serum urate during an acute gout flare?
options: Xanthine oxidase activity in the liver falls during the acute inflammatory response
Acute-phase proteins increase urate reabsorption in the renal tubules
Activated neutrophils convert uric acid to allantoin in the circulation
Inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 increase the kidney's fractional excretion of urate
notes: A fall in xanthine oxidase activity in the liver is not the recognised mechanism; the drop in serum urate is mainly from increased excretion by the kidney.
This is the wrong way round: more tubular reabsorption would raise serum urate, not lower it.
Humans have no uricase, so urate cannot be turned into allantoin; that is why humans get gout and most other mammals do not.
questions.why: In an acute flare, systemic inflammation (IL-6) increases renal urate excretion, and urate is also being laid down as crystals. Both lower serum urate, so a normal level does not exclude gout. Repeat it 2 to 4 weeks after the flare.

questions.stem: Before a joint procedure on Mr Tan's left ring finger DIP joint, a digital nerve block is planned for analgesia. The block needs to cover sensation to the skin around the distal ring finger, including its dorsum. Which nerves provide sensation to this area?
options: The ulnar nerve alone, through its palmar and dorsal digital branches
The median nerve to the radial half and the ulnar nerve to the ulnar half
The median nerve alone, through its common palmar digital branches
The radial nerve to the dorsum and the median nerve to the volar surface
notes: The ulnar nerve supplies only the ulnar half of the ring finger; the radial half belongs to the median nerve.
The median nerve supplies only the radial half of the ring finger, so blocking it alone leaves the ulnar side with sensation.
The radial nerve's dorsal branches stop around the proximal phalanx; the palmar digital nerves supply the dorsum at the DIP joint.
questions.why: The ring finger is split: the median nerve supplies its radial half and the ulnar nerve its ulnar half. Their palmar digital branches also curve dorsally to supply the nail bed and the dorsum of the distal phalanx. A digital block must therefore reach both sides of the finger.

questions.stem: Ms Thomas, 56, has bilateral hip, knee and hand pain that is worse on weight-bearing, with morning stiffness under 30 minutes. You move to examine her hips with her lying supine on the GP couch. Which manoeuvre is most sensitive for early hip osteoarthritis?
options: Thomas test for a fixed flexion deformity of the hip
Trendelenburg test standing on each leg in turn
Passive internal rotation with the hip and knee flexed to 90 degrees
Straight leg raise to 70 degrees with ankle dorsiflexion
notes: A fixed flexion deformity is a late sign of advanced hip disease, so it misses early osteoarthritis.
The Trendelenburg test assesses hip abductor (gluteus medius) function and is not a sensitive test for early joint disease.
The straight leg raise tests for lumbosacral nerve root tension in radicular pain, and she has no leg symptoms.
questions.why: Internal rotation is the first movement lost in hip osteoarthritis. Testing it passively with the hip and knee flexed to 90 degrees often reproduces groin pain and shows reduced range early, before other signs appear.

questions.stem: Ms Thomas, 56, has nodal hand osteoarthritis and knee osteoarthritis. CRP, ESR, RF and anti-CCP are normal, eGFR is over 90, and she has no GI, kidney or cardiac history. She has started exercise and is working on weight loss, and she asks for something for the knee and hand pain. Which medicine is the most appropriate first choice?
options: Paracetamol 1 g orally four times daily, taken regularly
Topical diclofenac gel to the painful knees and hands, 3 to 4 times daily
Tramadol 50 mg orally up to four times daily as needed
Glucosamine sulfate 1500 mg orally once daily
notes: Paracetamol gives at most a small, clinically trivial benefit in osteoarthritis and is no longer preferred first-line.
Opioids, including tramadol, are not recommended for osteoarthritis: benefit is small and the risk of harm and dependence is significant.
Glucosamine is not recommended because good-quality trials show no meaningful benefit over placebo.
questions.why: For knee and hand osteoarthritis, a topical NSAID is the first-line medicine. It relieves pain about as well as an oral NSAID, with far less systemic GI, kidney and cardiovascular risk. Use it alongside exercise and weight loss.

questions.stem: Ms Thomas, 56, has bony Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes. Her hand X-ray shows joint space narrowing, marginal osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis, with no erosions or periarticular osteopenia, and her CRP is 4 mg/L. Which underlying process best explains these findings?
options: Autoimmune synovitis with pannus eroding bone at the joint margins
Urate crystal deposition provoking neutrophil-driven inflammation
Enthesitis at tendon insertions with new bone formation
Cartilage loss under mechanical load, with reactive bone remodelling
notes: Rheumatoid pannus causes marginal erosions, periarticular osteopenia and raised inflammatory markers, and none of these are present.
Gout causes acute hot swollen joints and punched-out erosions with overhanging edges, which she has never had.
Enthesitis with new bone formation is typical of spondyloarthritis such as psoriatic arthritis, and she has no psoriasis, nail changes or erosive change.
questions.why: Osteoarthritis is a whole-joint disease. Articular cartilage breaks down, and the subchondral bone remodels in response, forming osteophytes (the nodes) and sclerosis. Because the inflammation is only low grade, CRP stays normal and there are no erosions.

questions.stem: Examining the hands of Ms Thomas, 56, you note squaring at the base of each thumb, caused by adduction and subluxation of the base of the first metacarpal, and pain on grinding the thumb base. She can no longer open jars. Which joint is affected, and which bones form it?
options: First carpometacarpal joint: trapezium with the base of the first metacarpal
First metacarpophalangeal joint: first metacarpal head with proximal phalanx
Scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joint: scaphoid with the trapezium and trapezoid
Radiocarpal joint: distal radius with the scaphoid and the lunate
notes: The first MCP joint lies further along the thumb and does not cause squaring at the base of the thumb.
The STT joint is often involved alongside the CMC joint, but it lies deeper in the carpus and does not produce the squared thumb base.
The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is not typically involved in nodal osteoarthritis and would not cause thumb-base squaring.
questions.why: Thumb-base squaring and a positive grind test point to the first carpometacarpal (trapeziometacarpal) joint. It is a saddle joint between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal, and one of the most common sites of hand osteoarthritis.

questions.stem: Katie, 28, is in ED with 4 days of progressive weakness in both legs. On examination her legs are spastic, and pinprick is reduced from both feet up to the tops of both thighs. Her arms are normal. What should you do next in the sensory examination?
options: Do Romberg's test to confirm a dorsal column sensory deficit
Test pinprick up the trunk from the groin towards the nipples to find a level
Compare each leg dermatome with the other side to find a single affected root
Test two-point discrimination on both soles to grade the sensory loss
notes: Katie cannot stand, so Romberg's test is unsafe and impossible here. It also would not help localise the lesion.
Loss in both legs together with spasticity points to a cord lesion, not a single root, so comparing dermatomes side to side misses the key finding.
Grading loss on the soles adds nothing to localisation. The step that matters is finding the upper border of the sensory loss on the trunk.
questions.why: When sensation is abnormal throughout both legs, keep testing up the trunk to find a sensory level. Useful landmarks are L1 at the inguinal ligament, T10 at the umbilicus and T4 at the nipples. A truncal level puts the lesion in the spinal cord and tells you which part of the spine to image.

questions.stem: Katie, 28, has a short, enhancing intramedullary lesion at T7-T8 on MRI. Nothing is compressing the cord. She is afebrile, and her CRP and white cell count are normal. Neurology agree this is an acute demyelinating myelitis. Her sensory level is rising. What is the first-line acute treatment?
options: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days, then taper over 2 weeks
IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg divided over 5 days
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days
IV dexamethasone 10 mg stat, then 4 mg orally 6-hourly
notes: A low-dose oral steroid course is not the standard treatment for an acute, disabling myelitis. High-dose pulsed methylprednisolone is used.
IVIG is not first-line for MS-related myelitis. If steroids fail, the escalation is plasma exchange.
This dexamethasone regimen is used for malignant spinal cord compression, and the MRI has excluded compression.
questions.why: Once compression and infection have been excluded, an acute demyelinating relapse is treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone, 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days, on neurology advice. Monitor her blood glucose while she is on it. Plasma exchange is the next step if she does not respond.

questions.stem: Katie, 28, has an enhancing demyelinating lesion in her thoracic cord. She asks how inflammation can stop her legs working when nothing is pressing on the cord. Her weakness is spastic, with brisk reflexes and no wasting. What best explains her acute weakness?
options: Loss of myelin abolishes saltatory conduction, causing conduction block in tracts
Inflammation destroys anterior horn cells, denervating the leg muscles
Cord swelling occludes the anterior spinal artery, infarcting the cord
Antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
notes: Loss of anterior horn cells gives lower motor neuron signs (flaccidity, wasting, areflexia), not the spasticity and brisk reflexes Katie has.
Anterior spinal artery infarction is sudden, spares the dorsal columns and is not an enhancing demyelinating plaque. Katie's dorsal column loss is the most prominent deficit.
A neuromuscular junction disorder causes fatigable weakness with normal reflexes and no sensory level, sphincter problems or upper motor neuron signs.
questions.why: Myelin lets the action potential jump from node to node (saltatory conduction). In an inflamed, demyelinated segment the current leaks away and conduction slows or fails, which blocks the descending corticospinal signals. Function can return as inflammation settles, sodium channels redistribute along the axon and remyelination occurs.

questions.stem: Katie's right leg is weaker and more spastic than her left, but her pinprick loss is worse on the left. MRI shows an eccentric right dorsolateral lesion at the T7-T8 vertebral level. Which feature of the pain and temperature pathway explains why her pinprick loss is worse on the side opposite the lesion?
options: They ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns and cross in the medulla
They ascend uncrossed in the spinothalamic tract and cross in the thalamus
They cross at the pyramidal decussation alongside the corticospinal fibres
They cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments of entry
notes: Fine touch, vibration and proprioception take this route (dorsal columns, crossing in the medulla). Pain and temperature fibres cross in the cord.
The spinothalamic tract already carries crossed fibres. Crossing happens in the cord, not the thalamus, which is why a cord lesion gives a contralateral deficit.
The pyramidal decussation is a motor crossing for corticospinal fibres. It explains why her weakness is on the same side as the lesion, not why her pinprick loss is opposite.
questions.why: Pain and temperature fibres synapse in the dorsal horn, then cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments and ascend in the contralateral spinothalamic tract. A right-sided cord lesion therefore reduces pinprick on the left, while corticospinal and dorsal column deficits stay on the right.

questions.stem: Peter, 39, has consented to a perianal examination in left lateral with the practice nurse chaperoning. When you gently part his buttocks you see a linear split at 6 o'clock. He flinches, and the anal verge is visibly puckered and tight. You had planned a digital rectal examination. What is the best next step in the station?
options: Proceed with DRE using generous lidocaine gel and a slow single-finger insertion
Stop, defer the DRE, explain why to Peter and document it with a plan to re-examine
Pass a lubricated proctoscope to view the anal canal and exclude a second lesion
Ask Peter to bear down so that the full length of the split can be seen
notes: Even with local anaesthetic gel, a DRE in acute fissure is very painful and adds nothing to a diagnosis already visible on inspection.
Proctoscopy is even more painful than a DRE in acute fissure and isn't needed to make the diagnosis; it can wait for review.
Straining doesn't help show a fissure and is uncomfortable. Bearing down is used to show prolapsing haemorrhoids or rectal prolapse.
questions.why: A visible fissure with sphincter spasm and severe tenderness is enough for the diagnosis. Forcing a DRE or proctoscopy hurts, makes the spasm worse and adds nothing now. Defer it, tell the patient, document it and re-examine once healed or less tender.

questions.stem: Peter, 39, returns to his GP after 2 weeks. He has used psyllium, drinks more water and takes warm sitz baths, and his stools are now soft. Every bowel motion is still painful and the posterior midline fissure has not healed. He takes no other medicines. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
options: Paracetamol with codeine 30 mg, up to four times daily for 2 weeks
Refer now for lateral internal sphincterotomy under general anaesthetic
Glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% ointment applied to the anal canal 12-hourly for up to 8 weeks
Hydrocortisone-containing haemorrhoid ointment applied twice daily until healed
notes: Codeine causes constipation and harder stools, which tears the fissure again. It should be avoided in anal fissure.
Sphincterotomy is kept for chronic fissures where topical treatment (and often botulinum toxin) has failed, because it carries a risk of incontinence.
Corticosteroid haemorrhoid preparations don't relax the internal sphincter or help healing, and long-term use thins the anoderm.
questions.why: When conservative care fails, the next step is to relax the sphincter with a topical agent: GTN 0.2% ointment (or diltiazem 2%) to the anal canal every 12 hours for up to 8 weeks. Warn about headache, and it must not be used with PDE5 inhibitors.

questions.stem: Peter, 39, developed a posterior midline anal fissure after passing a hard stool 4 days ago. Each bowel motion is so painful that he now puts off going to the toilet. Which mechanism best explains why the fissure is failing to heal?
options: Internal sphincter hypertonia raises anal pressure and cuts anodermal blood flow
External sphincter spasm obstructs venous drainage of the internal haemorrhoids
Infection of the anal crypt glands spreads into the intersphincteric space
Coeliac-related mucosal atrophy impairs epithelial turnover in the anal canal
notes: The persistent hypertonia in a fissure is in the internal sphincter (smooth muscle). Venous obstruction is a mechanism for haemorrhoids, not fissures.
Infection of the anal glands is the cryptoglandular mechanism of perianal abscess and fistula, and he has no signs of either.
Coeliac disease affects the small bowel mucosa, not the squamous anoderm of the anal canal, and his disease is controlled on a gluten-free diet.
questions.why: Pain causes spasm of the internal anal sphincter. The spasm raises resting pressure and reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm, which is poorly perfused to start with, so the tear becomes ischaemic. Holding on hardens the stool and tears it again. Treatment relaxes the sphincter and softens the stool.

questions.stem: Peter, 39, has an acute posterior midline anal fissure running from the anal verge into the distal anal canal, below the dentate line. He describes 10/10 sharp, cutting pain with each bowel motion. Which nerves carry this sharp, well-localised pain?
options: Visceral afferents travelling with the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4)
Sympathetic afferents travelling with the inferior hypogastric plexus
Cutaneous branches of the ilioinguinal nerve (L1)
Inferior rectal (anal) branches of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4)
notes: Pelvic splanchnic visceral afferents supply the mucosa above the dentate line and carry only poorly localised, dull sensation.
The inferior hypogastric plexus carries autonomic fibres to the rectum and upper anal canal, not somatic pain from the anoderm.
The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the groin, anterior scrotum and medial thigh, not the anal canal.
questions.why: Below the dentate line the anoderm has somatic innervation from the inferior rectal branches of the pudendal nerve, so lesions there cause sharp, well-localised pain. Above the line the innervation is visceral, which is why internal haemorrhoids are usually painless.

questions.stem: Sam, 20, is seen in a GP clinic after severe breathlessness towards the end of his first 20 km run. He is now well. He has no chest pain, palpitations, dizziness or syncope. Before you move on to the examination, which further question best screens for an inherited cardiac cause such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
options: Does anyone in your family have high cholesterol or take tablets for their heart?
Have you or anyone in your family ever had a clot in the legs or lungs?
Has anyone in your family died suddenly or unexpectedly at a young age?
Did you have asthma, eczema or bad hay fever when you were a child?
notes: High cholesterol is a risk factor for coronary disease later in life (Sam's dad takes a statin). It does not screen for the inherited cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias that cause exertional events in young athletes.
This screens for venous thromboembolism, which is a separate dangerous differential, not for inherited heart disease.
This screens for atopy and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, which is a respiratory differential, not an inherited cardiac cause.
questions.why: Sudden unexplained death in a young relative is the key family history red flag for an inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy (for example HCM or long QT) in a young athlete with exertional symptoms. If present, he needs an ECG and cardiology review before he trains hard again.

questions.stem: Sam, 20, returns to the GP 3 weeks later. He now gets cough and chest tightness for 10 to 15 minutes after most of his training runs, and it is spring. His resting spirometry last visit was normal, with no significant bronchodilator response. You suspect exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Give salbutamol 200 micrograms via spacer 15 minutes before each run and review
Refer for a bronchial provocation test such as a mannitol or exercise challenge
Start budesonide-formoterol 200/6 micrograms, one inhalation as needed
Repeat resting spirometry with bronchodilator response in 4 weeks
notes: This is treatment on suspicion, not confirmation. A symptomatic response to a reliever is non-specific, and the diagnosis would stay unproven.
This is a treatment, not a diagnostic test. Guidelines advise confirming variable airflow limitation objectively before labelling him with asthma.
Resting spirometry is often normal in EIB because the bronchoconstriction is triggered by exercise. Repeating it is unlikely to show anything and delays the diagnosis.
questions.why: Normal resting spirometry does not exclude EIB. The diagnosis is confirmed with an indirect bronchial provocation test (mannitol, exercise or eucapnic voluntary hyperpnoea challenge) before committing him to inhaler treatment.

questions.stem: Sam, 20, a runner with spring hay fever, is referred for a mannitol challenge to look for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Inhaled dry-powder mannitol is used because it mimics the main trigger of bronchoconstriction during exercise. What is that mechanism?
options: Direct stimulation of muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle
IgE-mediated mast cell reaction to pollen inhaled during the run
Diaphragm fatigue reducing tidal volume at high minute ventilation
Airway water loss makes lining fluid hyperosmolar, releasing mast cell mediators
notes: This is how methacholine works, as a direct challenge. Mannitol and exercise are indirect stimuli that act through mediator release.
Allergen exposure can worsen airway inflammation in atopic people, but the trigger in EIB is the osmotic effect of hyperventilation, not an allergen.
Respiratory muscle fatigue does not cause bronchoconstriction, and mannitol has no effect on the diaphragm.
questions.why: Breathing large volumes of relatively dry air during exercise evaporates water from the airway surface. The lining fluid becomes hyperosmolar, and mast cells release leukotrienes, histamine and prostaglandins, which cause bronchoconstriction. Mannitol reproduces this osmotic stimulus.

questions.stem: Sam, 20, is tall and slim and became acutely breathless while running. The GP requests an erect PA chest X-ray to exclude a primary spontaneous pneumothorax, and the radiologist specifically comments that lung markings reach the chest wall at the apices. Where are the subpleural blebs that usually rupture to cause this condition typically located?
options: Apices of the upper lobes
Bases of the lower lobes
Lingula of the left upper lobe
Right middle lobe near the horizontal fissure
notes: The bases are not the usual site of blebs. Air in an erect patient also rises to the apex, so a basal pneumothorax is mainly seen on supine films (the deep sulcus sign).
The lingula is not the typical site of blebs in primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
The middle lobe is not the typical site, and the horizontal fissure is not a site of predilection for blebs.
questions.why: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax usually comes from rupture of subpleural blebs at the lung apices. Tall, thin young men are thought to have greater mechanical stress at the apex. On an erect film, air also collects at the apex, so that is where a small pneumothorax is looked for first.

questions.stem: You are examining the hands of Ms Little, a 35-year-old hairdresser, with her hands resting on a pillow in the rheumatology clinic. Her knuckles look puffy and she says they are tender. Which manoeuvre is the quickest screen for synovitis across all of her MCP joints at once?
options: Phalen's test: hold both wrists in full flexion for 60 seconds
Prayer sign: press the palms together with the wrists extended
Gently squeeze the 2nd to 5th MCP joints together from the sides
Finkelstein's test: ulnar deviate the wrist with the thumb in a fist
notes: Phalen's test checks for median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel. It does not test for MCP synovitis.
The prayer sign looks at wrist extension and flexor tendon or joint restriction, not at the MCP joints.
Finkelstein's test is for de Quervain's tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment, not for MCP synovitis.
questions.why: The MCP squeeze test is gentle sideways compression across the 2nd to 5th metacarpal heads. Pain on squeezing suggests MCP synovitis and is a useful early sign of RA, often present before any deformity. Ask about pain first and watch her face while you squeeze.

questions.stem: The consultant agrees that Ms Little, 35, has seropositive, erosive RA and wants to start methotrexate. Her GP bloods include FBC, UEC, LFT, CRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP and ANA. Along with a chest X-ray and a pregnancy test, which further test is needed before her first dose?
options: Hepatitis B and C serology
HLA-B27
Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies
Serum urate
notes: HLA-B27 helps when axial spondyloarthritis is suspected. It does not change the methotrexate work-up, and she has no back pain.
Her ANA is negative and nothing suggests SLE, so anti-dsDNA adds nothing before starting methotrexate.
Serum urate is for suspected gout. She has symmetrical RA with no tophi or acute monoarthritis, and urate is not a methotrexate pre-treatment test.
questions.why: Before starting methotrexate (or any DMARD), check hepatitis B and C serology, because immunosuppression can reactivate hepatitis B and methotrexate is hepatotoxic. A chest X-ray, a pregnancy test and baseline FBC, UEC and LFT are also needed.

questions.stem: Ms Little, 35, has 3 months of active RA. Her Hb is 112 g/L with an MCV of 84 fL, platelets are 432 × 10^9/L and CRP is 24 mg/L. Her eGFR is above 90 and her LFTs are normal. Which mechanism best explains her anaemia?
options: Warm IgG autoantibodies causing extravascular haemolysis
Low renal erythropoietin production from interstitial nephritis
Vitamin B12 malabsorption from autoimmune gastritis
IL-6 raises hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin and traps iron in stores
notes: Autoimmune haemolysis is more a feature of SLE than RA. She has a negative ANA and no evidence of haemolysis.
Her eGFR is above 90 with normal electrolytes, so a lack of erythropoietin from kidney disease does not fit.
Pernicious anaemia causes a macrocytic anaemia, but her MCV is a normal 84 fL.
questions.why: This is anaemia of chronic disease. Inflammatory IL-6 makes the liver produce more hepcidin, which breaks down ferroportin, so iron stays locked in macrophages and enterocytes and red cell production slows. The result is a mild normocytic anaemia that tracks with disease activity.

questions.stem: Ms Little, 35, has active wrist synovitis from RA and asks why you tested for carpal tunnel syndrome. If flexor tenosynovitis compressed her median nerve within the carpal tunnel, which sensory pattern would you expect?
options: Palmar thumb, index, middle and radial half of ring finger, plus the thenar skin
Palmar thumb, index, middle and radial half of ring finger, sparing the thenar skin
Little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger, front and back
Dorsum of the first web space between the thumb and index finger
notes: Loss of feeling over the thenar skin points to a median nerve lesion above the wrist, because the palmar cutaneous branch runs outside the carpal tunnel.
This is ulnar nerve territory (compression at Guyon's canal or the elbow), not the median nerve.
The dorsum of the first web space is supplied by the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
questions.why: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves the nerve above the flexor retinaculum and runs superficial to it, so the skin over the thenar eminence keeps its feeling in carpal tunnel syndrome. Sensory loss affects the palmar thumb, index finger, middle finger and radial half of the ring finger.

questions.stem: You are examining Josh, 23, in a GP clinic. He has jaundice from acute hepatitis and you want to check for the hepatic flap (asterixis), a sign of encephalopathy and possible acute liver failure. How should you elicit it?
options: Ask him to squeeze two of your fingers firmly in each hand for 10 seconds
Ask him to hold his arms out, palms up and eyes closed, for 20 seconds
Ask him to hold his arms out, wrists cocked back and fingers spread, for 15 seconds
Ask him to touch your finger, then his nose, repeatedly with each hand
notes: A sustained grip that waxes and wanes (milkmaid grip) is a sign of chorea, not hepatic encephalopathy.
Holding the arms out with palms up and eyes closed tests for pronator drift, a sign of an upper motor neuron lesion.
Finger-nose testing looks for cerebellar signs (dysmetria and intention tremor), not the flap of metabolic encephalopathy.
questions.why: Asterixis is a failure to hold a posture. With the arms outstretched, wrists dorsiflexed and fingers spread for about 15 seconds, it shows as irregular flapping. Finding it would mean encephalopathy, which needs hospital assessment for acute liver failure.

questions.stem: Josh, 23, has confirmed acute hepatitis A. His jaundice began 2 days ago. He shares a kitchen and bathroom with three healthy housemates aged 22 to 24. None has liver disease or immunosuppression, and none has been vaccinated against hepatitis A. What should the housemates be offered?
options: One dose of hepatitis A vaccine as soon as possible, ideally within 2 weeks of exposure
Normal human immunoglobulin intramuscularly as soon as possible, instead of vaccine
Two vaccine doses a month apart, started once serology shows they are non-immune
No prophylaxis: advise hand hygiene and review only if they develop symptoms
notes: Normal human immunoglobulin is for contacts under 12 months old, immunocompromised contacts or those with chronic liver disease; healthy young adults get the vaccine.
Waiting for serology delays prophylaxis past its 2-week window, and the second dose of hepatitis A vaccine is given 6 to 12 months later, not after a month.
Household contacts sharing a kitchen and bathroom are at real risk, and vaccine given within 2 weeks can prevent infection, so they should be offered it.
questions.why: Under the Australian Immunisation Handbook, healthy household and sexual contacts aged 12 months or more get hepatitis A vaccine as post-exposure prophylaxis, ideally within 2 weeks of exposure. Normal human immunoglobulin is kept for infants under 12 months, people who are immunocompromised and people with chronic liver disease.

questions.stem: Josh, 23, has acute hepatitis A. He is well, with an ALT of 1,240 U/L, an INR of 1.1 and an albumin of 41 g/L. Your GP supervisor says the INR is a better guide than the albumin to how well his liver is coping right now. What best explains this?
options: Albumin is lost in the urine during acute hepatitis, so its level is unreliable
The INR mainly reflects vitamin K absorption, which falls early in any jaundice
Prothrombin is made only by hepatocytes, while albumin is also made in muscle
Factor VII has a half-life of about 6 hours, while albumin's is about 3 weeks
notes: Albumin is not lost in the urine in acute hepatitis; urinary loss suggests nephrotic syndrome.
Poor vitamin K absorption matters mainly in long-standing cholestasis with pale stools. Josh's normal INR reflects hepatocyte synthesis, not vitamin K uptake.
Albumin is made only in the liver, not in muscle, so this does not explain why the INR changes sooner.
questions.why: The INR depends on liver-made clotting factors, especially factor VII, whose half-life is only a few hours, so it rises within a day or two of synthetic failure. Albumin lasts about 3 weeks, so it stays normal early in acute liver failure and better reflects chronic disease.

questions.stem: Josh, 23, has jaundice and a dull right upper quadrant ache. To look for cholecystitis you test for Murphy's sign, placing your fingers over the surface marking of the gallbladder fundus as he breathes in. Where is this?
options: Right mid-clavicular line, level with the umbilicus
Tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, at the lateral border of rectus abdominis
Right 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, above the costal margin
Midline just below the xiphisternum, over the epigastrium
notes: The umbilical level in the right mid-clavicular line is well below the gallbladder; palpating here is how you begin feeling for an enlarged liver edge.
The right 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line is about where the upper border of liver dullness lies, not the gallbladder.
The epigastrium overlies the stomach, the left lobe of the liver and the pancreas, not the gallbladder fundus.
questions.why: The gallbladder fundus lies at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the lateral border of rectus abdominis meets the costal margin (near the transpyloric plane). An inflamed gallbladder meets the examining fingers on inspiration, so the breath catches.

questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, a 63-year-old electrician seen in general practice, has 6 weeks of right neck pain spreading to his lateral forearm and thumb, with tingling in his thumb and index finger. Before testing power, you want a provocation test that supports compression of a right cervical nerve root in its foramen. Which manoeuvre should you perform?
options: Flex the neck fully forward and ask about electric shocks down the spine or into the limbs
Hold both wrists fully flexed for 60 seconds and ask about tingling in the hand
Extend the neck, rotate and side-bend it to the right, then press gently down on the head
Flex the shoulder to 90 degrees, internally rotate it and ask about pain at the shoulder
notes: This is Lhermitte's sign, which suggests disease of the cord (myelopathy or demyelination) rather than compression of a nerve root in its foramen.
This is Phalen's test for carpal tunnel syndrome. It does not explain neck pain, pain radiating from the shoulder or weakness above the wrist.
This is the Hawkins-Kennedy test for subacromial impingement, a shoulder problem. It does not stress the cervical foramen.
questions.why: This is Spurling's test. Extending, rotating and side-bending the neck towards the painful side narrows that foramen, and adding axial load reproduces the radicular pain down the arm. It is specific for cervical radiculopathy. Avoid it if there has been trauma or the neck may be unstable.

questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, 63, comes back to his GP 10 days later. His right shoulder abduction and elbow flexion are 4/5 and stable, his right biceps reflex is reduced, and he has no upper motor neuron signs. MRI shows right C4-5 and C5-6 foraminal stenosis with a normal cord. His pain is 4/10 on paracetamol. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Analgesia, physiotherapy, modified duties and a non-urgent spinal surgical referral
Same-day transfer to the emergency department for urgent decompressive surgery
Analgesia and physiotherapy only, reviewing if the pain lasts beyond 6 months
Regular slow-release oxycodone, strict bed rest and a soft cervical collar
notes: He has no myelopathy, his cord is normal and his weakness is stable. Emergency decompression is for cord compression or rapidly progressive weakness.
A persisting motor deficit with concordant root compression on MRI warrants specialist input. A plan that only reviews pain misses the weakness.
Opioids are not recommended for routine use in radiculopathy, and bed rest and collars delay recovery. He should stay active.
questions.why: Most cervical radiculopathy settles with conservative care. Even so, an objective motor deficit with a concordant MRI warrants routine referral to a spinal surgeon. Progressive weakness or signs of myelopathy would make the referral urgent.

questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, 63, finds that his right arm pain eases when he rests his right hand on top of his head. His MRI shows right C5-6 foraminal stenosis compressing the right C6 nerve root, with a normal spinal cord. What best explains why this posture relieves his pain?
options: It relaxes the supraspinatus, easing impingement of its tendon under the acromion
Elevating the arm widens the costoclavicular space around the brachial plexus
Raising the arm flexes the neck, which widens the canal around the spinal cord
Shoulder abduction slackens the plexus and lowers tension on the compressed root
notes: Raising the arm overhead makes subacromial impingement worse, not better. His pain also runs below the elbow to the thumb, which a rotator cuff problem would not explain.
Raising the arm narrows the costoclavicular space. That is why arm elevation brings on thoracic outlet symptoms rather than relieving them.
Resting the hand on the head does not meaningfully flex the neck. His cord is also normal, so canal space is not the cause of his pain.
questions.why: This is the shoulder abduction relief sign. Raising the arm shortens the path from the foramen to the limb, which reduces traction and tension on the compressed nerve root and so eases radicular pain. It points to radiculopathy rather than a shoulder problem.

questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, 63, has an MRI of his cervical spine for right arm radicular pain. It reports severe narrowing of the right intervertebral foramen at C5-6, between the C5 and C6 vertebrae. Which nerve root leaves the spinal canal through this foramen?
options: C5 root, since cervical roots exit below the pedicle of their numbered vertebra
C6 root, since cervical roots exit above the pedicle of their numbered vertebra
C7 root, since the root passes the disc and exits at the foramen one level down
C4 root, since roots exit one level above the cord segment they arise from
notes: Exiting below the numbered vertebra is the thoracic and lumbar pattern. The C5 root exits at C4-5, which is where his moderate stenosis is.
A root that passes the disc and exits a level lower is how a lumbar disc affects the traversing root. A foraminal lesion in the neck compresses the root that exits at that level.
Roots are named for the foramen they exit through, not for a mismatch with cord segments. The C4 root exits at C3-4.
questions.why: There are 8 cervical roots but only 7 cervical vertebrae. Each cervical root exits above the vertebra of the same number, so the C6 root leaves at C5-6 and C8 leaves at C7-T1. From T1 downwards, roots exit below their vertebra.

questions.stem: Jane, 62, sees you at the GP with 5 to 6 months of new constipation, straining, blood mixed through her stool and tiredness. Her brother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 48. She says, "I was hoping to get one of those bowel test kits." What is the best response?
options: Give her the kit today and refer for colonoscopy only if the result is positive
Say it is likely her haemorrhoids again and give the kit for peace of mind
Explain the kit is for people without symptoms and she needs a colonoscopy
Give her the kit and suggest she repeats it in two years if it is negative
notes: Waiting for an FOBT result delays a colonoscopy she needs now, and a false negative could stop the referral altogether.
Blood mixed through the stool and a change in habit are not explained by haemorrhoids, and an FOBT does not suit a patient with symptoms.
This applies the screening interval to a patient with symptoms; she needs a diagnostic test now, not routine screening.
questions.why: An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms. A patient with symptoms (change in habit, blood mixed in the stool) needs a diagnostic colonoscopy, because a negative FOBT does not rule out cancer and would falsely reassure her.

questions.stem: Jane's bloods show Hb 108 g/L, MCV 76 fL and ferritin 8 µg/L. TSH, calcium and kidney function are normal. You are referring her for an urgent colonoscopy. Which further investigation should also be arranged for her iron deficiency anaemia?
options: Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies, together with coeliac serology
Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level to screen for cancer
CT colonography to image the whole colon as well
Faecal calprotectin to look for bowel inflammation
notes: CEA is too insensitive and nonspecific to diagnose cancer; it is used for staging and follow-up once cancer is confirmed.
CT colonography repeats the colonoscopy, cannot take biopsies and does not look at the upper GI tract.
Calprotectin helps tell IBD from IBS in diarrhoea; it does not look for an upper GI source of iron loss.
questions.why: Iron deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman needs both ends of the gut looked at: colonoscopy plus gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies, and coeliac serology. This finds upper GI cancer, peptic ulcer or coeliac disease, and two lesions can occur together.

questions.stem: Jane, 62, with iron deficiency anaemia (ferritin 8 µg/L), is started on oral ferrous sulfate while she waits for endoscopy. She is advised to take it on alternate days rather than twice daily. What is the main reason alternate-day dosing can improve absorption?
options: Daily iron fully saturates transferrin, so the extra iron is excreted in bile
Iron is absorbed in the terminal ileum, which needs 48 hours between doses
Daily dosing suppresses erythropoietin, so less iron is taken up by marrow
Each dose raises hepcidin for about a day, blocking ferroportin in enterocytes
notes: Her transferrin saturation is 5%, far from saturated, and the body has no regulated way to excrete excess iron in bile.
Non-haem iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not the terminal ileum.
Oral iron does not suppress erythropoietin; the limit on the dose schedule is gut absorption, not uptake by the marrow.
questions.why: An oral iron dose raises hepcidin for about 24 hours. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, the channel that moves iron out of duodenal enterocytes, so a dose taken the next day is poorly absorbed. Spacing doses avoids this and causes fewer GI side effects.

questions.stem: Jane's colonoscopy shows a tumour at the rectosigmoid junction, above the dentate line. Biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma, and the surgeon plans a resection with its regional lymph nodes. To which lymph nodes does this tumour first drain?
options: Superficial inguinal nodes in the femoral triangle
Nodes along the superior rectal vessels to the inferior mesenteric nodes
Internal iliac nodes along the middle rectal vessels
Superior mesenteric nodes at the root of the small bowel mesentery
notes: Superficial inguinal nodes drain the anal canal below the dentate line, not a tumour at the rectosigmoid.
Drainage to the internal iliac nodes along the middle rectal vessels is mainly from the lower rectum, not the rectosigmoid junction.
Superior mesenteric nodes drain the midgut up to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, not the hindgut.
questions.why: Lymph from the sigmoid and upper rectum drains alongside the superior rectal and inferior mesenteric vessels to the inferior mesenteric nodes. This is why the resection includes a high tie of the inferior mesenteric artery with its mesentery.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has 3 months of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation, with a resting heart rate of 56. In the examination you tell the examiner you will look for the reflex sign of hypothyroidism. Which technique best shows it?
options: Knee jerk with Jendrassik reinforcement, looking for a brisk, wide-amplitude response
Plantar response with a blunt stimulus, looking for an upgoing great toe
Ankle jerk with her kneeling on a chair, watching for a slow relaxation phase
Biceps jerk with her arm relaxed, looking for spread to finger flexion
notes: Brisk, wide-amplitude reflexes suggest hyperthyroidism or an upper motor neurone lesion, and reinforcement only helps when a reflex is hard to get.
An upgoing plantar is an upper motor neurone sign and plays no part in hypothyroidism.
Spread of a reflex to nearby muscles is an upper motor neurone sign; it does not show the delayed relaxation seen in hypothyroidism.
questions.why: Hypothyroidism slows the relaxation phase of the reflex (it is 'hung up'), not the contraction. The ankle jerk with the patient kneeling on a chair, feet hanging free, shows this best.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, of average build with no heart disease, has TSH 52 mIU/L, free T4 4.3 pmol/L and strongly positive anti-TPO antibodies. Her sodium and potassium are normal, and she has no pigmentation, postural drop or hypos. Which treatment plan is best?
options: Levothyroxine about 100 micrograms daily before breakfast; recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks
Levothyroxine 25 micrograms daily, increasing by 25 micrograms monthly on free T4 alone
Liothyronine 20 micrograms twice daily; recheck free T3 and TSH in 2 weeks
Levothyroxine about 100 micrograms daily with breakfast; recheck TSH in 2 weeks
notes: Starting low and titrating slowly is for older patients or those with ischaemic heart disease; here it just delays recovery, and TSH, not free T4 alone, guides the dose.
Liothyronine is not first-line replacement: its short half-life gives swings in T3, and levothyroxine is the standard treatment.
Food reduces levothyroxine absorption, and TSH has not reached steady state at 2 weeks, so the result would mislead dosing.
questions.why: A young patient without heart disease can start the full replacement dose of levothyroxine, about 1.6 micrograms/kg (around 100 micrograms), on an empty stomach. TSH takes about 6 weeks to settle, so check it 6 to 8 weeks after each dose change.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has Hashimoto thyroiditis and an anaemia with Hb 104 g/L and MCV 118 fL. Her B12 and folate results are pending. A colleague suggests starting folic acid now to save time. Why is giving folic acid alone risky if she turns out to be B12 deficient?
options: It corrects the anaemia while B12-dependent nerve damage keeps progressing
It competes with B12 for uptake in the terminal ileum, worsening the deficiency
It drives such rapid red cell production that it causes severe hypokalaemia
It stimulates parietal cell autoantibodies and speeds up the atrophic gastritis
notes: Folate is absorbed in the proximal small bowel by a different mechanism, and it does not block uptake of the B12-intrinsic factor complex.
Hypokalaemia can occur when severe megaloblastic anaemia is treated, but it is not why folate alone is avoided. The worry is irreversible nerve damage.
Folic acid has no effect on the autoimmune process in pernicious anaemia.
questions.why: Folate can bypass the methylfolate trap and restore DNA synthesis, so the blood count improves. It cannot replace B12's role with methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in making myelin, so subacute combined degeneration progresses without being noticed.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto thyroiditis and a macrocytic anaemia (MCV 118 fL). Pernicious anaemia is suspected. In this condition, autoimmune gastritis destroys the cells that make intrinsic factor. Which part of the gut is mainly affected?
options: Gastric antrum, where the gastrin-secreting G cells lie
Proximal duodenum, where B12 is transferred onto intrinsic factor
Terminal ileum, where the B12-intrinsic factor complex is absorbed
Gastric body and fundus, where the parietal cells lie
notes: The antrum is typically spared in autoimmune gastritis. Its G cells overproduce gastrin in response to the low acid.
B12 does bind intrinsic factor in the duodenum, but the intrinsic factor is made in the stomach. The duodenum is not the autoimmune target.
The terminal ileum is where B12 is absorbed, and it is affected in Crohn disease or resection. It is not the site of the lesion in pernicious anaemia.
questions.why: Parietal cells, which secrete acid and intrinsic factor, sit in the oxyntic mucosa of the gastric body and fundus. Autoimmune gastritis attacks this area and spares the antrum, so gastrin rises as acid output falls.

questions.stem: Abdul, 30, is in your GP room mid-attack with 10/10 strictly left orbital pain for 2 hours, rocking in his chair. His history fits cluster headache. You now tell the examiner what you are examining. Which examination step is most likely to show a sign that supports this diagnosis?
options: Fundoscopy of both eyes looking for papilloedema
Palpation of both temporal arteries for tenderness and pulse
Comparing pupil size and eyelid height on both sides in dim light
Passive neck flexion looking for meningism
notes: Fundoscopy is an essential red-flag screen for raised intracranial pressure, but here it is expected to be normal and does not support cluster headache.
Temporal artery palpation screens for giant cell arteritis, which is very unlikely at 30 and would not support cluster headache.
Checking for meningism screens for subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis. It is expected to be negative and gives no positive support for cluster headache.
questions.why: During an attack many patients have a partial Horner's on the side of the pain (miosis and mild ptosis), so compare the two pupils and lids. The difference shows best in dim light, because the small pupil fails to dilate.

questions.stem: Abdul, 30, has episodic cluster headache with a normal ECG and normal MRI brain. He comes to the GP clinic 15 minutes into a typical left orbital attack and wants relief now. Which acute treatment is most appropriate?
options: Oxygen 2 L/min via nasal prongs for 15 minutes
Oral sumatriptan 50 mg, repeated after 2 hours if needed
100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask for 15 minutes
Oral ibuprofen 400 mg with paracetamol 1 g
notes: Low-flow oxygen through nasal prongs doesn't deliver a high enough concentration to abort a cluster attack.
Oral triptans are absorbed too slowly to help a cluster attack. The subcutaneous (6 mg) or intranasal route is needed.
Simple oral analgesics don't work for cluster attacks, and Abdul has already found paracetamol useless.
questions.why: High-flow 100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min through a non-rebreather for 15 minutes aborts many cluster attacks. Subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg is the other first-line option. Oral drugs act too slowly for attacks that peak quickly.

questions.stem: During his attacks, Abdul, 30, has a watering red left eye and a runny, blocked left nostril, on the same side as his left orbital pain. What mechanism best explains these features?
options: Trigeminal-autonomic reflex driving parasympathetic outflow via the facial nerve
Sympathetic overactivity from the superior cervical ganglion on the left side
Passive fluid leak from venous congestion of the left cavernous sinus
Mast cell histamine release in the left nasal and conjunctival mucosa
notes: Tearing and nasal secretion are parasympathetic functions. In cluster headache the sympathetic supply is actually underactive, which is why a partial Horner's syndrome appears.
Venous congestion of the cavernous sinus doesn't explain active glandular secretion, and Abdul's MRI showed normal cavernous sinuses.
Histamine release from mast cells is the mechanism of allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. It doesn't explain strictly one-sided features tied to a pain attack.
questions.why: Pain input from the trigeminal nerve activates the superior salivatory nucleus. Parasympathetic fibres then travel via the facial nerve (greater petrosal nerve) and pterygopalatine ganglion to the lacrimal gland and nasal mucosa, causing tearing, redness and rhinorrhoea on the same side.

questions.stem: During an attack, Abdul, 30, has mild drooping of his left upper eyelid and a small left pupil. Both resolve once the attack settles. This is a partial Horner's syndrome. Loss of sympathetic supply to which muscle causes the mild ptosis?
options: Levator palpebrae superioris
Orbicularis oculi
Inferior tarsal muscle
Superior tarsal muscle
notes: The levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the oculomotor nerve. Paralysis of it causes marked or complete ptosis, not the mild droop of Horner's.
The orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids and is supplied by the facial nerve. Weakness of it causes incomplete eye closure, not ptosis.
The inferior tarsal muscle helps hold down the lower lid. Losing its supply slightly raises the lower lid, so it doesn't cause the upper lid droop.
questions.why: The superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle is smooth muscle with a sympathetic supply. It adds a few millimetres of upper lid elevation, so sympathetic loss gives only mild ptosis. Complete ptosis points to the levator and the oculomotor nerve.

questions.stem: Peter, 42, has 2 days of painless bright red blood on the toilet paper. Partway through your history he asks: "Could this be bowel cancer? My dad died of cancer." You have established that his father died of testicular cancer at 56 and that no one in the family has had bowel cancer or polyps. What is the best response?
options: Reassure him it is almost certainly haemorrhoids, so no further tests will be needed
Tell him his father's cancer puts him at high risk, so he needs urgent screening
Acknowledge his worry, say his dad's cancer doesn't raise his risk, and explain the checks
Offer a home iFOBT kit today so he knows quickly whether a cancer is present
notes: This is false reassurance: haemorrhoids found on proctoscopy don't clear the bowel above, and an adult with new rectal bleeding should still have a colonoscopy.
Testicular cancer is not linked to colorectal cancer risk, so this is wrong and needlessly alarming.
The iFOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms; he already has visible bleeding, and a negative result would not exclude cancer.
questions.why: Address the worry honestly: testicular cancer in a father does not raise his colorectal cancer risk. But new rectal bleeding still needs examination and colonoscopy, so explain the plan instead of offering blanket reassurance.

questions.stem: Peter, 42, has had about 4 days of painless bright red blood on the paper. Proctoscopy shows grade I internal haemorrhoids with fresh blood at 3 o'clock and normal lower rectal mucosa. Hb 151 g/L, ferritin 142 µg/L, CRP 2 mg/L. No change in bowel habit, no weight loss and no family history of bowel cancer. Alongside fibre, fluids and psyllium, what investigation should the GP arrange?
options: Colonoscopy referral to gastroenterology or colorectal surgery
iFOBT now, with colonoscopy referral only if it is positive
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for a colonic mass
No further tests unless bleeding persists after 6 months of fibre
notes: An iFOBT is for screening people without symptoms; with visible bleeding a positive result is expected and a negative one does not exclude a lesion.
CT is not the first-line test for the colonic mucosa; it can miss polyps and small cancers, and it cannot take a biopsy.
Waiting months before investigating new rectal bleeding risks delaying the diagnosis of a polyp or cancer above the reach of the proctoscope.
questions.why: A proctoscope sees only the anal canal and lower rectum, and finding haemorrhoids does not prove they are the only cause. Adults with new rectal bleeding, including those under 50, should be referred for colonoscopy.

questions.stem: Peter, 42, has had intermittent constipation for years and eats a low-fibre diet at work. Proctoscopy shows congested internal vascular cushions at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock that bleed but do not prolapse on straining. Which mechanism best explains how his haemorrhoids developed?
options: Portal hypertension opening portosystemic anastomoses in the anal canal
A tear in the anoderm from hard stool, with internal sphincter spasm
Obstruction and infection of anal glands in the intersphincteric space
Straining and hard stool engorging the cushions and stretching their supports
notes: Portal hypertension causes anorectal varices, a different condition, and Peter has no features of liver disease.
This is the mechanism of an anal fissure, which is painful and was not seen on proctoscopy.
This is how a perianal abscess and fistula form, which cause pain, swelling or discharge, not painless bleeding.
questions.why: Haemorrhoids are normal anal vascular cushions. Straining and hard stool slow venous outflow, engorge the cushions and push them down, which weakens the supporting connective tissue. The congested cushions then bleed and, in later grades, prolapse.

questions.stem: Peter's proctoscopy shows bleeding internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line, and his bleeding is painless. By contrast, an anal fissure or thrombosed external haemorrhoid below the dentate line is very painful. Which nerve carries pain sensation from the anal canal below the dentate line?
options: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4 parasympathetic)
Inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve)
Inferior hypogastric plexus (sympathetic fibres)
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1 to L2)
notes: Pelvic splanchnic nerves give visceral (autonomic) supply above the dentate line, where sharp somatic pain is not felt.
Sympathetic fibres from the inferior hypogastric plexus supply the rectum and upper anal canal, not the somatically sensitive anoderm.
The genitofemoral nerve supplies the scrotum and upper anterior thigh, not the anal canal.
questions.why: Below the dentate line the anoderm has somatic innervation from the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4), so lesions there hurt. Above it, the supply is visceral and autonomic and does not sense somatic pain, which is why internal haemorrhoids are painless.

questions.stem: Evelyn, 16, tells you in the ED, "I just can't stop throwing up. I think I've got gastro." She is breathing deeply and quickly but is alert. You have a few minutes of focused history. Which question is most likely to uncover the underlying diagnosis?
options: Have you had any diarrhoea, and has anyone at home been sick?
Is the pain worse if I press on the lower right side of your tummy?
Have you been thirstier, or weeing more often, over the last few weeks?
Have you had any headache, or any trouble with your vision?
notes: Worth asking to test her gastro theory, but a negative answer only makes gastro less likely. It does not point to the actual cause.
Screens for appendicitis, which doesn't fit her mild generalised soreness and wouldn't explain the deep, fast breathing.
Screens for raised intracranial pressure as a cause of vomiting, but it doesn't target the osmotic symptoms that point to DKA.
