questions.why: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis with a predilection for the coronary arteries, causing dilatation and aneurysm.

questions.stem: A pleural fluid sample has fluid:serum protein ratio 0.3, fluid:serum LDH ratio 0.4, and fluid LDH below two-thirds of the upper limit of the serum normal. In a patient with ankle oedema, which is the likely cause?
options: Congestive cardiac failure
Parapneumonic effusion
Pulmonary malignancy
Pulmonary embolism
notes: Parapneumonic effusions are exudates and meet Light's criteria.
Malignant effusions are typically exudates.
PE usually causes an exudate, occasionally a transudate, and is a less likely cause here.
questions.why: Light's criteria are not met (protein ratio <0.5, LDH ratio <0.6, fluid LDH <2/3 upper serum limit), so this is a transudate. Cardiac failure is the commonest cause.

questions.stem: A healthy 5-month-old with no eczema is to start solids. According to ASCIA guidance, what is the best advice about introducing peanut and egg?
options: Introduce them around 6 months, but not before 4 months, as part of the diet
Delay peanut until 12 months of age
Delay egg until 2 years of age
Introduce only after skin prick testing
notes: Delaying peanut increases allergy risk and is not recommended.
Delaying egg is not recommended and may increase risk of egg allergy.
Routine testing is not required in low-risk infants; it is only considered for high-risk infants.
questions.why: ASCIA advises introducing allergenic foods (peanut butter paste, well-cooked egg) in the first year, when the infant is ready at about 6 months and not before 4 months. Delay does not prevent allergy.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has a hot swollen knee, fever 38.8°C and refuses to weight-bear. What is the most important next step?
options: Joint aspiration for microscopy and culture before antibiotics
Oral anti-inflammatories and review in 48 hours
Knee MRI before any intervention
Start oral antibiotics and discharge
notes: Delay risks cartilage destruction.
MRI delays definitive diagnosis and drainage.
Oral outpatient treatment is inappropriate before diagnosis and drainage.
questions.why: Suspected septic arthritis needs urgent joint aspiration or washout for Gram stain and culture, then IV antibiotics. Do not delay for imaging.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with methamphetamine intoxication is agitated, sweaty and paranoid, HR 128, temp 37.8°C. Verbal de-escalation in a quiet room has failed. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral or parenteral benzodiazepine, such as diazepam or midazolam
Intramuscular naloxone
Intravenous propranolol to control tachycardia
Intravenous thiamine and glucose
notes: Naloxone reverses opioids, which are not implicated here.
Beta-blockers risk unopposed alpha stimulation and are avoided.
Thiamine and glucose are not indicated without alcohol-related or hypoglycaemic features.
questions.why: After failed de-escalation, benzodiazepines are first-line for stimulant agitation, treating agitation, tachycardia and hypertension. Antipsychotics are second-line.

questions.stem: Which mechanism of adrenaline is most important for reversing upper airway oedema and hypotension in anaphylaxis?
options: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction reducing mucosal oedema and raising vascular tone
Beta-2 mediated inhibition of IgE production
Muscarinic blockade reducing bronchial secretions
Direct inhibition of histamine synthesis
notes: Adrenaline does not reduce IgE production.
Adrenaline is not antimuscarinic.
It does not inhibit histamine synthesis; it opposes its effects physiologically.
questions.why: Alpha-1 agonism causes vasoconstriction, raising blood pressure and reducing mucosal oedema; beta-1 raises output and beta-2 causes bronchodilation and limits mediator release.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old returns from Bali with 5 days of fever, severe myalgia and retro-orbital pain. Platelets are 60 ×10⁹/L, haematocrit rising, and she has abdominal pain and persistent vomiting. Which is the best next step?
options: Admit for fluid monitoring as warning signs of severe dengue are present
Prescribe ibuprofen and discharge
Start empirical ceftriaxone for typhoid and discharge
Give prophylactic platelet transfusion
notes: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk and are avoided in dengue.
Ceftriaxone does not address the likely dengue and she needs admission.
Prophylactic platelets are not recommended without significant bleeding.
questions.why: Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting and rising haematocrit with falling platelets are dengue warning signs; admit for monitored fluids around defervescence. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with heart failure takes perindopril and frusemide. He starts regular ibuprofen for knee pain and develops gastroenteritis. Creatinine rises from 100 to 220 micromol/L. Which prescribing combination is described by the 'triple whammy'?
options: ACE inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID
Beta-blocker, diuretic and NSAID
ACE inhibitor, statin and NSAID
Digoxin, diuretic and ACE inhibitor
notes: Beta-blockers are not part of the triple whammy.
Statins are not involved in the renal haemodynamic mechanism.
Digoxin is not part of the triple whammy, though it accumulates in AKI.
questions.why: An ACEi or ARB, a diuretic and an NSAID together, especially with volume depletion, markedly increase the risk of acute kidney injury. Withhold them during dehydrating illness.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains hepatic steatosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)?
options: Insulin resistance increasing adipose lipolysis and hepatic de novo lipogenesis
Increased hepatic beta-oxidation exceeding triglyceride supply
Excess VLDL export from hepatocytes
Impaired hepatic glucose uptake causing hypoglycaemia
notes: Beta-oxidation is typically impaired or overwhelmed, not excessive.
VLDL export is insufficient relative to input, not excessive.
Hyperglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia are typical, not hypoglycaemia.
questions.why: Insulin resistance increases free fatty acid flux from adipose tissue and hepatic de novo lipogenesis, while export and oxidation are inadequate, so triglyceride accumulates.

questions.stem: A man is oliguric 24 hours after a long operation with intraoperative hypotension. Urine sodium is high and urine osmolality is similar to plasma. Which process best explains this?
options: Renal tubular epithelial injury impairing concentration
Activated renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
Obstruction of the bladder outlet
Increased ADH secretion
notes: Activated RAAS in prerenal AKI gives low urine sodium and concentrated urine.
Obstruction is a postrenal cause and does not typically give this pattern; a bladder scan would show it.
Raised ADH produces concentrated urine, not isosmolar urine.
questions.why: Ischaemic acute tubular necrosis impairs sodium reabsorption and concentrating ability, giving high urinary sodium and isosmolar urine. Prerenal states give avid sodium retention.

questions.stem: Which is a feature of a complex febrile seizure?
options: Duration of 2 minutes
Generalised tonic-clonic activity
Occurring at age 2 years
Focal features or recurrence within 24 hours
notes: A 2-minute seizure is brief, which fits a simple seizure.
Generalised tonic-clonic activity is typical of simple febrile seizures.
Age 2 years is within the typical window of 6 months to 6 years.
questions.why: Complex febrile seizures are focal, last longer than 15 minutes, or recur within 24 hours. Simple ones are generalised, brief and single.

questions.stem: Benzodiazepines reduce anxiety by enhancing which neurotransmitter action?
options: Serotonin reuptake inhibition
Glutamate NMDA receptor blockade
GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency
Noradrenaline release
notes: That is the SSRI mechanism.
NMDA blockade is the mechanism of ketamine, not benzodiazepines.
Benzodiazepines do not increase noradrenaline release.
questions.why: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening and producing neuronal inhibition. Tolerance and dependence follow with prolonged use.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with sudden severe right iliac fossa pain and vomiting. Urine hCG is negative. Ultrasound shows a 7 cm ovarian cyst with an enlarged ovary; Doppler shows arterial flow is present. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Serum CA-125 and repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks
Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian conservation
Analgesia, antiemetics and discharge with review in 1 week
Laparotomy with right salpingo-oophorectomy
notes: Delay risks ovarian loss, and CA-125 is not useful in a young woman with acute pain.
Discharge risks ovarian necrosis; suspected torsion needs prompt surgical assessment.
Oophorectomy is not first-line; detorsion usually salvages the ovary, and laparoscopy is preferred.
questions.why: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis; preserved Doppler flow does not exclude it. Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion conserves the ovary, even if it looks dusky.

questions.stem: Which pathophysiological feature underlies the hyperandrogenism and anovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome?
options: Hyperinsulinaemia and raised LH driving ovarian theca androgen production
Low LH with high FSH causing follicular arrest
Excess cortisol suppressing the ovarian axis
Elevated prolactin inhibiting GnRH pulses
notes: PCOS typically has a raised LH:FSH ratio, not low LH with high FSH.
Cortisol excess is Cushing syndrome, a differential rather than the PCOS mechanism.
Hyperprolactinaemia is a differential for oligomenorrhoea, not the mechanism of PCOS.
questions.why: Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia and raised LH pulsatility stimulates theca cells to make androgens, and reduces SHBG, increasing free androgen. This impairs follicle maturation.

questions.stem: Which measure best predicts impending neuromuscular respiratory failure in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
options: Serial forced vital capacity
Arterial pCO2 on room air
Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry
Chest X-ray
notes: Hypercapnia is a late sign, after the patient is already failing.
Saturation stays normal until late because of compensatory tachypnoea.
A chest X-ray does not measure respiratory muscle strength.
questions.why: Respiratory muscle weakness causes a falling vital capacity before hypoxia or hypercapnia. Hypercapnia and desaturation are late signs.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man drinks 3 standard drinks most evenings, with 6 on Saturdays. He has a positive AUDIT-C, no withdrawal history and no dependence. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Refer for inpatient withdrawal management
Start naltrexone and review in one year
Brief intervention advising no more than 10 drinks a week and 4 on any day
Reassure, as his intake is within NHMRC limits
notes: No dependence or withdrawal history, so inpatient withdrawal is unnecessary.
Pharmacotherapy is for moderate to severe use disorder, not first-line here.
He exceeds both the weekly and single-day limits.
questions.why: He drinks about 21 to 27 standard drinks a week, above the NHMRC limits of 10 a week and 4 on any day. A brief intervention with feedback and advice is first-line.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a 1.5 mm Breslow thickness invasive melanoma on his back, diagnosed on excisional biopsy with narrow margins. What is the recommended wide excision margin?
options: 5 mm
1 cm
1 to 2 cm
3 cm
notes: Appropriate for in situ melanoma (5–10 mm), not an invasive 1.5 mm lesion.
1 cm alone is for thin melanomas up to 1 mm; 1.5 mm allows 1–2 cm.
3 cm is not recommended; 2 cm is the maximum even for thicker melanomas.
questions.why: Australian guidelines recommend 1–2 cm margins for melanoma 1.01–2 mm thick (1 cm for ≤1 mm... 5–10 mm for in situ). Margins above 2 cm give no benefit.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m², urine ACR 25 mg/mmol and BP 128/78 on perindopril at maximal dose. HbA1c is 7.4%. Which addition most reduces her risk of kidney disease progression?
options: Dapagliflozin
Amlodipine
Glibenclamide
Spironolactone
notes: Amlodipine lowers BP but gives no renoprotection beyond BP, and her BP is controlled.
Sulfonylureas do not slow CKD and risk hypoglycaemia at reduced eGFR.
Spironolactone adds hyperkalaemia risk; it is not the first add-on over an SGLT2 inhibitor.
questions.why: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) added to an ACEi/ARB slow CKD progression and reduce cardiovascular events in diabetic kidney disease, even at modest glycaemic effect.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has nephrotic syndrome from biopsy-proven membranous nephropathy. He has serum albumin 18 g/L, a sudden left flank pain and haematuria. Doppler shows no hydronephrosis. Which complication should be suspected first?
options: Renal vein thrombosis
Acute pyelonephritis
Ureteric calculus
Renal papillary necrosis
notes: Infection risk is raised, but fever and pyuria would be expected rather than an acute thrombotic picture.
A calculus is possible, but hydronephrosis is absent and the nephrotic hypercoagulable state is the stronger link.
Papillary necrosis occurs with diabetes, analgesics or sickle cell disease, not nephrotic syndrome.
questions.why: Membranous nephropathy with low albumin (<20-25 g/L) carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis and VTE due to urinary loss of antithrombin and a hypercoagulable state. Flank pain and haematuria are typical.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 24 weeks' gestation has 2 days of right-sided abdominal pain and vomiting. Examination shows right flank tenderness. Ultrasound is non-diagnostic and she is stable. What is the most appropriate next imaging?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis
Plain abdominal X-ray
MRI abdomen without gadolinium
Repeat ultrasound in 48 hours
notes: CT delivers fetal radiation; use only if MRI is unavailable.
X-ray is low yield and gives radiation.
Delay risks perforation, which carries high fetal loss.
questions.why: In pregnancy, ultrasound first, then non-contrast MRI if non-diagnostic, avoiding radiation. CT is reserved for when MRI is unavailable or the patient is unstable.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman, 5 days into amoxicillin-clavulanate for cellulitis, has 8 watery stools daily with abdominal cramping. Stool PCR is positive for toxigenic C. difficile. Creatinine and white cell count are mildly raised and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, and stop the inciting antibiotic if possible
Oral loperamide and oral rehydration alone
Intravenous metronidazole alone
Ciprofloxacin orally for 5 days
notes: Loperamide is avoided and does not treat the infection.
IV metronidazole alone is not first line; metronidazole is now second-line.
Fluoroquinolones are a risk factor for C. difficile, not treatment.
questions.why: Current Australian guidance favours oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin for C. difficile, and the inciting antibiotic should be stopped where possible. Antimotility agents are avoided.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest single predictor of future suicide in a patient presenting after self-harm?
options: Female sex
A history of previous self-harm
Being employed
Living with family
notes: Women attempt more often, but men die by suicide more often.
Employment is generally protective.
Living with family is generally protective; living alone raises risk.
questions.why: Previous self-harm is the strongest predictor of later suicide. Risk factors are used for formulation, but no tool predicts who will die.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has weight gain, bruising and proximal weakness. She takes no steroids. Which is an appropriate initial screening test for Cushing syndrome?
options: Random serum cortisol
Plasma ACTH
Late-night salivary cortisol
High-dose dexamethasone suppression test
notes: Random cortisol varies diurnally and cannot screen.
ACTH is used after biochemical confirmation to find the cause.
High-dose suppression helps localise cause, not screen.
questions.why: Screening uses late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol or a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Confirm abnormal results before localising.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man on clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia presents with fever and sore throat. His neutrophil count is 0.8 × 10^9/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue clozapine and repeat the count in one week
Reduce the clozapine dose by half and give paracetamol
Switch to olanzapine the same day without further tests
Cease clozapine and urgently refer for haematology review and management of neutropenia
notes: Continuing risks life-threatening infection.
Dose reduction does not treat agranulocytosis; cessation is required.
A febrile neutropenic patient needs urgent assessment first, and switching blindly is inappropriate.
questions.why: Neutrophils below 1.0 × 10^9/L on clozapine, with fever, suggest severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis. Stop clozapine and manage urgently with haematology input.

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes beta-thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency in a patient with microcytosis?
options: Raised red cell count with normal or high ferritin
Low ferritin with raised red cell count
Raised red cell distribution width with low red cell count
Low transferrin saturation with high ferritin
notes: Low ferritin indicates iron deficiency, which typically has a low red cell count.
Raised RDW with low RCC fits iron deficiency.
Low saturation with high ferritin suggests inflammation, not thalassaemia trait.
questions.why: Thalassaemia trait gives a high red cell count with marked microcytosis and normal iron stores; iron deficiency has low ferritin and a low red cell count.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with BMI 38 has had 8 months of irregular heavy bleeding. Pelvic ultrasound shows endometrial thickness 14 mm and no fibroids. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Serum FSH level
Repeat ultrasound in 3 months
Endometrial sampling
CA-125 measurement
notes: FSH is unreliable in perimenopause and does not exclude endometrial pathology.
Waiting delays diagnosis in a high-risk woman.
CA-125 is not a screening test for endometrial cancer and is non-specific.
questions.why: Women over 45, or younger with risk factors such as obesity, with persistent AUB need endometrial sampling to exclude hyperplasia or cancer. A thickened endometrium raises concern.

questions.stem: A displaced intracapsular neck of femur fracture carries a high risk of avascular necrosis. Disruption of which vessels is mainly responsible?
options: Nutrient artery of the femoral shaft
Retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery
Artery of the ligamentum teres
Superior gluteal artery
notes: The nutrient artery supplies the shaft, not the femoral head blood supply after a neck fracture.
The ligamentum teres artery is minor in adults and does not sustain the head.
The superior gluteal artery supplies gluteal muscles and is not the key head supply.
questions.why: The femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular vessels from the medial circumflex femoral artery, which run along the neck within the capsule and are torn in displaced intracapsular fractures.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has 3 days of ascending leg weakness and paraesthesia, areflexia, and a recent diarrhoeal illness. What CSF finding is typical?
options: Raised protein with normal cell count
Raised neutrophils with low glucose
Oligoclonal bands with lymphocytosis
Low protein with high lymphocytes
notes: Neutrophils and low glucose indicate bacterial meningitis.
Oligoclonal bands suggest multiple sclerosis.
Pleocytosis (>50 cells) should prompt consideration of another diagnosis such as HIV or Lyme.
questions.why: Albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein, normal white cells) is typical of Guillain-Barré, though it may be normal in the first week.

questions.stem: Which pathological protein deposit is the hallmark of dementia with Lewy bodies?
options: Alpha-synuclein
Hyperphosphorylated tau only
Beta-amyloid plaques only
TDP-43 in the hippocampus only
notes: Tau tangles characterise Alzheimer disease (and some FTD), not Lewy body disease.
Amyloid plaques are the Alzheimer hallmark.
TDP-43 inclusions occur in some FTD and ALS, not Lewy body dementia.
questions.why: Lewy bodies are intraneuronal aggregates of alpha-synuclein (cortical and brainstem). Alzheimer disease shows amyloid plaques and tau tangles; FTD shows tau, TDP-43 or FUS.

questions.stem: A patient has euvolaemia, plasma osmolality 255 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 450 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 60 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains the hyponatraemia in SIADH?
options: Excess ADH causing free water retention via aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting ducts
Aldosterone deficiency causing renal sodium wasting
Reduced GFR from low effective arterial volume
Primary excess water intake with maximally dilute urine
notes: Aldosterone deficiency gives hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, with hyperkalaemia; volume status here is euvolaemic.
Low effective arterial volume drives ADH in heart failure or cirrhosis, but those are hypervolaemic states, not SIADH.
Primary polydipsia gives maximally dilute urine (<100 mOsm/kg), not 450.
questions.why: Inappropriate ADH inserts aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct, retaining free water and diluting plasma sodium. Urine is inappropriately concentrated (>100 mOsm/kg) with urinary Na >30 mmol/L.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old attends for scheduled vaccines. He has a runny nose and a temperature of 37.9°C, is feeding well and is otherwise well. His older sibling had anaphylaxis to egg years ago. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give the scheduled vaccines today
Defer all vaccines until he is afebrile for 2 weeks
Defer MMR until egg allergy testing is done
Give vaccines only in hospital under observation
notes: Minor illness without systemic upset is not a reason to delay immunisation.
Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR, and the sibling's history is irrelevant anyway.
Routine hospital observation is unnecessary without a past anaphylactic reaction to a vaccine.
questions.why: Minor illness with low-grade fever is not a contraindication. Only anaphylaxis to a vaccine or component, or specific immunocompromise for live vaccines, are true contraindications.

questions.stem: Why does lithium accumulate to toxic levels when eGFR falls?
options: It is renally excreted unchanged and reabsorbed with sodium in the proximal tubule
It is metabolised by hepatic CYP3A4, which fails in CKD
It is highly protein bound and displaced by uraemic toxins
It is secreted by P-glycoprotein into bile
notes: Lithium is not hepatically metabolised.
Lithium is not protein bound.
Biliary secretion is not a route of lithium elimination.
questions.why: Lithium is almost entirely cleared by the kidney and reabsorbed like sodium, so reduced GFR or volume depletion raises levels. It has a narrow therapeutic index.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents after an overdose. He now has ongoing intent to die, a plan, refuses help and wants to leave. He has severe depression and no capacity to weigh the risk. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Discharge with a safety plan and GP follow-up in a week
Assess under mental health legislation for involuntary treatment
Discharge to his family with a no-suicide contract
Allow him to leave and offer a crisis line number
notes: Safety planning is for lower risk, not ongoing intent with refusal of care.
No-suicide contracts have no evidence and are not protective.
Letting him leave fails the duty of care when risk is high and capacity is impaired.
questions.why: With persisting intent, a mental illness and impaired decision-making, he should be assessed for involuntary treatment under the state Mental Health Act. Safety plans and contracts do not suffice for imminent risk.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with an intact uterus starts menopausal hormone therapy for hot flushes. Why must a progestogen be added to her oestrogen?
options: To prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from unopposed oestrogen
To prevent breast cancer from oestrogen
To increase bone density beyond that from oestrogen
To reduce the risk of venous thromboembolism
notes: Progestogen does not protect the breast; combined therapy carries a small increase in breast cancer risk.
Bone benefit comes from oestrogen; progestogen adds little.
Oral oestrogen raises VTE risk; adding progestogen does not lower it.
questions.why: Unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial proliferation, raising hyperplasia and cancer risk. A progestogen induces secretory change and shedding; it is not needed after hysterectomy.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old has had fever for 6 days and irritability with a rash, but only 2 other classic features. CRP is high and echo is normal. What is the best next step?
options: Treat as incomplete Kawasaki disease with IVIG
Discharge with paracetamol and review
Wait for more criteria before treating
Start oral antibiotics only
notes: This risks missed treatment and coronary aneurysm.
Waiting delays therapy; incomplete presentations are common in infants and need prompt treatment.
Antibiotics alone do not treat Kawasaki disease.
questions.why: Infants under 12 months with prolonged fever and raised inflammatory markers often have incomplete Kawasaki disease. Treat early with IVIG, since coronary risk is highest in infants and a normal early echo does not exclude it.

questions.stem: A CTG shows repetitive late decelerations. What is the underlying physiological mechanism?
options: Head compression stimulating vagal tone
Cord compression causing baroreceptor reflex
Uteroplacental insufficiency causing chemoreceptor-mediated vagal response to hypoxaemia
Maternal sympathetic activation from pain
notes: Head compression produces early decelerations that mirror contractions.
Cord compression produces variable decelerations.
Maternal pain does not cause the characteristic lagging deceleration.
questions.why: Late decelerations reflect reduced uteroplacental oxygen transfer during contractions; fetal hypoxaemia triggers a chemoreceptor-mediated vagal response, lagging the contraction.

questions.stem: A low-FODMAP diet is used to reduce symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome. Which mechanism best explains why poorly absorbed short-chain carbohydrates cause bloating and diarrhoea?
options: They are osmotically active and fermented by colonic bacteria to produce gas
They directly damage the small bowel villi and cause malabsorption
They stimulate gastrin release and increase gastric acid secretion
They inhibit pancreatic lipase and cause steatorrhoea
notes: Villous damage is the mechanism in coeliac disease, not with FODMAPs; the mucosa is normal.
FODMAPs do not act through gastrin or acid secretion.
Lipase inhibition causes fat malabsorption (e.g. orlistat), not FODMAP symptoms.
questions.why: FODMAPs are poorly absorbed, draw water into the lumen osmotically and are fermented by colonic bacteria, producing gas and distension. This triggers symptoms in a visceral hypersensitive gut.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on dapagliflozin presents with vomiting and malaise after 2 days of poor intake. Glucose 11 mmol/L, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L, ketones 5.0 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observe and recommence dapagliflozin when eating
Give IV sodium bicarbonate and oral fluids
Give IV fluids only, as glucose is below 14 mmol/L
Stop dapagliflozin; treat as DKA with IV fluids, insulin with dextrose, and potassium
notes: Continuing the drug risks persisting ketosis; it must be ceased.
Bicarbonate is not routine at pH 7.15 and oral fluids are inadequate.
Insulin is needed to switch off ketogenesis despite near-normal glucose.
questions.why: This is SGLT2-inhibitor euglycaemic DKA. Stop the drug and treat as DKA with fluids, fixed-rate insulin plus dextrose to clear ketones, and potassium replacement.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has clinic BP readings of 152/94 mmHg on two visits, with no end-organ damage. What is the best next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Start perindopril immediately
Ambulatory or home BP monitoring
Repeat clinic BP in 12 months
Renal angiography
notes: Treatment should follow confirmation, unless BP is severely raised or there is end-organ damage.
A 12-month delay is inappropriate for readings this high without confirmation.
Renal angiography is for suspected renovascular disease, not routine confirmation.
questions.why: Australian guidelines recommend confirming raised clinic BP with ambulatory (preferred) or home BP monitoring before diagnosing hypertension, to exclude white-coat hypertension.

questions.stem: Ticagrelor is added to aspirin after an acute coronary syndrome. What is ticagrelor's mechanism of action?
options: Reversible antagonism of the platelet P2Y12 receptor
Irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1
Inhibition of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors
Inhibition of factor Xa
notes: This is aspirin's mechanism, which ticagrelor complements.
Tirofiban is the GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor, given IV.
Rivaroxaban and apixaban inhibit factor Xa; ticagrelor does not.
questions.why: Ticagrelor reversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor and does not need metabolic activation. Clopidogrel and prasugrel block it irreversibly.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with obesity (BMI 38 kg/m²) on semaglutide has sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Cease semaglutide and check serum lipase
Continue semaglutide and start a proton pump inhibitor
Reduce the semaglutide dose by half
Arrange outpatient gallbladder ultrasound only
notes: Continuing the drug risks worsening possible pancreatitis.
Dose reduction is inadequate when pancreatitis is suspected.
Imaging may follow, but acute assessment and stopping the drug come first.
questions.why: GLP-1 RAs are associated with pancreatitis and gallbladder disease. Suspected pancreatitis requires stopping the drug and checking lipase; do not restart if confirmed.

questions.stem: Which pharmacological property of buprenorphine explains its ceiling effect on respiratory depression and its risk of precipitated withdrawal?
options: High-affinity partial mu-opioid agonism
Full mu-opioid agonism with short half-life
Kappa-receptor agonism only
Non-competitive NMDA antagonism
notes: Full agonism describes methadone, which has no ceiling effect.
Kappa activity does not explain these features.
NMDA antagonism is a secondary property of methadone, not buprenorphine's ceiling.
questions.why: Buprenorphine binds mu receptors with high affinity but low intrinsic activity, so it displaces full agonists and can precipitate withdrawal while limiting respiratory depression.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains how statins lower plasma LDL cholesterol?
options: Inhibit intestinal cholesterol absorption via NPC1L1
Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors
Activate lipoprotein lipase to clear triglycerides
Bind bile acids in the gut, preventing reabsorption
notes: That is ezetimibe's mechanism.
Fibrates act through PPAR-alpha to increase lipoprotein lipase activity.
That is the mechanism of bile acid sequestrants such as colestyramine.
questions.why: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis, which upregulates LDL receptors and increases LDL clearance from plasma.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman (65 kg) develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension after a wasp sting. She has had one IM adrenaline dose with no improvement after 5 minutes. What is the next step?
options: Repeat adrenaline 0.5 mg IM now
Give hydrocortisone 200 mg IV and observe
Give promethazine IM and reassess in 15 minutes
Start adrenaline IV infusion straight away without further IM doses
notes: Steroids and antihistamines are not first-line and do not treat shock.
Antihistamines are adjuncts only and delay adrenaline.
Infusion is for refractory cases after repeated IM doses, with expert/ICU input.
questions.why: Adult dose is 0.5 mg (0.01 mg/kg) IM into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response. Start an infusion if there is refractory anaphylaxis after multiple IM doses, with fluids.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man with heart failure becomes dyspnoeic, hypertensive (190/100) with raised JVP and bilateral crackles 2 hours into his second unit of red cells. SpO2 is 88%. After stopping the transfusion, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Sit upright, give oxygen and intravenous frusemide
Give intravenous adrenaline 1 mg
Restart transfusion at a slower rate
Give intravenous fluid bolus
notes: Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, which has hypotension, wheeze and urticaria rather than hypertension and raised JVP.
Transfusion should not be restarted until stable and reassessed; it worsens overload.
Fluid bolus would worsen pulmonary oedema.
questions.why: This is TACO: hypertension, raised JVP and pulmonary oedema. Stop the transfusion, sit upright, give oxygen and a diuretic such as frusemide.

questions.stem: Oral rehydration solution is effective even in secretory diarrhoea such as cholera. Which mechanism underlies this?
options: Sodium–glucose cotransport in the enterocyte drives water absorption
Glucose inhibits chloride secretion by blocking CFTR
Glucose directly stimulates colonic aldosterone release
Sodium is absorbed by passive diffusion through tight junctions only
notes: Glucose does not block CFTR; secretion continues but absorption is enhanced.
Aldosterone is not released by glucose in the colon in this way.
Coupled cotransport, not passive paracellular diffusion, is the mechanism.
questions.why: SGLT1 couples sodium and glucose uptake, which remains intact in secretory diarrhoea, and water follows osmotically. This is the basis of ORS.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with severe haemophilia A presents with a swollen painful knee after minor trauma. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Urgent factor VIII replacement before imaging, then haematology advice
Aspirate the joint first and then give factor VIII
Oral tranexamic acid and review in 48 hours
Fresh frozen plasma
notes: Aspiration is not routine and is done only after factor replacement if needed.
Tranexamic acid alone is inadequate for a significant joint bleed in severe haemophilia.
FFP contains low factor VIII concentration; specific factor concentrate is preferred.
questions.why: Suspected haemarthrosis in haemophilia needs prompt factor VIII (recombinant) replacement, ideally within hours, before investigations, with early haematology input. Early treatment preserves the joint.

questions.stem: A patient has a small bowel obstruction and profuse vomiting. Which acid-base and electrolyte disturbance is most likely from loss of gastric contents and third-space fluid?
options: Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis with hyperkalaemia
Hyperkalaemic metabolic alkalosis
notes: That pattern occurs with diarrhoea or saline excess, not vomiting.
Respiratory alkalosis is not the primary disturbance here.
Potassium is lost, not retained, with vomiting and aldosterone activation.
questions.why: Vomiting loses H+ and Cl-, causing hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; volume depletion drives aldosterone-mediated K+ loss. Late ischaemia may cause lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: Midazolam is used for sedation of acute behavioural disturbance. Through which mechanism does it act?
options: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors
Enhances GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency
Blocks histamine H1 and muscarinic receptors only
Inhibits NMDA receptors
notes: That is the mechanism of antipsychotics such as haloperidol or droperidol.
Antihistamine action is not the benzodiazepine mechanism.
NMDA antagonism is the mechanism of ketamine.
questions.why: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A, increasing channel opening frequency and causing sedation. Antipsychotics such as droperidol act at D2.

questions.stem: Lithium is almost entirely renally cleared. Which change most likely raises serum lithium concentration?
options: Starting a thiazide diuretic
Increasing dietary salt intake
Starting acetazolamide
Pregnancy in the third trimester
notes: Sodium loading increases lithium excretion and lowers levels.
Acetazolamide increases lithium excretion and lowers levels.
Increased GFR in pregnancy lowers levels.
questions.why: Thiazides reduce sodium and volume, increasing proximal lithium reabsorption and raising levels. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and dehydration act likewise.

questions.stem: Which finding is the earliest and most sensitive marker of glomerular filtration barrier damage in diabetic kidney disease?
options: Raised serum creatinine
Reduced urine output
Albuminuria on urine albumin:creatinine ratio
Red cell casts in the urine
notes: Creatinine rises late, after substantial nephron loss.
Urine output is usually preserved in CKD until advanced stages.
Red cell casts indicate glomerulonephritis, not typical diabetic nephropathy.
questions.why: Albuminuria reflects loss of charge and size selectivity of the glomerular barrier and appears before eGFR falls. The urine ACR is the key early marker and also predicts progression.

questions.stem: What is the main mechanism by which mifepristone contributes to early medical abortion?
options: Prostaglandin E1 agonism causing cervical softening
Progesterone receptor antagonism, withdrawing decidual support
Oxytocin receptor activation causing uterine contraction
Inhibition of hCG secretion by the trophoblast
notes: That is misoprostol's action, given 24–48 hours after mifepristone.
Oxytocin receptor activation is not how either drug acts; oxytocin is not used in early medical abortion.
Mifepristone does not inhibit hCG secretion; hCG falls as a consequence of decidual and trophoblast detachment.
questions.why: Mifepristone blocks progesterone receptors, causing decidual breakdown, cervical softening and increased uterine sensitivity to prostaglandin. Misoprostol (a PGE1 analogue) then causes contractions and expulsion.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has low back pain. Which finding is the most concerning red flag for spinal infection or malignancy?
options: Night pain with unexplained weight loss and fever
Pain worse after prolonged sitting
Pain beginning after lifting a box
Stiffness that eases within minutes of moving
notes: Pain with sitting and varying with posture suggests a mechanical cause.
A clear mechanical trigger suggests musculoskeletal strain.
Brief morning stiffness is mechanical; inflammatory back pain stiffness lasts over 30 minutes.
questions.why: Fever, weight loss, night or constant pain suggest infection or malignancy. Mechanical pain that varies with posture and movement is typically benign.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with iron deficiency anaemia and type 1 diabetes has bloating. She has avoided gluten for 3 months and her GP's tTG-IgA is negative (total IgA normal). What is the best next step?
options: Exclude coeliac disease, as the negative result is reliable
Start gluten challenge for at least 6 weeks, then repeat tTG-IgA
Order HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing to confirm the diagnosis
Proceed to duodenal biopsy while she remains gluten-free
notes: Testing on a gluten-free diet gives false negatives.
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 has a high negative predictive value but cannot confirm diagnosis.
Biopsy can be falsely normal if gluten has been avoided.
questions.why: Serology and biopsy are unreliable once gluten is withdrawn. Eat gluten daily (about 6 weeks) before repeat testing. HLA typing only helps exclude disease.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old university student has fever, headache and a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. The GP is 40 minutes from hospital and she has no known allergy. What is the best action before transfer?
options: Give IV or IM benzylpenicillin immediately, then transfer
Perform a lumbar puncture in the surgery first
Wait for hospital blood cultures before any antibiotic
Give oral amoxicillin and transfer
notes: LP delays treatment and is risky in shock or rash with sepsis.
Delaying antibiotics increases mortality.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate for this emergency.
questions.why: Suspected meningococcal disease needs immediate parenteral benzylpenicillin (or ceftriaxone) before transfer; do not delay for investigations. Lumbar puncture is not appropriate in a shocked patient.

questions.stem: Why does intermittent claudication in peripheral arterial disease occur with exercise and settle with rest?
options: Fixed stenosis cannot increase flow to meet muscle demand
Venous valves fail during walking
Nerve compression occurs when standing
Muscle spasm from low calcium
notes: Venous valve failure causes venous insufficiency, with heaviness and oedema.
Nerve compression describes neurogenic claudication, which eases with sitting or flexion rather than just stopping.
Calcium-related spasm does not explain exertional, rest-relieved pain.
questions.why: A fixed atherosclerotic stenosis allows adequate flow at rest but cannot increase it with exertion, so ischaemic pain occurs and eases once demand falls.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old ex-smoker with COPD, on a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, remains breathless with one exacerbation in the past year. According to COPD-X stepwise therapy, what is the usual next step?
options: Add a long-acting beta2 agonist (LAMA/LABA)
Start long-term oral prednisolone
Start long-term azithromycin only
Add regular theophylline
notes: Long-term oral corticosteroids cause harm and are not recommended.
Azithromycin is considered later for frequent exacerbations despite optimal inhaled therapy.
Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and is not a routine next step.
questions.why: For persistent symptoms or exacerbations on monotherapy, COPD-X advises dual long-acting bronchodilator therapy (LAMA plus LABA).

questions.stem: A pituitary macroadenoma expands upward and compresses the optic chiasm. Which retinal fibres are damaged first, producing bitemporal hemianopia?
options: Nasal retinal fibres from each eye, which cross
Temporal retinal fibres from each eye, which cross
Nasal retinal fibres from each eye, which stay uncrossed
Temporal retinal fibres from the ipsilateral eye only
notes: Temporal retinal fibres do not cross; they pass laterally in the chiasm.
Nasal fibres cross; they do not stay uncrossed.
Unilateral temporal fibre loss would give a nasal field defect in one eye, not bitemporal loss.
questions.why: Nasal retinal fibres, carrying the temporal visual fields, decussate at the chiasm and are compressed centrally. Temporal fibres stay ipsilateral.

questions.stem: What best explains the non-blanching purpuric rash of meningococcaemia?
options: Endotoxin-induced DIC and vascular injury causing bleeding into the skin
Type I hypersensitivity with mast cell degranulation
Direct bacterial invasion of the epidermis causing blistering
Immune complex deposition in the glomeruli
notes: Mast cell degranulation causes blanching urticaria.
Epidermal blistering describes staphylococcal scalded skin or bullous impetigo.
Glomerular immune complexes do not cause the purpuric rash.
questions.why: Neisseria meningitidis lipo-oligosaccharide triggers endothelial injury, microthrombi and DIC, causing petechiae and purpura that do not blanch.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman on gliclazide with eGFR 30 is brought in confused. BGL is 2.1 mmol/L. She cannot swallow safely and has no IV access yet. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Intramuscular glucagon 1 mg
Oral glucose gel and observe
Subcutaneous octreotide 100 micrograms
Oral sucrose drink then discharge
notes: Unsafe swallow with reduced consciousness makes oral gel an aspiration risk.
Octreotide is used for recurrent sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia after glucose, not as first-line rescue.
Oral route unsafe, and discharge is wrong given prolonged sulfonylurea effect in renal impairment.
questions.why: With no IV access and an unsafe swallow, IM glucagon 1 mg is appropriate (IV 10% glucose once access is gained). Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia recurs, so she needs admission and observation.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has had 1 day of vomiting and watery diarrhoea. He is alert, mildly reduced skin turgor, slightly dry mucous membranes, normal capillary refill and has vomited twice in ED. He refuses fluids. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give ondansetron then trial oral rehydration solution
Start intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride bolus 20 mL/kg
Give loperamide and discharge with oral fluids
Send stool culture and start oral azithromycin
notes: A bolus is for shock or severe dehydration; he has normal perfusion and should first have oral or nasogastric rehydration.
Loperamide is not recommended in young children with gastroenteritis.
Most gastroenteritis is viral and self-limiting; antibiotics and routine culture are not indicated.
questions.why: Mild to moderate dehydration with vomiting: a single dose of ondansetron improves oral rehydration success and reduces need for IV fluids. Antimotility drugs and routine antibiotics are not recommended.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains how methylphenidate improves symptoms of ADHD?
options: Blocks dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake in the prefrontal cortex
Blocks postsynaptic D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway
Enhances GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening
Inhibits monoamine oxidase A irreversibly
notes: D2 blockade is the mechanism of antipsychotics, which do not treat core ADHD symptoms.
Enhancing GABA-A is the mechanism of benzodiazepines, which are not used for ADHD.
Irreversible MAO inhibition is the mechanism of older antidepressants, not stimulants.
questions.why: Methylphenidate blocks dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, increasing synaptic catecholamines in frontostriatal circuits. Lisdexamfetamine also increases release.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and BMI 34 has steatosis on ultrasound and mildly raised ALT. Which is the best next step to assess for advanced fibrosis?
options: Calculate FIB-4 from age, AST, ALT and platelets
Repeat liver ultrasound in 6 months
Liver biopsy immediately
Serum ferritin to stage fibrosis
notes: Ultrasound is insensitive for fibrosis.
Biopsy is reserved for unclear cases after non-invasive tests.
Ferritin does not stage fibrosis.
questions.why: FIB-4 is the first-line non-invasive fibrosis screen in primary care; indeterminate or high scores prompt elastography (FibroScan).

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with moderate dementia refuses to move into residential care. She understands the information and can retain it, but says she is 'perfectly safe' and cannot weigh the risks. What is the best next step?
options: Find she lacks capacity for this decision, as she cannot use and weigh the information
Find she has capacity because she understands and retains the information
Proceed under her son's wishes without further assessment
Assume capacity is lost because she has a dementia diagnosis
notes: Understanding and retention alone are not enough; she must also use and weigh the information.
Family cannot decide without a formal capacity assessment and legal authority.
A diagnosis of dementia does not alone mean incapacity; capacity is assessed per decision.
questions.why: Capacity is decision-specific and requires understanding, retaining, using/weighing information and communicating a choice. Inability to weigh risks means she lacks capacity for this decision; involve the substitute decision-maker.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma with a 4 cm adrenal mass and is awaiting adrenalectomy. Which preoperative regimen is most appropriate?
options: Alpha-blocker such as phenoxybenzamine, then add beta-blocker if tachycardic
Beta-blocker alone
Hydrochlorothiazide and fluid restriction
No medication; proceed to surgery urgently
notes: Beta-blockade alone leaves unopposed alpha stimulation, risking hypertensive crisis.
Diuretics and fluid restriction worsen volume contraction and postoperative hypotension.
Unprepared surgery risks intraoperative hypertensive crisis.
questions.why: Alpha-blockade for 1–2 weeks (with salt and fluid loading) comes first; beta-blocker is added only afterwards for tachycardia.

questions.stem: A GP examines a 4-year-old with multiple bruises and a patterned handprint on the thigh. The explanation is vague. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Report to the state child protection authority and arrange paediatric assessment
Wait to gather proof before involving any agency
Seek the parents' consent before making any report
Document findings and review the child in 4 weeks
notes: Proof is not required; reasonable suspicion is enough.
Parental consent is not required for a report.
Delay leaves the child at risk.
questions.why: Where there is reasonable belief of significant harm, doctors must notify child protection services (mandatory in most states and territories) and arrange urgent assessment. Proof and parental consent are not required.

questions.stem: A child with faltering growth has a normal length but a low weight. Which cause is most likely to produce this pattern?
options: Growth hormone deficiency
Inadequate energy intake
Hypothyroidism
Turner syndrome
notes: Growth hormone deficiency impairs linear growth, with relatively preserved weight.
Hypothyroidism causes short stature, with weight relatively preserved or increased.
Turner syndrome causes short stature from early on, not isolated low weight.
questions.why: Inadequate energy intake affects weight first, then head circumference and length last. Endocrine causes and genetic short stature affect length early.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old on dialysis has weakness. K+ is 7.4 mmol/L and ECG shows broad QRS and peaked T waves. IV calcium has been given. What is the next best treatment to lower serum potassium?
options: IV insulin with glucose
Oral calcium resonium alone
IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol
notes: Binders act too slowly for an emergency with ECG changes.
Saline does not reliably lower potassium and risks overload in dialysis patients.
Bicarbonate is of limited benefit unless severe acidosis exists.
questions.why: Insulin with glucose (plus nebulised salbutamol) rapidly shifts potassium into cells after membrane stabilisation. Definitive removal needs dialysis in this patient.

questions.stem: A GP suspects a patient's rash is an adverse reaction to a newly marketed medicine. How should the GP report this in Australia?
options: Report to the TGA (for example via the Adverse Event Reporting System online)
Report only to the medicine's pharmacy of dispensing
Wait for confirmation by dechallenge before reporting any event
Report only if the reaction is serious and fatal
notes: The TGA is the national reporting body; pharmacy notification alone does not meet this.
Causation need not be proven before reporting a suspected reaction.
Non-serious reactions are also valuable to report, especially for new medicines.
questions.why: Health professionals can report suspected adverse reactions to the TGA online, and reporting is encouraged for suspected reactions, especially to new medicines. Proof of causation is not required.

questions.stem: Burkholderia pseudomallei causes melioidosis. Which statement best explains its distribution and risk factors?
options: It lives in soil and surface water, and diabetes impairs host neutrophil defence
It is transmitted person to person by respiratory droplets
It lives only in livestock and spreads through milk
It is a mosquito-borne virus
notes: Person-to-person spread is very rare.
Milk spread describes brucellosis.
It is a bacterium, not a virus.
questions.why: B. pseudomallei is an environmental Gram-negative bacillus in tropical soil and water. Infection follows inhalation or inoculation, mostly in the wet season, and diabetes is the major risk factor.

questions.stem: Which event is the usual initiating step in the pathogenesis of native valve infective endocarditis?
options: Bacteraemia infecting normal, undamaged endothelium directly
Endothelial injury with deposition of a sterile platelet–fibrin thrombus
Immune complex deposition on the valve leaflets
Papillary muscle rupture causing turbulent flow
notes: Wrong: most organisms cannot adhere to healthy endothelium (S. aureus is a partial exception); a damaged surface is usually needed first.
Wrong: immune complexes cause the secondary phenomena such as glomerulonephritis and Roth spots, not the initial vegetation.
Wrong: this is a complication of valve disease or infarction, not the initiating step.
questions.why: Endothelial damage from turbulent flow or injury forms a sterile platelet–fibrin thrombus (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis); transient bacteraemia then seeds it to form a vegetation.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with JAK2-positive polycythaemia vera has a haematocrit of 0.58 and no prior thrombosis. She is on no treatment. Which regimen is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Venesection to haematocrit below 0.45 plus low-dose aspirin
Venesection alone without aspirin
Warfarin with target INR 2–3
Imatinib
notes: Aspirin is recommended unless contraindicated, as it reduces arterial and venous thrombotic events.
Anticoagulation is not first-line prophylaxis without a thrombotic event.
Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in CML, not PV.
questions.why: Initial PV management is venesection to keep haematocrit under 0.45 plus low-dose aspirin to reduce thrombosis. Cytoreduction (e.g. hydroxycarbamide) is added for high-risk disease (age over 60 or prior thrombosis).

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has a sudden severe occipital headache that peaked within a minute while exercising, 3 hours ago, with neck stiffness. She is alert, neurologically normal. Non-contrast CT brain at 2 hours is reported normal. What is the next step?
options: Discharge with simple analgesia
Lumbar puncture, or CT angiography, to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
Start sumatriptan for migraine
MRI in the outpatient setting
notes: Discharge risks missing a sentinel bleed or aneurysm with high rebleed mortality.
Triptans are vasoconstrictors and inappropriate before SAH is excluded.
Outpatient delay is unsafe; the work-up should be completed urgently.
questions.why: Thunderclap headache needs SAH excluded. CT within 6 hours of onset by an expert is highly sensitive, but here the CT was at 2 hours with high suspicion, so LP (xanthochromia) or CTA is still needed per local protocol.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is in cardiac arrest with VF. He has had two shocks and CPR is ongoing with IV access and adrenaline already due. Per ANZCOR, which drug is given after the third shock?
options: Amiodarone 300 mg IV
Calcium chloride 10 mL of 10% IV
Sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol IV
Atropine 3 mg IV
notes: Calcium is only for specific causes such as hyperkalaemia, not routine VF.
Bicarbonate is not routine; it is for select causes such as TCA overdose or hyperkalaemia.
Atropine is no longer used in cardiac arrest algorithms.
questions.why: ANZCOR ALS: in shock-refractory VF/pVT give adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock, then adrenaline every second cycle.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman discloses in a private consultation that her partner has choked her and threatened to kill her. She has two children, is not ready to leave and does not want police involved. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Make a safety plan and offer referral to 1800RESPECT or a local service
Notify police immediately against her wishes
Advise her to leave tonight
Document nothing to avoid the record being accessed
notes: Adult competent patients' confidentiality applies; police are contacted without consent only if there is a serious imminent threat to life.
Telling her to leave is directive; the period around leaving is high-risk and the decision is hers, supported by a plan.
Accurate, factual documentation is recommended; it can support later legal action.
questions.why: Strangulation and death threats are high-risk indicators. Respect autonomy, assess immediate risk, make a safety plan, offer referrals (1800RESPECT) and document factually. Mandatory reporting applies to children at risk in some jurisdictions.

questions.stem: In benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, brief vertigo is triggered by head movement. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Endolymph excess distending the cochlear duct
Inflammation of the vestibular nerve after a viral illness
Ischaemia of the cerebellar vermis
Displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal
notes: Endolymphatic hydrops describes Ménière disease, with hearing loss and tinnitus.
This describes vestibular neuritis, which causes prolonged continuous vertigo.
Cerebellar ischaemia causes persistent vertigo with ataxia, not brief positional episodes.
questions.why: Otoconia displaced from the utricle enter a semicircular canal (usually posterior) and cause abnormal endolymph movement with head position change, producing brief vertigo.

questions.stem: Why is a pressure immobilisation bandage applied after an Australian elapid snakebite?
options: It slows lymphatic flow, delaying venom reaching the circulation
It neutralises venom at the bite site
It prevents local tissue necrosis by increasing perfusion
It occludes arterial inflow to the limb
notes: Bandaging does not neutralise venom; only antivenom does.
Venom is not limited by perfusion; the aim is to reduce lymphatic spread, not boost perfusion.
The bandage should be firm like a sprain wrap, not a tourniquet; distal pulses should remain.
questions.why: Elapid venom is large and moves mainly via lymphatics; pressure and immobilisation reduce lymph flow and muscle movement, delaying systemic envenomation. Arterial flow must not be occluded.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has 40 minutes of central chest pain. ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in V2–V5. He is at a hospital with no PCI capability; transfer to a PCI centre will take over 3 hours. No contraindications. What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?
options: Fibrinolysis, then transfer to a PCI centre
Wait for troponin result before deciding
Heparin and aspirin only, then transfer for angiography next day
Transfer for primary PCI without any fibrinolysis
notes: STEMI is diagnosed on ECG and reperfusion should not wait for troponin.
Antithrombotics alone do not reperfuse an occluded artery in STEMI.
Delay beyond 120 minutes makes PCI-only inferior when fibrinolysis is available and safe.
questions.why: When primary PCI cannot be achieved within about 120 minutes of first contact, fibrinolysis should be given promptly (ideally within 30 minutes), followed by transfer to a PCI centre.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has hypertension, hypokalaemia and a suppressed renin. Excess of which hormone best explains her hypertension?
options: Aldosterone, causing sodium retention and potassium loss
Cortisol, causing insulin resistance
Adrenaline, causing vasoconstriction through alpha receptors
Angiotensin II, causing efferent arteriolar constriction
notes: Cortisol excess (Cushing) can cause hypokalaemia, but suppressed renin with this picture points to aldosterone.
Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension without the typical hypokalaemia and suppressed renin.
Angiotensin II would be raised with high renin, as in renal artery stenosis, not suppressed.
questions.why: Primary aldosteronism causes sodium and water retention and renal potassium loss, with renin suppressed by volume expansion. Screen with aldosterone-renin ratio.

questions.stem: At what age does a typically developing child usually first walk independently?
options: 12 to 15 months
6 to 8 months
9 to 10 months
20 to 24 months
notes: 6 to 8 months is the age of sitting without support.
9 to 10 months is typically crawling and pulling to stand.
Walking has usually occurred well before this; this age is when running and kicking emerge.
questions.why: Most children walk independently by about 12 to 15 months. Failure to walk by 18 months warrants assessment.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 at 28 weeks is RhD negative with no anti-D antibodies on screening. She has had no bleeding. Which routine prophylaxis is recommended in Australia?
options: Anti-D 625 IU IM at 28 weeks only
Anti-D 250 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks
Anti-D 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks
Anti-D after birth only, if the baby is RhD positive
notes: A single dose at 28 weeks is not the schedule; a second dose is given at 34 weeks.
250 IU is the dose for sensitising events before 12 weeks, not routine antenatal prophylaxis.
Postnatal-only prophylaxis misses sensitisation during pregnancy; antenatal doses are also recommended.
questions.why: Australian guidelines recommend routine antenatal anti-D 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks for RhD-negative non-sensitised women. Postnatal anti-D is still given if the baby is RhD positive.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has a stab wound to the left chest. He is gasping, SpO2 82%, HR 140, BP 70/40, trachea deviated right, absent left breath sounds. What is the immediate management?
options: Wait for a chest X-ray to confirm
Left chest decompression (finger thoracostomy or needle)
Intubate and ventilate first
Rapid 2 L crystalloid bolus
notes: Delay for imaging in an unstable patient is dangerous.
Positive pressure ventilation before decompression can cause arrest.
Fluid does not relieve the obstruction.
questions.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; immediate decompression, preferably finger thoracostomy in the 4th/5th intercostal space, anterior to mid-axillary line, then an intercostal catheter. Positive pressure ventilation first can worsen it.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has dysuria and urethral discharge. Urine NAAT is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. He has no drug allergies. Which is the most appropriate treatment per current Australian guidelines?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM with azithromycin 1 g orally
Azithromycin 1 g orally alone
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally single dose
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IM
notes: Azithromycin alone promotes resistance and is not adequate.
Quinolone resistance is widespread in Australia.
Penicillin treats syphilis, not gonorrhoea, given resistance.
questions.why: Because of resistance, uncomplicated gonorrhoea is treated with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 1 g orally. Also test for other STIs, arrange contact tracing and test of cure.

questions.stem: Hepatitis B serology shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive and anti-HBs positive. How is this interpreted?
options: Chronic infection with high infectivity
Vaccine-induced immunity
Resolved past infection
Acute infection in the window period
notes: Chronic infection has persistent HBsAg.
Vaccination produces anti-HBs only, without anti-HBc.
Window period has HBsAg and anti-HBs both negative, with anti-HBc present but no anti-HBs.
questions.why: Anti-HBc with anti-HBs and negative HBsAg means natural infection that has cleared. Vaccination gives anti-HBs alone. Reactivation can occur with immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A healthy woman at 33 weeks' gestation, in autumn, has had no vaccines this pregnancy. What is the best advice?
options: Give dTpa, influenza and RSV (RSVpreF) vaccines now
Give influenza now; defer dTpa and RSV until after birth
Give dTpa and MMR vaccine now
Give RSV vaccine now; give dTpa after birth
notes: Delaying dTpa and RSV vaccine until after birth loses the passive antibody protection for the newborn.
MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
dTpa should be given in pregnancy, not after birth, so the newborn gets maternal antibody.
questions.why: dTpa, influenza and RSVpreF (28 to 36 weeks) are all recommended in pregnancy, and can be co-administered. dTpa is best at 20 to 32 weeks but can be given later.

questions.stem: Which hormone, produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy and is measured in a urine or serum pregnancy test?
options: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
Human placental lactogen
Oestriol
Relaxin
notes: Human placental lactogen rises later and alters maternal glucose metabolism; it is not the pregnancy test marker.
Oestriol is a placental oestrogen; it does not maintain the corpus luteum.
Relaxin softens ligaments and is not the pregnancy test hormone.
questions.why: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast rescues the corpus luteum so progesterone continues until the placenta takes over at about 8–10 weeks. It is the basis of pregnancy tests.

questions.stem: In Australian workers' compensation, what is the role of the treating GP when completing a medical certificate for an injured worker?
options: Certify capacity for work and suggest suitable duties, not just total incapacity
Decide whether the claim is accepted
Direct the employer's rehabilitation budget
Certify only complete time off work
notes: Liability decisions are made by the insurer.
The GP doesn't control budgets; rehabilitation providers and insurers do.
Certificates should specify capacity, not default to total incapacity, since work is generally good for health.
questions.why: The GP certifies diagnosis and work capacity, recommending suitable or modified duties, as early safe return to work aids recovery. The insurer decides liability, not the GP.

questions.stem: Varenicline helps people quit smoking. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Irreversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase
Blockade of dopamine reuptake in the nucleus accumbens
Partial agonism at α4β2 nicotinic receptors
Full agonism at α7 nicotinic receptors
notes: Not an MAO inhibitor.
Dopamine reuptake blockade is closer to bupropion's proposed action, which is not varenicline's.
Its key action is at α4β2, as a partial rather than full agonist.
questions.why: Varenicline is a partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors. It eases withdrawal and craving while blunting the reward from smoking.

questions.stem: In HFE haemochromatosis, which change in hepcidin explains the increased iron absorption?
options: Inappropriately low hepcidin, so ferroportin stays active
High hepcidin, which upregulates ferroportin
Low hepcidin, which downregulates divalent metal transporter
Absent transferrin, which frees iron for absorption
notes: High hepcidin degrades ferroportin and reduces absorption.
Low hepcidin does not downregulate iron uptake; absorption increases.
Transferrin is present, and saturation is high, not absent.
questions.why: HFE mutation reduces hepcidin production. Without hepcidin, ferroportin is not degraded, so enterocytes and macrophages release excess iron.

questions.stem: Which criterion for a population screening program is most essential to justify screening for a condition?
options: Accepted treatment that improves outcomes if started early
A highly sensitive test regardless of cost
A high lifetime prevalence in older adults
Availability of the test in private clinics
notes: Test performance matters but cost-effectiveness and acceptability are also needed; sensitivity alone is not sufficient.
Prevalence is relevant but does not justify screening without effective early treatment.
Access via private clinics is irrelevant to program justification.
questions.why: Wilson–Jungner principles require an important condition with a detectable latent phase and accepted, effective treatment that improves outcomes when started early.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has fever, confusion, haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 12 x10^9/L, raised LDH and schistocytes on the film. INR and fibrinogen are normal, and creatinine is mildly raised. What is the most appropriate urgent treatment?
options: Platelet transfusion and observation
Urgent plasma exchange with corticosteroids
Oral prednisolone alone for ITP
Intravenous immunoglobulin alone
notes: Platelet transfusion may fuel microthrombi and is avoided in TTP unless life-threatening bleeding.
ITP lacks haemolysis and schistocytes; steroids alone are inadequate in TTP.
IVIG treats ITP but is not definitive for TTP.
questions.why: This is TTP (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, normal coagulation). Urgent plasma exchange with corticosteroids is lifesaving; send ADAMTS13 first and avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding.

questions.stem: Which drug used in Alzheimer disease acts by increasing synaptic acetylcholine?
options: Memantine
Donepezil
Quetiapine
Selegiline
notes: Memantine blocks NMDA receptors, reducing glutamate excitotoxicity.
Quetiapine is an antipsychotic with no cholinergic enhancing action.
Selegiline is an MAO-B inhibitor, not a cholinesterase inhibitor.
questions.why: Donepezil inhibits acetylcholinesterase, raising synaptic acetylcholine. Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist.

questions.stem: Why does septic arthritis cause rapid joint destruction if untreated?
options: Bacterial toxins and neutrophil enzymes degrade articular cartilage
Synovial fluid hyperviscosity compresses the cartilage
Immune complexes deposit in subchondral bone
Urate crystals erode the cartilage matrix
notes: Fluid hyperviscosity is not the mechanism; purulent effusion raises pressure but enzymes are key.
Immune complex deposition characterises some inflammatory arthritides, not acute bacterial destruction.
Urate crystals cause gout, a non-infective mimic.
questions.why: Bacterial products and host neutrophil proteases and cytokines degrade cartilage proteoglycans within days, so urgent washout and antibiotics are needed.

questions.stem: Dengue haemorrhagic features and plasma leakage are most often seen at which time in a secondary dengue infection with a different serotype?
options: Around defervescence, days 3 to 7
On the first day of fever
Several weeks after recovery
During the incubation period
notes: Early febrile phase precedes leakage.
Leakage is not delayed weeks.
Incubation is before symptoms.
questions.why: Antibody-dependent enhancement in heterotypic secondary infection increases immune activation, causing capillary leak at the critical phase near defervescence (days 3-7).

questions.stem: A 26-year-old returns from India with 8 days of stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, constipation and abdominal pain. Blood cultures grow Salmonella Typhi. Which is the best empirical antibiotic choice given regional resistance?
options: Ceftriaxone intravenously
Ciprofloxacin orally
Amoxicillin orally
Doxycycline orally
notes: Fluoroquinolone resistance is very common from South Asia.
Amoxicillin has high resistance and is not empirical therapy.
Doxycycline is not effective treatment for typhoid.
questions.why: Typhoid acquired in South Asia is frequently quinolone-resistant and increasingly multidrug or extensively drug-resistant, so ceftriaxone is the empirical choice until susceptibilities return.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents 24 hours after sudden right facial droop involving the forehead, with an inability to close the right eye. There is no limb weakness and ear examination is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral prednisolone and eye protection
Oral aciclovir alone
Urgent CT brain and aspirin
Observation only without eye care
notes: Antivirals alone are not beneficial; they are not recommended as sole therapy.
Forehead involvement with no other deficits indicates a lower motor neurone lesion, not stroke.
Eye care is essential, and steroids improve outcomes if started early.
questions.why: This is Bell's palsy, with lower motor neurone signs. Prednisolone started within 72 hours improves recovery, and eye lubrication and taping at night prevent corneal damage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a required element of valid consent to treatment?
options: The patient has decision-making capacity
The patient is over 18 years
A family member has agreed
The consent is in writing
notes: Mature minors can consent; age alone does not determine validity.
Family agreement is not required for a capable adult.
Verbal or implied consent can be valid; writing is for evidence or high-risk procedures.
questions.why: Valid consent requires capacity, voluntariness and adequate information. Age and writing are not strict requirements; capacity is decision-specific.

questions.stem: Which maternal marker indicates the highest infectivity and risk of perinatal hepatitis B transmission?
options: Anti-HBs
Anti-HBc IgG alone
HBeAg positivity with high HBV DNA
Anti-HBe
notes: Anti-HBs indicates immunity.
Isolated anti-HBc reflects past exposure and is not a marker of high infectivity.
Anti-HBe suggests lower replication and lower infectivity.
questions.why: HBeAg positivity and high viral load reflect active replication and the greatest transmission risk. Maternal antiviral therapy is considered in the third trimester with high DNA.

questions.stem: In cirrhosis with portal hypertension, which mechanism is the main driver of sodium and water retention leading to ascites?
options: Splanchnic vasodilatation causing effective arterial underfilling and RAAS activation
Raised plasma oncotic pressure from increased hepatic albumin synthesis
Primary renal tubular defect causing sodium wasting
Reduced hepatic aldosterone production
notes: Albumin synthesis falls in cirrhosis, lowering oncotic pressure rather than raising it.
The kidney retains sodium avidly, not wastes it.
Hepatic clearance of aldosterone is reduced, so levels rise, not fall.
questions.why: Portal hypertension causes splanchnic vasodilatation (nitric oxide), lowering effective arterial volume; RAAS and ADH activate, retaining sodium and water. Hypoalbuminaemia also contributes.

questions.stem: What landmark distinguishes an inguinal hernia from a femoral hernia?
options: Position relative to the pubic tubercle
Position relative to the inferior epigastric vessels only
Position relative to the anterior superior iliac spine
Position relative to the umbilicus
notes: Epigastric vessels separate direct from indirect, not inguinal from femoral.
The ASIS marks the inguinal ligament origin but not the hernia distinction.
Umbilicus is relevant to umbilical hernias.
questions.why: Inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernias lie below and lateral to it, through the femoral canal.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with asthma presents with severe wheeze, speaking single words and SpO2 88% on air. She has had no response to initial care. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Oxygen, repeated salbutamol and ipratropium, and systemic corticosteroid
Oral montelukast and observation
Intravenous antibiotics and chest physiotherapy
Nebulised budesonide only and discharge
notes: Montelukast has no role in acute severe asthma.
Infection is not the primary problem; antibiotics and physiotherapy do not treat bronchospasm.
Inhaled steroid alone is inadequate and discharge is unsafe at this severity.
questions.why: Life-threatening or severe asthma needs oxygen, frequent salbutamol with ipratropium, and early systemic corticosteroids, with escalation if there is no response.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man on long-term amiodarone for atrial fibrillation develops progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. HRCT shows bilateral ground-glass change and a low DLCO. Infection is excluded. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Increase the amiodarone dose
Stop amiodarone and consider corticosteroids
Add nitrofurantoin prophylaxis
Continue amiodarone and start diuretics
notes: This would worsen toxicity.
Nitrofurantoin itself causes pulmonary toxicity.
There is no evidence of heart failure; continuing the drug risks progression.
questions.why: Suspected amiodarone pulmonary toxicity: stop the drug, switch rhythm control, and consider corticosteroids if symptomatic or severe. Seek cardiology input.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents one hour after amitriptyline overdose. She is drowsy, with BP 85/50 mmHg and QRS 140 ms on ECG. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
options: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Intravenous flumazenil
Intravenous amiodarone
Intravenous physostigmine
notes: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdoses as it may precipitate seizures.
Amiodarone can worsen conduction block and QT prolongation.
Physostigmine risks seizures and asystole in tricyclic overdose.
questions.why: A wide QRS or hypotension in tricyclic overdose reflects sodium channel blockade. Treat with intravenous sodium bicarbonate.

questions.stem: Most patients with polycythaemia vera carry an acquired JAK2 V617F mutation. What is the main effect of this mutation on haemopoietic progenitor cells?
options: Constitutive cytokine-independent signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway
Loss of function of the erythropoietin gene
Fusion of BCR and ABL1 producing a tyrosine kinase
Impaired iron uptake by erythroid precursors
notes: The mutation does not affect the erythropoietin gene; erythropoietin is suppressed, not lost, because of autonomous red cell production.
BCR-ABL1 defines chronic myeloid leukaemia, not PV.
Iron uptake is not the defect; PV may cause iron deficiency from overproduction, but that is secondary.
questions.why: JAK2 V617F is a gain-of-function mutation causing constitutive JAK-STAT signalling, so progenitors proliferate without needing erythropoietin. Serum erythropoietin is therefore low in PV.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with septic shock from pneumonia is bleeding from line sites. Platelets 22 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, INR 2.1. Antibiotics and fluids are given. Which is the most appropriate additional management?
options: Platelets and fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate or concentrate) for active bleeding
Tranexamic acid infusion
Therapeutic unfractionated heparin
Vitamin K only
notes: Antifibrinolytics are generally avoided in DIC as they risk thrombosis in a prothrombotic state.
Therapeutic heparin would worsen bleeding with this profile.
Vitamin K alone will not correct consumptive coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia.
questions.why: Treat the cause first. In DIC with active bleeding, replace platelets (keep over 50), fibrinogen (keep over 1.5 g/L) and factors with plasma as required.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has sudden right arm weakness and aphasia 90 minutes ago. BP is 170/95 mmHg, glucose 6.5 mmol/L. Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Aspirin 300 mg and observe on a ward
Intravenous tenecteplase now, with CT angiography to assess for large vessel occlusion
Lower BP below 140/90 mmHg before any treatment
Wait for MRI before deciding on thrombolysis
notes: Antiplatelet alone is inadequate in an eligible patient; aspirin is withheld until after thrombolysis and follow-up imaging.
BP of 170/95 is already below the 185/110 mmHg threshold; no lowering is needed.
Waiting for MRI delays treatment; time is brain, and non-contrast CT is sufficient.
