questions.why: Within 4.5 hours with haemorrhage excluded and no contraindications, give IV thrombolysis (tenecteplase) without delay, and image vessels for ECR candidacy. BP must be below 185/110 mmHg.

questions.stem: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people have higher rates of end-stage kidney disease. Which early marker is used to screen for kidney damage, starting earlier than in the general population?
options: Serum urea
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
Urine specific gravity
Serum potassium
notes: Urea rises late and is affected by diet and hydration.
Specific gravity measures concentration and is not a screening marker for kidney damage.
Potassium rises only in advanced disease.
questions.why: Albuminuria (urine ACR) is the earliest marker of kidney damage, along with eGFR. Guidelines advise screening Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people from age 30, or earlier if risk factors exist.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with COPD exacerbation has had 1 hour of optimal medical therapy. ABG on 28% oxygen: pH 7.28, PaCO2 70 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 32 mmol/L. He is drowsy but rousable. What is the next step?
options: Start non-invasive ventilation
Increase oxygen to a non-rebreather mask
Intubate immediately
Give IV sodium bicarbonate
notes: High-flow oxygen can worsen hypercapnia; target saturation 88–92%.
Intubation is for NIV failure or contraindications, not first line here.
Bicarbonate is not indicated; ventilation corrects the acidosis.
questions.why: Acute hypercapnic acidosis (pH below 7.35, PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) persisting after optimal therapy is the indication for NIV in COPD exacerbation. Intubate if NIV fails.

questions.stem: Denosumab reduces bone resorption by which mechanism?
options: Binds RANKL, preventing osteoclast formation and activation
Binds hydroxyapatite and is taken up by osteoclasts
Stimulates osteoblasts via PTH receptor
Inhibits sclerostin to increase bone formation
notes: This describes bisphosphonates.
This describes teriparatide.
This describes romosozumab.
questions.why: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL, inhibiting osteoclast differentiation and function. Its effect is reversible, so stopping causes rapid bone turnover and rebound vertebral fractures.

questions.stem: Warfarin prolongs the INR by reducing the activity of which group of coagulation factors?
options: II, VII, IX and X
I, V, VIII and XIII
XI, XII, prekallikrein and HMWK
III, IV, V and VIII
notes: Factors I, V, VIII and XIII are not vitamin K dependent; this is a mixed group.
These are contact pathway factors; they are not vitamin K dependent and do not affect INR with warfarin.
Factors III and IV are tissue factor and calcium, and V and VIII are not vitamin K dependent.
questions.why: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C and S). Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so INR rises first.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has back pain, fatigue, creatinine 220 µmol/L, corrected calcium 3.0 mmol/L, Hb 85 g/L and a high ESR. Urine dipstick is negative for protein. Which pair of tests is the best initial investigation for suspected myeloma?
options: Serum protein electrophoresis with serum free light chains
Bone scan with serum ferritin
Urine culture with renal ultrasound
Serum PSA with lumbar spine MRI
notes: Bone scans often miss lytic lesions as they are purely osteolytic; ferritin does not diagnose myeloma.
These would not identify a paraprotein.
PSA addresses prostate metastases, but the CRAB features and ESR point towards myeloma.
questions.why: Initial work-up of suspected myeloma is serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains (plus urine). Light chains are missed by dipstick, so a negative dipstick does not exclude Bence Jones proteinuria.

questions.stem: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program uses an immunochemical faecal occult blood test, which needs no dietary restriction, unlike the older guaiac test. What property of the immunochemical test explains this?
options: It detects the peroxidase activity of haem in the stool
It detects tumour-specific DNA mutations shed into the stool
It uses antibodies specific for human globin
It measures faecal calprotectin from mucosal neutrophils
notes: This describes the guaiac test, which reacts with dietary peroxidases and red meat and so needs dietary restriction.
That describes a stool DNA test, which is not used in the national program.
Calprotectin is a marker of intestinal inflammation, not a bowel cancer screening test.
questions.why: The iFOBT uses antibodies against human globin, so dietary animal blood and plant peroxidases do not react. Globin is also digested in the upper GI tract, so it favours lower bowel bleeding.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman using methamphetamine daily asks to cut down but is not ready to stop. She injects occasionally. Which harm minimisation advice is most appropriate?
options: Offer sterile needles and syringes and blood-borne virus testing
Advise stopping all contact until she commits to abstinence
Prescribe dexamfetamine as the standard first-line treatment
Advise that smoking rather than injecting carries no risk
notes: Requiring abstinence first is not harm minimisation and disengages patients.
Substitution with dexamfetamine is not standard and is not first-line.
Smoking still carries cardiac, psychosis and dependence risks.
questions.why: Harm minimisation includes sterile injecting equipment, BBV testing and vaccination, and psychosocial support such as CBT and contingency management. No medication is approved for methamphetamine use disorder.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains the sympathomimetic toxidrome (hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia) and euphoria caused by methamphetamine?
options: Reversal of monoamine transporters, releasing dopamine and noradrenaline
Direct agonism of mu-opioid receptors
Enhanced GABA-A receptor chloride conductance
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at synapses
notes: Mu-opioid agonism gives sedation, miosis and respiratory depression.
GABA-A enhancement causes sedation, as with alcohol and benzodiazepines.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition gives a cholinergic toxidrome with bradycardia and secretions.
questions.why: Methamphetamine enters terminals, disrupts vesicular storage and reverses DAT/NET, flooding synapses with dopamine and noradrenaline.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has fever, confusion and a new focal seizure over two days. Neck stiffness is absent. CT head is normal. After lumbar puncture, which empirical treatment is most appropriate?
options: Intravenous aciclovir
Intravenous ceftriaxone alone
Oral valaciclovir
Intravenous dexamethasone alone
notes: Ceftriaxone alone leaves HSV untreated; aciclovir is needed.
Oral valaciclovir is inadequate for suspected encephalitis, which needs IV therapy.
Steroids alone do not treat the infection and are not indicated for suspected HSV encephalitis.
questions.why: Fever, altered mentation and seizures suggest HSV encephalitis, so give IV aciclovir promptly without waiting for results. Many add ceftriaxone until bacterial meningitis is excluded.

questions.stem: Why does dehydration or sodium depletion raise serum lithium concentration?
options: Proximal tubules reabsorb lithium with sodium, so lithium retention increases
Lithium is metabolised by the liver and hepatic blood flow falls
Lithium binds albumin and is displaced
Lithium is secreted in the loop of Henle and secretion falls
notes: Lithium is not metabolised; it is excreted unchanged by the kidney.
Lithium is not protein bound.
Lithium is reabsorbed, not secreted, along the proximal nephron.
questions.why: Lithium is handled like sodium in the proximal tubule and is renally cleared. Sodium depletion increases proximal reabsorption of both, so levels rise.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has a routine midstream urine showing E. coli >10^8 CFU/L. She has no urinary symptoms and is afebrile. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Treat with targeted antibiotics according to susceptibilities
No treatment; repeat culture at 28 weeks
Treat only if she develops dysuria or fever
Single-dose fosfomycin only if nitrites are positive
notes: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy, unlike in most non-pregnant adults.
Waiting for symptoms risks progression to pyelonephritis, which is why screening is done.
Treatment depends on culture and susceptibilities, not a dipstick nitrite result.
questions.why: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated, as it increases the risk of pyelonephritis, preterm birth and low birthweight. Choose an agent by susceptibility and safe in pregnancy, then confirm cure.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has fever, loin pain and a 5 mm obstructing ureteric stone on CT, with hydronephrosis, BP 85/50 mmHg and HR 120. What is the most appropriate next step after IV fluids and antibiotics?
options: Urgent decompression with stent or nephrostomy
Oral tamsulosin and review in a week
Elective ureteroscopy next week
Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy tomorrow
notes: Medical expulsive therapy is inappropriate in septic obstruction.
Delay risks septic shock; definitive treatment waits until infection is treated.
Lithotripsy in infected obstruction can worsen sepsis; decompress first.
questions.why: An obstructed infected kidney is a urological emergency; urgent decompression (stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) is needed with antibiotics. Definitive stone treatment follows once sepsis resolves.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is confused and dehydrated. Corrected calcium is 3.4 mmol/L. What is the first-line initial management?
options: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride
Oral cinacalcet
Intravenous furosemide
Oral calcium-restricted diet
notes: Cinacalcet is used in primary or parathyroid carcinoma hypercalcaemia, not as acute first-line in malignancy.
Furosemide is only used after rehydration if fluid overloaded; it risks worsening volume depletion.
Dietary calcium is irrelevant in acute malignant hypercalcaemia.
questions.why: Severe hypercalcaemia causes volume depletion, so rehydration with IV normal saline comes first, followed by an IV bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman develops confusion two weeks after starting sertraline. Sodium is 122 mmol/L with concentrated urine. Which mechanism most likely explains this?
options: Reduced aldosterone secretion
Inappropriate ADH secretion causing water retention
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Primary polydipsia suppressing ADH
notes: Aldosterone deficiency causes hypovolaemic hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, not typical of SSRIs.
Nephrogenic DI causes dilute urine and hypernatraemia.
Polydipsia gives dilute urine, not concentrated.
questions.why: SSRIs can cause SIADH, producing euvolaemic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine. Risk is highest in older women in the first weeks.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman, day 2 after hip fracture repair, is agitated at night, pulling at her drip, and disoriented. Vitals are normal. She is aggressive only when staff approach. What is the best initial management?
options: Regular lorazepam
Physical restraints for safety
Non-drug measures and a search for the cause
Regular haloperidol
notes: Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
Restraints increase agitation, injury and prolonged delirium.
Antipsychotics are a short-term last resort if non-drug measures fail and there is risk, not regular first-line.
questions.why: First-line delirium care is identifying and treating causes (pain, constipation, retention, infection, drugs) with non-drug measures: reorientation, glasses, sleep, mobilisation. Drugs are reserved for distress or danger.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has ALT 620 U/L, AST 540 U/L, ALP 110 U/L (normal) and bilirubin 35 µmol/L after a paracetamol overdose. Which pattern is this?
options: Cholestatic
Hepatocellular
Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Infiltrative
notes: Cholestasis has ALP/GGT predominance.
Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia has normal enzymes.
Infiltrative disease typically raises ALP with normal or mildly raised ALT.
questions.why: Markedly raised aminotransferases with near-normal ALP indicates hepatocellular injury. Cholestatic patterns show ALP and GGT disproportionately raised.

questions.stem: Chronic kidney disease occurs earlier in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Which developmental mechanism contributes, through low birthweight and prematurity?
options: Reduced nephron number at birth
Excess glomerular basement membrane
Congenital renal artery stenosis
Reduced tubular reabsorption capacity
notes: Not a recognised mechanism; low nephron endowment, not excess basement membrane, links low birthweight to CKD.
Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension, not a feature of low birthweight programming.
Tubular capacity is not the primary issue; the problem is fewer glomeruli to share the filtration load.
questions.why: Nephrogenesis finishes by about 36 weeks, so prematurity or growth restriction leaves fewer nephrons. Remaining nephrons hyperfilter and scar, raising lifetime CKD risk.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man had a left hemispheric TIA 5 days ago. Carotid duplex and CT angiography show 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. He is fit for surgery. What is the best management?
options: Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks of the event
Medical therapy alone, as stenosis is under 90%
Carotid endarterectomy after 3 months
Warfarin to target INR 2.5
notes: Benefit is established for 70–99% symptomatic stenosis; best medical therapy is also given but surgery is added.
Benefit decays with delay; waiting 3 months forfeits the early risk reduction.
Anticoagulation is not superior to antiplatelets for carotid atherosclerosis.
questions.why: Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70–99% benefits most from endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of symptoms, alongside best medical therapy.

questions.stem: By which mechanism do SGLT2 inhibitors predispose to euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis?
options: Glycosuria lowers glucose and insulin while raising glucagon, promoting ketogenesis
They block hepatic gluconeogenesis, causing lactate accumulation
They stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion, causing hypoglycaemia
They inhibit lipolysis, reducing ketone clearance
notes: Lactic acidosis relates to metformin, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
Insulin secretion is not stimulated; that is sulfonylurea action.
SGLT2 inhibitors promote, not inhibit, lipolysis and ketogenesis.
questions.why: Urinary glucose loss lowers glucose and insulin and raises glucagon, driving lipolysis and ketogenesis despite normal glucose. Illness, fasting and surgery increase risk.

questions.stem: Tacrolimus is used after kidney transplantation. Through which mechanism does it suppress rejection?
options: Inhibiting calcineurin and reducing T-cell IL-2 production
Inhibiting inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase in lymphocytes
Blocking the IL-2 receptor on activated T cells
Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase
notes: That describes mycophenolate.
That describes basiliximab.
That describes methotrexate.
questions.why: Tacrolimus binds FKBP12 and inhibits calcineurin, so NFAT is not activated and IL-2 transcription falls. Its toxicities include nephrotoxicity, tremor and diabetes.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old has had 3 days of coryza and cough, with tachypnoea, subcostal recession and widespread crackles and wheeze. Oxygen saturation is 94% in room air and feeding is reduced but adequate. What is the best management?
options: Nebulised salbutamol trial
Oral dexamethasone
Supportive care with minimal handling and no oxygen
Low-flow oxygen to keep saturation above 98%
notes: Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and are not recommended.
Corticosteroids are not effective in bronchiolitis.
Oxygen is indicated only if saturation is persistently below 90%; targeting above 98% is unnecessary.
questions.why: PREDICT/Australasian guidance: bronchiolitis is managed supportively. Oxygen is not needed if saturations are 90% or above; avoid bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics.

questions.stem: Which mechanism of action best explains why carbamazepine can control focal seizures but may worsen generalised absence seizures?
options: Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels
Enhancement of GABA-A receptor chloride conductance
Blockade of T-type calcium channels in thalamus
Inhibition of synaptic vesicle protein SV2A
notes: GABA-A enhancement is the benzodiazepine and barbiturate mechanism, and these do not worsen absence seizures.
T-type calcium blockade is how ethosuximide treats absence seizures; carbamazepine lacks this action.
SV2A binding is levetiracetam's mechanism; it is broad-spectrum and does not worsen absence seizures.
questions.why: Carbamazepine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, limiting high-frequency firing in focal seizures. It can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures, which depend on thalamocortical T-type calcium currents.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has had 3 hours of a painful, pale, cold left leg with absent pulses and reduced sensation and power. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Oral aspirin and outpatient duplex
Elevate the leg and apply warm packs
Wait for CT angiography before anticoagulating
Intravenous unfractionated heparin and urgent vascular review
notes: Outpatient assessment is unacceptable in a threatened limb.
Warming and elevation worsen ischaemia and delay treatment.
Heparin should not wait for imaging in a threatened limb.
questions.why: Suspected embolic acute limb ischaemia with a threatened limb needs immediate heparin to prevent propagation, analgesia and urgent vascular surgical revascularisation.

questions.stem: Which hormone, released from duodenal I cells in response to fat in the duodenum, causes gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi?
options: Secretin
Cholecystokinin
Gastrin
Motilin
notes: Secretin stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion in response to duodenal acid.
Gastrin, from G cells, stimulates gastric acid secretion.
Motilin drives the migrating motor complex in fasting, not gallbladder emptying after meals.
questions.why: Cholecystokinin is released in response to fat and protein; it contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. This explains biliary colic after fatty meals.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting and drowsiness. Glucose 28 mmol/L, pH 7.1, ketones 5.0 mmol/L, K+ 3.0 mmol/L. Fluids are running. What is the most appropriate next step regarding insulin?
options: Start IV insulin infusion now alongside potassium replacement
Give IV insulin bolus of 10 units and then infusion
Delay insulin until potassium is above 5.5 mmol/L
Delay insulin until potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L
notes: Starting insulin with K+ 3.0 mmol/L risks dangerous hypokalaemia and arrhythmia.
Boluses are not recommended; and it does not address the low potassium.
Insulin is withheld only if K+ is below about 3.3 mmol/L, not until above 5.5 mmol/L.
questions.why: With K+ below 3.3 mmol/L, insulin would drive potassium intracellularly and risk arrhythmia, so replace potassium first and start insulin once K+ is at least 3.3 mmol/L.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man on methadone for opioid use disorder is counselled on overdose prevention. Which is the most appropriate item to supply?
options: Take-home naloxone with instructions for family
Take-home flumazenil
Extra methadone doses for emergencies
Oral activated charcoal sachets
notes: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
Extra methadone increases overdose risk.
Activated charcoal is not a community overdose measure and risks aspiration.
questions.why: Take-home naloxone (intranasal or injectable) should be offered to people at risk of opioid overdose and their contacts, available without prescription in Australia.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with known HFrEF presents with acute pulmonary oedema, SpO2 88% on air, BP 150/90, and is warm and wet. What is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
options: Intravenous furosemide with oxygen
Intravenous metoprolol
Oral spironolactone
Intravenous verapamil
notes: IV beta-blockers can worsen acute decompensation.
Spironolactone is too slow to treat acute pulmonary oedema.
Verapamil is negatively inotropic and harmful in HFrEF.
questions.why: Congested, normotensive acute decompensation needs IV loop diuretic and oxygen if hypoxic; consider nitrates and NIV if severe.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has bilateral enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts. His mother and brother have the same condition. What is the most likely mode of inheritance?
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Mitochondrial
notes: Autosomal recessive PKD presents in neonates or infants and parents are usually unaffected.
X-linked recessive disease would mainly affect males and not pass from mother to son in this pattern.
Mitochondrial inheritance passes through the mother to all children and is not the pattern of ADPKD.
questions.why: ADPKD (PKD1 or PKD2 mutations) is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk. Autosomal recessive PKD presents in infancy.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman's cervical screening test shows oncogenic HPV (not 16/18) detected, with LBC showing negative or low-grade changes. What is the recommended management?
options: Routine screening in 5 years
Immediate colposcopy
Repeat HPV test in 12 months
Hysterectomy planning
notes: Routine 5-yearly screening is for HPV not detected.
Colposcopy is indicated for HPV 16/18 or for high-grade cytology.
Not indicated.
questions.why: Oncogenic HPV (not 16/18) with negative/low-grade LBC is intermediate risk: repeat HPV testing in 12 months. Colposcopy is for HPV 16/18 or higher-grade cytology.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has 3 days of lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia and mucopurulent discharge. She has cervical motion tenderness and temperature 37.8°C, is tolerating oral fluids, and hCG is negative. What is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
options: Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once, then doxycycline and metronidazole orally for 14 days
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days alone
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid orally for 5 days
notes: Azithromycin alone does not cover anaerobes or reliably treat gonorrhoea, and one dose is too short for PID.
Doxycycline alone misses gonorrhoea and anaerobes and is too short a course.
This does not cover chlamydia or gonorrhoea adequately and is not a PID regimen.
questions.why: Mild-to-moderate PID is treated empirically with ceftriaxone IM plus doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days, covering gonorrhoea, chlamydia and anaerobes. Treat early to protect fertility.

questions.stem: Treponema pallidum is transmitted across the placenta. Which feature of the organism and maternal disease best explains why congenital syphilis can occur in a mother with no symptoms?
options: Latent infection still permits spirochaetaemia that can seed the fetus
The organism is only released from genital ulcers
Maternal IgG blocks placental transfer of the organism
Fetal infection occurs only at delivery through the birth canal
notes: Ulcers are infectious by contact, but haematogenous spread occurs without lesions.
Maternal IgG does not prevent transplacental spread of treponemes.
Congenital syphilis is acquired transplacentally, not mainly at delivery.
questions.why: Treponemes can circulate in the blood during early and sometimes latent infection, crossing the placenta from about the second trimester. Maternal screening is therefore essential even without symptoms.

questions.stem: A smoker has hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and low serum osmolality. Which lung cancer type most typically causes this paraneoplastic syndrome through ectopic ADH?
options: Small cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma
Adenocarcinoma
Large cell carcinoma
notes: Squamous cell cancer is classically linked with PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia.
Adenocarcinoma is associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy and thromboembolism, not typical SIADH.
Large cell carcinoma can secrete hCG (gynaecomastia) but is not the classic SIADH cause.
questions.why: Small cell lung cancer arises from neuroendocrine cells and secretes ADH (SIADH) and ACTH. Squamous cell cancer typically causes PTHrP hypercalcaemia.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has asthma with symptoms twice weekly, using salbutamol only. She has had no recent exacerbations. According to the Australian Asthma Handbook, which is the preferred reliever approach?
options: As-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol
Regular daily oral montelukast alone
Regular salmeterol twice daily
Salbutamol as needed with no other change
notes: Montelukast is not preferred first-line and does not replace an inhaled corticosteroid-containing reliever.
LABA without an inhaled corticosteroid is unsafe in asthma.
SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended as it increases exacerbation risk.
questions.why: The Handbook recommends as-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol as the preferred reliever for adults with mild asthma, reducing exacerbations compared with salbutamol alone.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent haemarthroses. APTT is prolonged and PT is normal; the APTT corrects with normal plasma. Which role of factor VIII explains this?
options: Cofactor for factor IXa in activating factor X in the intrinsic pathway
Cofactor for factor VIIa in the extrinsic pathway
Cross-linking fibrin
Activating protein C
notes: The extrinsic pathway involves tissue factor and VIIa, measured by PT, which is normal.
Fibrin cross-linking is factor XIII.
Protein C is activated by thrombin-thrombomodulin and is anticoagulant.
questions.why: Factor VIII is a cofactor for factor IXa in the tenase complex activating factor X. Deficiency (X-linked haemophilia A) prolongs APTT with normal PT.

questions.stem: A traveller plans 3 months working in rural Papua New Guinea and the Torres Strait islands during the wet season. Which prevention measure is most appropriate against Japanese encephalitis?
options: Japanese encephalitis vaccination and mosquito avoidance
Doxycycline prophylaxis
Ribavirin prophylaxis
Mosquito avoidance alone is sufficient
notes: Doxycycline does not prevent viral infection.
Ribavirin is not used for prophylaxis.
Prolonged stay in risk areas warrants vaccination too.
questions.why: Japanese encephalitis vaccine is recommended for those spending prolonged time in Torres Strait or PNG at risk, together with repellents and protective clothing.

questions.stem: Leptospira interrogans is shed in the urine of rodents and livestock. Through which route does it most commonly enter humans in Queensland cane and banana farms?
options: Abraded skin or mucous membranes exposed to contaminated water or soil
Inhalation of dried faecal dust
Bite from an infected mosquito
Ingestion of unpasteurised milk
notes: Inhalation of dust describes Q fever and psittacosis, not usual leptospirosis.
Leptospirosis is not mosquito-borne.
Unpasteurised milk is a brucellosis route.
questions.why: Leptospires enter through cuts, abraded skin or mucous membranes after contact with water or soil contaminated by animal urine. This explains flood and wet-season exposure.

questions.stem: Abrupt cessation of chronic heavy alcohol intake causes tremor, tachycardia and seizures. Which change in neurotransmission best explains this?
options: Reduced GABA-A inhibition with increased NMDA glutamate activity
Increased GABA-A inhibition with reduced glutamate activity
Reduced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens only
Increased serotonin reuptake in the raphe nuclei
notes: This is the acute intoxicated state, not withdrawal; adaptation reverses it on cessation.
Dopamine changes relate to reward and craving, not the autonomic hyperactivity and seizures of withdrawal.
Serotonin reuptake changes do not explain withdrawal hyperexcitability.
questions.why: Chronic alcohol enhances GABA-A and inhibits NMDA; adaptation downregulates GABA and upregulates NMDA, so cessation leaves CNS hyperexcitability. This is why benzodiazepines (GABA-A agonists) treat withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma presents with hypotension, vomiting and lethargy after pituitary surgery. Sodium is 124 mmol/L. Both cortisol and thyroxine are low. Which replacement should be given first?
options: Hydrocortisone before levothyroxine
Levothyroxine before hydrocortisone
Testosterone before either
Desmopressin before either
notes: Starting levothyroxine first can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Gonadal replacement is not urgent and comes later.
Desmopressin is for diabetes insipidus, not indicated by these findings.
questions.why: Glucocorticoid must be replaced before thyroid hormone, because levothyroxine increases cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer has 3 days of thoracic back pain, now with bilateral leg weakness and a sensory level at T8. He is still able to walk with help. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Dexamethasone and urgent whole-spine MRI
Outpatient MRI within 2 weeks
Lumbar puncture and CSF cytology
Oral analgesia and physiotherapy review
notes: Delay risks irreversible paralysis; imaging must be urgent, within hours.
Lumbar puncture risks neurological deterioration with a compressive lesion and doesn't define it.
Analgesia alone ignores a cord compression emergency.
questions.why: Suspected malignant spinal cord compression is an emergency: give high-dose dexamethasone and arrange urgent whole-spine MRI, then oncology/neurosurgical and radiotherapy review to preserve function.

questions.stem: Which hypersensitivity mechanism underlies immediate reactions such as urticaria and anaphylaxis occurring within an hour of a penicillin dose?
options: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
Immune complex deposition
T cell-mediated delayed reaction
IgG-mediated cytotoxicity
notes: Immune complexes (type III) cause serum sickness days later.
T cell-mediated type IV reactions are delayed, like contact dermatitis or SCARs.
Type II cytotoxic reactions cause haemolytic anaemia, not urticaria.
questions.why: Type I hypersensitivity involves pre-formed specific IgE on mast cells, releasing histamine and tryptase on re-exposure. This is why immediate reactions are the main concern for delabelling.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has 8 months of amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Pregnancy test is negative, prolactin is 3800 mIU/L (repeated), and MRI shows a 7 mm pituitary microadenoma. Visual fields are normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Cabergoline
Transsphenoidal surgery
Pituitary radiotherapy
Combined oral contraceptive pill alone
notes: Surgery is second-line for dopamine agonist resistance or intolerance.
Radiotherapy is rarely used and is slow with a risk of hypopituitarism.
The pill may restore bleeding but does not treat the tumour or galactorrhoea.
questions.why: Dopamine agonists, usually cabergoline, are first-line for symptomatic prolactinoma, normalising prolactin and shrinking the tumour. Surgery is reserved for resistance or intolerance.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has 3 days of vomiting and diarrhoea. He takes perindopril, indapamide and regular ibuprofen. BP 95/60 mmHg, dry mucous membranes. Creatinine 220 µmol/L (baseline 90). Urine sodium is low, urine osmolality high. What is the most likely cause?
options: Acute tubular necrosis
Prerenal acute kidney injury
Post-renal obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy
Acute interstitial nephritis from ibuprofen
notes: ATN gives high urine sodium and isosmolar urine with muddy brown casts; it may follow prolonged prerenal injury.
Obstruction would not explain hypotension with concentrated, low-sodium urine.
AIN usually has rash, eosinophilia or white cells in urine, and tubular dysfunction with high urine sodium.
questions.why: Volume depletion plus ACEi, diuretic and NSAID reduces renal perfusion. Low urine sodium and concentrated urine show intact tubular function, typical of prerenal injury.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has oligomenorrhoea and hirsutism. Ultrasound shows polycystic-appearing ovaries. TSH and prolactin are normal. According to the 2023 international guideline, which finding is needed to confirm PCOS?
options: Raised testosterone with a normal ultrasound
Raised LH:FSH ratio on day 3 bloods
Anti-Müllerian hormone above 10 pmol/L
Two of three: irregular cycles, hyperandrogenism, or ultrasound features
notes: Testosterone alone is not diagnostic; two criteria are needed.
LH:FSH ratio is not a diagnostic criterion.
AMH can serve as an alternative to ultrasound, but a threshold alone does not confirm PCOS without another feature.
questions.why: Rotterdam criteria need two of three features. Ultrasound or AMH can replace the ultrasound criterion in adults, and exclusion of other causes (thyroid, prolactin, congenital adrenal hyperplasia) is required.

questions.stem: By which mechanism do NSAIDs predispose to peptic ulcer disease?
options: Direct stimulation of gastrin release
Increased gastric acid secretion by parietal cells
Reduced prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection via COX-1 inhibition
Impaired gastric emptying causing acid reflux
notes: NSAIDs do not act mainly by raising gastrin.
Acid secretion is not primarily increased; the defence is weakened.
Delayed emptying is not the main mechanism.
questions.why: COX-1 inhibition reduces gastric prostaglandins, which normally promote mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow. Mucosal defence falls, even with normal acid.

questions.stem: Which hypothalamic signal normally regulates prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary, so that a pituitary stalk lesion raises prolactin?
options: Dopamine inhibiting lactotrophs
TRH inhibiting lactotrophs
Somatostatin inhibiting lactotrophs
GHRH stimulating lactotrophs
notes: TRH stimulates prolactin release modestly; it is not the tonic inhibitor.
Somatostatin inhibits GH and TSH, not the main prolactin brake.
GHRH stimulates somatotrophs (GH), not lactotrophs.
questions.why: Prolactin is under tonic inhibition by hypothalamic dopamine. Stalk compression or dopamine antagonists remove this and raise prolactin; dopamine agonists treat prolactinoma.

questions.stem: HIV causes immunodeficiency by infecting a specific cell population. Which cell and surface molecule is the main target that explains the rise in opportunistic infections?
options: CD4 T lymphocytes via CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4
CD8 T lymphocytes via CD8
B lymphocytes via CD19
Neutrophils via CD16
notes: CD8 cells are not the main target.
B cells are not the main target of HIV.
Neutrophils are not infected; their function is largely preserved.
questions.why: HIV binds CD4 with a CCR5 or CXCR4 co-receptor, depleting CD4 T helper cells. Opportunistic infections rise as the count falls below about 200 cells/µL.

questions.stem: What is the main mechanism by which funnel-web spider venom causes autonomic storm?
options: Prolongs opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
Blocks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Inhibits acetylcholinesterase
Blocks presynaptic calcium channels
notes: Postsynaptic nicotinic blockade describes curare-like toxins, not funnel-web venom.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is organophosphate toxicity.
Calcium channel blockade is not the funnel-web mechanism.
questions.why: Delta-atracotoxin slows sodium channel inactivation, causing repetitive firing and massive autonomic neurotransmitter release.

questions.stem: Which component of Virchow's triad is most increased by prolonged immobility during and after surgery?
options: Venous stasis
Endothelial injury
Hypercoagulability
Platelet dysfunction
notes: Endothelial injury is more related to direct vessel trauma.
Hypercoagulability arises from the surgical stress response rather than immobility.
Platelet dysfunction is not part of Virchow's triad.
questions.why: Immobility and anaesthesia reduce venous flow in the calf, causing stasis. Surgery also adds hypercoagulability and endothelial injury.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease missed dialysis. He is dyspnoeic with crackles, K+ 7.2 mmol/L with peaked T waves, and urea 48 mmol/L. After IV calcium gluconate, what is the definitive treatment?
options: Oral calcium resonium alone
Urgent haemodialysis
Intravenous furosemide alone
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion
notes: Resin is slow and insufficient for life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
He is likely anuric or oliguric, so a diuretic will not work.
Bicarbonate has limited effect and adds sodium load.
questions.why: Refractory hyperkalaemia with fluid overload in an anuric patient needs urgent dialysis. Calcium protects the myocardium temporarily, and insulin-dextrose shifts potassium, but neither removes it.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has a barking cough and stridor at rest, with suprasternal and subcostal recession. He is distressed but alert and saturation is 97%. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 5 days
Nebulised budesonide 1 mg
Intravenous ceftriaxone
notes: Prednisolone courses are not the standard for croup; single-dose dexamethasone is preferred.
Nebulised budesonide is an alternative but oral dexamethasone is first line in Australia.
Croup is viral; antibiotics are not indicated.
questions.why: Moderate croup (stridor at rest with recession) is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (up to 0.6 mg/kg may be used); add nebulised adrenaline if severe.

questions.stem: Phaeochromocytomas arise from which cells, accounting for their catecholamine secretion?
options: Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells
Zona glomerulosa cells
Zona fasciculata cells
Juxtaglomerular cells
notes: Zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone.
Zona fasciculata produces cortisol.
Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin.
questions.why: Phaeochromocytomas arise from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla and secrete adrenaline, noradrenaline or dopamine.

questions.stem: Absolute CVD risk estimates the chance of events from atherosclerosis. Which is the earliest step in atherosclerotic plaque formation?
options: Retention and oxidation of LDL particles in the subendothelial intima
Smooth muscle migration forming a fibrous cap
Plaque rupture with overlying thrombosis
Calcification of the plaque core
notes: The fibrous cap forms later, after foam cells and a lipid core have developed.
Rupture and thrombosis are late complications that cause acute events.
Calcification is a late feature of established plaque.
questions.why: Endothelial dysfunction allows LDL to be retained and oxidised in the intima, which then recruits monocytes that become foam cells. Fibrous cap formation, calcification and rupture come later.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old had a 2-minute generalised seizure with a febrile viral illness and is now back to normal. You counsel the parents. What is the best advice about prevention of recurrence?
options: Give regular paracetamol to prevent recurrence
Start daily sodium valproate
Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence of febrile seizures
Start regular levetiracetam
notes: Paracetamol does not prevent recurrence, though it can be used for comfort.
Daily anticonvulsants are not indicated for simple febrile seizures.
Regular levetiracetam is not indicated for simple febrile seizures.
questions.why: Antipyretics do not reduce febrile seizure recurrence, and prophylactic anticonvulsants are not indicated for simple febrile seizures. Reassure and teach first aid.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with vomiting and poor intake has pH 7.30, Na 140, Cl 90, HCO3 14 mmol/L, normal albumin. The anion gap is 36 and the delta ratio is about 2.4. What does this indicate?
options: Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis
Pure normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
High anion gap acidosis with concurrent metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
notes: A pure HAGMA gives a delta ratio of about 1 to 2.
The anion gap is markedly raised, so this is not a normal gap acidosis.
Bicarbonate is low as the primary change, so this is not respiratory acidosis with compensation.
questions.why: A delta ratio above 2 means bicarbonate has fallen less than the gap has risen, indicating a concurrent metabolic alkalosis (here from vomiting).

questions.stem: In multiple myeloma, which free light chain finding explains the cast nephropathy seen on renal biopsy?
options: Filtered Bence Jones protein precipitating with Tamm–Horsfall protein in distal tubules
Immune complex deposition in glomerular basement membranes
Hypercalcaemia-induced afferent arteriolar dilatation
Renal artery stenosis from vascular infiltration
notes: Immune complex disease is not the mechanism of cast nephropathy.
Hypercalcaemia causes vasoconstriction and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, not afferent dilatation.
Renal artery stenosis is not a feature of myeloma.
questions.why: Excess monoclonal light chains are filtered and form casts with Tamm–Horsfall protein in distal tubules, causing obstruction and injury. Dipstick is often negative for protein as it detects albumin.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man on postoperative day 6 after anterior resection has fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain and rising CRP. Which complication is most likely?
options: Atelectasis
Anastomotic leak
Surgical site infection of the wound
Urinary tract infection
notes: Atelectasis causes fever in the first 48 hours.
Wound infection is usually day 5–7 with local erythema and discharge, but systemic abdominal pain after bowel anastomosis points to a leak.
UTI is possible but does not explain abdominal pain and tachycardia after bowel surgery.
questions.why: Anastomotic leak typically presents at days 5–7 with fever, tachycardia, pain and raised inflammatory markers; CT with contrast confirms it.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains why ketones accumulate in diabetic ketoacidosis?
options: Insulin deficiency drives unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis
Excess insulin suppresses ketone clearance by the kidney
Hyperglycaemia directly converts glucose into acetoacetate
Cortisol deficiency blocks beta-oxidation of fatty acids
notes: Insulin excess suppresses ketogenesis; it does not impair renal ketone clearance.
Ketones come from fatty acid oxidation, not direct glucose conversion.
Beta-oxidation is increased, not blocked, in DKA; counter-regulatory hormones are raised.
questions.why: Absent insulin removes inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase, so free fatty acids flood the liver and are converted to ketones, causing anion gap acidosis.

questions.stem: Why does primary adrenal insufficiency cause hyperkalaemia, but secondary adrenal insufficiency does not?
options: Cortisol deficiency directly impairs distal tubular potassium secretion
Raised ACTH inhibits renal potassium excretion
Aldosterone is lost only in primary disease, as the RAAS drives its release
Hyponatraemia shifts potassium out of cells
notes: Cortisol deficiency causes hyponatraemia via ADH, but the hyperkalaemia is from aldosterone loss.
ACTH has no inhibitory effect on renal potassium excretion; it causes pigmentation in primary disease.
Hyponatraemia does not cause a transcellular potassium shift.
questions.why: Aldosterone secretion depends mainly on angiotensin II and potassium, not ACTH. It is lost only when the adrenal cortex itself is destroyed, causing sodium loss and potassium retention.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with CKD has weakness. Potassium is 7.4 mmol/L and ECG shows broad QRS and peaked T waves. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Intravenous calcium gluconate
Oral sodium zirconium cyclosilicate alone
Intravenous insulin with glucose alone
Nebulised salbutamol alone
notes: Slow onset; it removes potassium but does not protect the heart immediately.
Shifts potassium but takes 15 to 30 minutes and does not protect the myocardium.
Shifts potassium, but is adjunctive and not first-line cardiac protection.
questions.why: With ECG changes, give IV calcium gluconate first to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin-dextrose, salbutamol and potassium removal. Calcium does not lower potassium.

questions.stem: How do SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin benefit patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
options: They cause glycosuria and natriuresis, reducing preload and hospitalisation
They block the beta-1 receptor to slow the heart rate
They antagonise aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor
They inhibit neprilysin to raise natriuretic peptides
notes: That is the beta-blocker mechanism.
That is the mineralocorticoid antagonists' mechanism (spironolactone, eplerenone).
That is sacubitril, part of ARNI.
questions.why: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF hospitalisation and cardiovascular death, irrespective of diabetes, partly through osmotic diuresis and natriuresis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency. She is afebrile with no flank pain, is not pregnant, and has no vaginal discharge. Which is the most appropriate empirical oral treatment per eTG?
options: Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
Cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 14 days
notes: Fluoroquinolones should be reserved for pyelonephritis or resistant organisms due to adverse effects and resistance.
Amoxicillin has high E. coli resistance and is not recommended empirically.
A 14-day course is far too long for uncomplicated cystitis.
questions.why: For uncomplicated cystitis, eTG first-line options include trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days, or alternatives such as cefalexin or nitrofurantoin. Fluoroquinolones are reserved because of resistance and adverse effects.

questions.stem: Which organism causes most community-acquired urinary tract infections, ascending from the periurethral flora via the urethra?
options: Escherichia coli
Staphylococcus saprophyticus
Proteus mirabilis
Enterococcus faecalis
notes: S. saprophyticus is the second most common cause in young sexually active women but is far less frequent than E. coli.
Proteus is associated with struvite stones and alkaline urine, and is a minority of UTIs.
Enterococcus is more often seen in healthcare-associated or catheter-related infection.
questions.why: Uropathogenic E. coli, using P fimbriae and type 1 pili to adhere to urothelium, causes about 70–80% of community UTIs. Remember that females have a short urethra close to the anus.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with known ulcerative colitis has 9 bloody stools daily, HR 110, temperature 38.2°C, CRP 80 mg/L. Intravenous hydrocortisone is started. What is the most appropriate additional step?
options: Daily abdominal X-ray and early surgical review
Oral mesalazine dose escalation
Loperamide for symptom control
Outpatient azathioprine commencement
notes: Oral mesalazine is inadequate for acute severe colitis.
Antimotility agents risk precipitating toxic megacolon.
Azathioprine is slow-acting and not for acute rescue; this patient needs inpatient care.
questions.why: This is acute severe colitis (Truelove and Witts). Admit, give IV corticosteroids, thromboprophylaxis, monitor for toxic megacolon, involve surgeons early, and escalate to infliximab or ciclosporin if no response by day 3.

questions.stem: Why must potassium be monitored closely and replaced early once an insulin infusion starts in diabetic ketoacidosis, even if the initial serum level is normal or high?
options: Insulin drives potassium into cells, unmasking total body depletion
Insulin increases renal potassium reabsorption
IV fluids cause potassium to bind to albumin
Ketones are cleared by the kidney together with potassium
notes: Insulin does not increase renal potassium reabsorption; its effect is cellular uptake.
Fluids dilute potassium but do not bind it to albumin.
Ketones are excreted as anions with sodium and potassium, but this is not why levels fall on insulin.
questions.why: Acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells and osmotic diuresis depletes total stores; insulin returns potassium into cells and serum levels fall rapidly.

questions.stem: Parkinson's disease results from loss of dopaminergic neurones in which structure?
options: Substantia nigra pars compacta
Caudate nucleus
Subthalamic nucleus
Cerebellar vermis
notes: The caudate receives the dopamine; it is not the site of primary neuronal loss.
The subthalamic nucleus is overactive downstream, not the site of loss.
Cerebellar disease causes ataxia and intention tremor, not parkinsonism.
questions.why: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta reduces striatal dopamine, producing bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor.

questions.stem: A GP assesses a 28-year-old with moderate depression and plans a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan. After preparing it, when is the earliest recommended review of the plan?
options: Within 4 weeks to 3 months
Within 12 months
Only when the patient requests it
After 6 sessions with a psychologist only
notes: Twelve months is too long for the initial review.
Review is scheduled by the GP, not left to patient request.
A further review follows the sessions, but the initial review is earlier.
questions.why: The GP should review the patient 4 weeks to 3 months after preparing the plan, then again after the course of services.

questions.stem: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii. Which feature of the organism best explains why abattoir workers can be infected without direct animal contact?
options: It forms a hardy spore-like form that persists in dust and spreads by aerosol
It is transmitted by a tick vector that infests carcasses
It produces a heat-stable enterotoxin in raw meat
It penetrates intact skin from contaminated water
notes: Ticks can carry it, but human infection is mainly by inhalation, not tick bite.
Q fever is not a toxin-mediated food poisoning.
Skin penetration from water describes leptospirosis, not Q fever.
questions.why: Coxiella burnetii forms resistant small-cell variants that survive in the environment and are inhaled as aerosols from birth products, hides and dust. Very few organisms are needed to infect.

questions.stem: A man on regular oral morphine develops hard stools and straining. Which mechanism best explains why opioid-induced constipation does not show tolerance over time?
options: Mu-receptor activation in the enteric nervous system reduces peristalsis and secretions
Opioids increase bile acid delivery to the colon, slowing transit
Opioids block cholinesterase in the gut wall
Opioids cause central vagal stimulation that raises sphincter tone only
notes: Opioids reduce, not increase, bile and pancreatic secretions; this is not the mechanism.
Opioids do not inhibit cholinesterase; they reduce acetylcholine release from enteric neurons.
The effect is mainly peripheral enteric, not central vagal, and involves more than sphincter tone.
questions.why: Mu-opioid receptors in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses reduce propulsion and secretion and increase sphincter tone. Tolerance to this effect is minimal, so prophylactic laxatives are needed for as long as opioids continue.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on day 6 after open appendicectomy for perforation has fever and a red, tender, swollen wound with purulent discharge. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the best initial management?
options: Open the wound and drain the pus
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam alone
Observe for 48 hours
Return to theatre for laparotomy
notes: Antibiotics alone are insufficient without drainage of pus.
Observation is inappropriate for a purulent infected wound.
Laparotomy is not needed when he is stable and the problem is superficial.
questions.why: Surgical site infection with pus needs source control: open the wound, drain and irrigate. Antibiotics are added for spreading cellulitis or systemic illness.

questions.stem: In an adult, the spinal cord ends at approximately which vertebral level, so that a lesion below it causes lower motor neurone signs from compression of the cauda equina?
options: L1–L2
L4–L5
S2
notes: The cord ends lower than T12; T12 is too high.
L4–L5 is where lumbar puncture is done, below the conus, but not where the cord ends.
S2 is the level of the end of the dural sac, not the spinal cord.
questions.why: The adult conus medullaris ends at about L1–L2. Below this the canal contains lumbosacral nerve roots (cauda equina), so compression gives LMN signs, not UMN signs.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man has 3 months of epigastric burning, relieved by food. He has no weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting or anaemia, takes no NSAIDs, and has not had treatment. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate gastroscopy
Test for H. pylori with stool antigen or urea breath test
Trial of lifelong high-dose proton pump inhibitor
CT abdomen
notes: No alarm features and young age; endoscopy is not first line.
Long-term PPI without testing misses a curable cause.
CT has no role in uncomplicated dyspepsia.
questions.why: Under 55 with no alarm features, test and treat H. pylori (urea breath test or stool antigen, off PPI for 2 weeks) is recommended for dyspepsia before endoscopy.

questions.stem: Testicular torsion most often occurs in adolescents because of which anatomical variant?
options: Short spermatic cord
Patent processus vaginalis only
Absent gubernaculum
Tunica vaginalis attached high on the cord (bell-clapper)
notes: A long, not short, cord permits twisting.
A patent processus relates to hernia or hydrocele, not classic torsion.
Gubernaculum absence is not the typical cause.
questions.why: In the bell-clapper deformity, the tunica vaginalis covers the testis and epididymis completely, so the testis hangs free and can rotate. It is often bilateral.

questions.stem: Why are young children more prone to acute otitis media than adults?
options: Their Eustachian tube is shorter, narrower and more horizontal
Their tympanic membrane is thicker and poorly vascularised
Their middle ear lacks a mucosal lining
Their Eustachian tube is longer and more vertical
notes: The tympanic membrane is not thicker in children, and thickness does not explain the susceptibility.
The middle ear has a mucosal lining at all ages.
The tube is shorter and more horizontal in children; it lengthens and becomes more vertical with age.
questions.why: In infants the Eustachian tube is short, narrow and horizontal, so it drains poorly and allows nasopharyngeal pathogens to reach the middle ear.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis?
options: Parathyroid hormone secretion by granulomas
Increased renal reabsorption of calcium due to loss of calcitonin
Osteoclast activation by tumour-derived PTH-related peptide
Activated macrophages in granulomas converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol
notes: PTH is suppressed in sarcoid hypercalcaemia.
Calcitonin loss is not a mechanism of this.
PTHrP is a paraneoplastic mechanism, for example in squamous cell lung cancer.
questions.why: Granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, unregulated by PTH, producing excess calcitriol and increased gut calcium absorption. PTH is suppressed.

questions.stem: In myasthenia gravis, what is the main autoantibody target?
options: Postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel
Muscle sodium channel
Neurofilament in the axon
notes: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
Sodium channel antibodies are not the cause of myasthenia gravis.
Axonal neurofilament is not the myasthenia target.
questions.why: Antibodies to the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor reduce receptor numbers, so end-plate potentials fail, causing fatigable weakness.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man who injects drugs has a 3 cm tender abscess on the forearm, no systemic features. Incision and drainage was done. Prior swab grew community-acquired MRSA. What is the most important management step?
options: Adequate incision and drainage alone is usually sufficient
Long-course IV vancomycin for all patients
Oral flucloxacillin for 7 days
Topical mupirocin to the wound only
notes: IV vancomycin is reserved for severe or systemic infection.
Flucloxacillin does not cover MRSA and is not required for a drained simple abscess.
Topical mupirocin is not treatment for an abscess.
questions.why: For simple abscesses without systemic features, drainage is the key treatment; antibiotics are added only for systemic illness, extensive cellulitis, or immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man has LDL-C 6.2 mmol/L, tendon xanthomata, and his father had an MI at 48. He is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Lifestyle advice alone and recheck in 12 months
Calculate 5-year risk and treat only if over 10%
Start a high-intensity statin and arrange cascade screening of relatives
Start fenofibrate as first-line therapy
notes: Lifestyle alone is insufficient in FH.
The risk calculator does not apply to people with clinically diagnosed FH, who are treated regardless.
Fibrates are not first-line for raised LDL-C.
questions.why: Clinically probable familial hypercholesterolaemia is treated regardless of the risk calculator: high-intensity statin, add ezetimibe if needed, and cascade-test first-degree relatives.

questions.stem: A woman taking an ACE inhibitor for hypertension finds she is 10 weeks pregnant. Which fetal toxicity is the main reason ACE inhibitors are avoided, particularly in the second and third trimesters?
options: Fetal renal dysfunction with oligohydramnios
Neural tube defects
Fetal thyroid goitre
Premature closure of the ductus venosus
notes: Neural tube defects are linked to valproate and carbamazepine (folate antagonism), not ACE inhibitors.
Fetal goitre is associated with antithyroid drugs or iodine excess, not ACE inhibitors.
Premature ductus arteriosus closure occurs with NSAIDs; the ductus venosus is not the target.
questions.why: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II, which maintains fetal glomerular filtration. This causes renal failure, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia and skull hypoplasia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old reports a childhood benign rash with amoxicillin over 10 years ago, with no systemic features or anaphylaxis. She is well now. Which is the most appropriate step per Australian antibiotic allergy guidance?
options: Direct oral amoxicillin challenge to delabel
Lifelong avoidance of all beta-lactams
Skin prick testing for all penicillins first
Use of vancomycin for future infections
notes: Avoidance perpetuates an inaccurate label and leads to inferior, broader-spectrum therapy.
Skin testing is not needed for low-risk histories; direct challenge is safe.
Vancomycin is inferior for beta-lactam-susceptible infections and worsens stewardship.
questions.why: Low-risk histories (such as remote benign rash) can be delabelled by direct oral challenge, per ASCIA/eTG tools such as PEN-FAST. Delabelling reduces broad-spectrum use and C. difficile risk.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms. Prostate is estimated at 70 mL on ultrasound, PSA 5.0 microgram/L, and he has no postural hypotension. Which drug combination best reduces his risk of progression and retention?
options: Tamsulosin alone
Dutasteride plus tamsulosin
Oxybutynin plus tamsulosin
Tadalafil alone
notes: An alpha-blocker gives quick symptom relief but does not shrink the gland or reduce retention risk long term.
Antimuscarinics treat overactive bladder symptoms and do not address gland size or progression.
Tadalafil improves symptoms but does not reduce prostate volume or progression.
questions.why: For a large prostate (more than about 30–40 mL) with bothersome symptoms, a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor plus an alpha-blocker reduces progression and retention risk. Dutasteride roughly halves PSA.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains how a group A streptococcal pharyngeal infection causes carditis in acute rheumatic fever?
options: Direct bacterial invasion of the heart valves
Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac myosin
Streptolysin O toxin directly lysing myocytes
Bacterial superantigen causing Kawasaki-type coronary vasculitis
notes: Wrong: the valves are not infected; cultures are sterile and the damage is autoimmune, which is why antibiotics do not treat the carditis.
Wrong: streptolysin O is the antigen behind the raised ASO titre, not the cause of the myocardial injury.
Wrong: this describes mechanisms proposed for Kawasaki disease or toxic shock, not the post-streptococcal autoimmune process of ARF.
questions.why: Immune response to group A streptococcal M protein cross-reacts with host cardiac proteins (e.g. myosin) in susceptible hosts: molecular mimicry. The heart is not infected.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man collapsed suddenly while swimming. His brother died suddenly aged 20. ECG shows QTc 510 ms. Which drug is the best long-term first-line therapy?
options: Flecainide
Digoxin
Nadolol
Verapamil
notes: Flecainide is not first-line for long QT syndrome and carries proarrhythmic risk.
Digoxin is proarrhythmic and does not reduce long QT risk.
Verapamil is not an established therapy for long QT syndrome.
questions.why: Syncope with swimming and a family history suggests long QT syndrome type 1. Non-selective beta-blockers such as nadolol are first-line, with an ICD for high-risk patients.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has an acute asthma exacerbation. Which change in the airways is the main reason salbutamol rapidly relieves wheeze?
options: Bronchial smooth muscle relaxation via beta-2 receptors
Reduced airway mucosal oedema via glucocorticoid action
Blockade of leukotriene receptors on eosinophils
Thinning of mucus through increased ciliary clearance
notes: Describes corticosteroid effect, which is slower and not how salbutamol works.
Describes montelukast, a preventer, not a reliever.
Mucociliary clearance is not the main mechanism of salbutamol's rapid effect.
questions.why: Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist that raises cAMP and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, giving rapid bronchodilation. Corticosteroids act on inflammation over hours.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains the clonus, hyperreflexia and hyperthermia seen in serotonin syndrome?
options: Excess 5-HT2A stimulation in the brainstem and spinal cord
Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway
Excess GABA-A receptor activation in the cortex
Ryanodine receptor dysfunction in skeletal muscle
notes: D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway is the proposed mechanism of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with rigidity and bradyreflexia.
GABA-A activation causes sedation and hypotonia, not neuromuscular hyperactivity.
Ryanodine receptor dysfunction underlies malignant hyperthermia, a different condition triggered by anaesthetic agents.
questions.why: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic stimulation, especially 5-HT2A (and 5-HT1A), causing neuromuscular hyperactivity and hyperthermia. D2 blockade underlies neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

questions.stem: Which early placental abnormality is thought to underlie pre-eclampsia?
options: Inadequate remodelling of spiral arteries by extravillous trophoblast
Excessive trophoblast invasion into the myometrium with low-resistance flow
Primary maternal renal glomerular injury causing proteinuria
Placental overproduction of pro-angiogenic placental growth factor
notes: Excess invasion describes placenta accreta spectrum, not pre-eclampsia.
Renal involvement is a consequence of endothelial dysfunction, not the primary defect.
Pre-eclampsia features low placental growth factor and high sFlt-1, not overproduction.
questions.why: Shallow trophoblast invasion leaves spiral arteries narrow, causing placental ischaemia and release of anti-angiogenic factors (sFlt-1), which cause maternal endothelial dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old bird breeder has 1 week of fever, dry cough, headache and relative bradycardia. Chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation. Which organism is most likely?
options: Chlamydia psittaci
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Legionella pneumophila
Coxiella burnetii
notes: Pneumococcus is common, but bird exposure points elsewhere.
Legionella is linked to water systems and potting mix, with hyponatraemia.
Q fever follows livestock exposure, not birds.
questions.why: Psittacosis follows exposure to infected birds (parrots, pigeons, poultry) and causes atypical pneumonia with headache and relative bradycardia. Treat with doxycycline.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has fluctuating alertness, well-formed visual hallucinations of children, mild parkinsonism and acting out his dreams. Memory is relatively preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Alzheimer disease
Vascular dementia
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia
notes: Alzheimer disease presents with early prominent amnesia, without these core features.
Vascular dementia has stepwise decline and focal signs with vascular risk factors.
bvFTD presents with disinhibition, apathy and loss of empathy, with early personality change.
questions.why: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism are core features of dementia with Lewy bodies. Avoid typical antipsychotics (severe sensitivity).

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine ACR 8 mg/mmol on two samples over 4 months. Which CKD stage and category is this?
options: Stage 2, albuminuria category A1
Stage 3a, albuminuria category A2
Stage 3b, albuminuria category A3
Stage 3a, albuminuria category A3
notes: eGFR 52 is below 60, so this is stage 3, not 2.
G3b is eGFR 30 to 44, and A3 requires ACR above 25 mg/mmol in men.
A3 requires ACR above 25 mg/mmol in men (35 in women); 8 is A2.
questions.why: eGFR 45 to 59 is G3a. In men, ACR 2.5 to 25 mg/mmol (women 3.5 to 35) is A2, moderately increased. Persistence over 3 months confirms CKD.

questions.stem: Which protein, secreted by the liver, is raised in iron overload and inhibits iron absorption by degrading ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages?
options: Transferrin
Hepcidin
Erythropoietin
Ferritin
notes: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; it is not an inhibitor of absorption and rises in iron deficiency.
Erythropoietin drives red cell production; it suppresses hepcidin rather than degrading ferroportin.
Ferritin stores iron intracellularly; it does not regulate ferroportin.
questions.why: Hepcidin binds ferroportin, causing its internalisation and degradation, so less iron leaves enterocytes and macrophages. It is raised in inflammation, which explains anaemia of chronic disease.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman on apixaban falls at home and hits her head. She is GCS 15, has no vomiting or neurological deficit, and a 2 cm scalp haematoma. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with head injury advice
Observe for 6 hours then discharge
CT head now
CT head only if symptoms develop
notes: Unsafe: anticoagulant use is a risk factor mandating imaging.
Observation alone does not exclude intracranial haemorrhage in an anticoagulated patient.
Waiting for symptoms risks delayed diagnosis of a bleed.
questions.why: Anticoagulated patients with head injury need urgent CT head, even if GCS 15 and asymptomatic, because of the risk of occult or delayed intracranial bleeding.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria starts an ACE inhibitor. Which mechanism most directly reduces intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria?
options: Efferent arteriolar dilatation
Afferent arteriolar constriction
Reduced proximal tubular sodium reabsorption
Increased mesangial contraction
notes: Afferent constriction is the effect of SGLT2 inhibitors via tubuloglomerular feedback, not ACE inhibitors.
Proximal sodium reabsorption is the target of SGLT2 inhibitors, not ACE inhibitors.
ACE inhibitors relax mesangial cells; contraction would reduce filtration surface area.
questions.why: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole. Blocking it dilates the efferent arteriole, lowering glomerular capillary pressure and albuminuria. Expect a small, acceptable rise in creatinine.

questions.stem: Why does broad-spectrum antibiotic use predispose to Clostridioides difficile infection?
options: It depletes protective colonic flora, allowing spore germination and toxin production
It directly stimulates toxin gene transcription
It raises gastric pH, allowing vegetative bacteria to survive
It suppresses neutrophil function in the gut
notes: Antibiotics do not directly upregulate toxin genes; the effect is through flora loss.
Raised gastric pH is a PPI-related risk factor and not the antibiotic mechanism.
Antibiotics do not primarily impair gut neutrophils.
questions.why: Disrupting the commensal microbiome removes colonisation resistance, so ingested spores germinate and produce toxins A and B. Narrow-spectrum, short courses reduce risk.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 18 months ago. He now has fatigue, a macrocytic anaemia and paraesthesia. Which long-term supplementation is essential after this operation?
options: Lifelong vitamin B12
Vitamin C
Vitamin K
Folate restriction
notes: Vitamin C deficiency is uncommon and does not cause macrocytosis with neuropathy.
Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not neuropathy or macrocytosis.
Folate is supplemented, not restricted.
questions.why: Bypass reduces intrinsic factor and acid, so B12 deficiency is common and lifelong supplementation (with iron, calcium, vitamin D) is needed.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old develops watery diarrhoea 6 days after starting clindamycin in hospital. Stool is positive for C. difficile toxin. Which is the first-line oral therapy per eTG for an initial episode?
options: Vancomycin orally
Metronidazole intravenously
Loperamide
Ciprofloxacin orally
notes: IV metronidazole is no longer first-line and is reserved as an adjunct in severe cases.
Antimotility agents risk toxic megacolon.
Fluoroquinolones are a high-risk cause of C. difficile.
questions.why: Oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin) is first-line for C. difficile infection, along with stopping the precipitating antibiotic where possible. Antimotility drugs should be avoided.

questions.stem: A well 55-year-old man with no family history asks about PSA testing. Which approach is best, in line with Australian guidance?
options: Offer testing every 2 years from 50 with informed discussion of harms and benefits
Test only if he has symptoms
Refuse testing as it is not recommended
Do a digital rectal exam only, avoiding PSA
notes: Asymptomatic men can choose testing after counselling; testing is not limited to symptoms.
Testing is not recommended routinely, but it is not refused if an informed man requests it.
DRE alone has poor sensitivity and is not recommended as a standalone screen.
questions.why: Australian guidelines recommend men aged 50–69 who choose to be tested have PSA every 2 years after shared decision-making about benefits and harms, including overdiagnosis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve on warfarin (INR target 3.0) presents at 5 weeks' gestation, planning to continue the pregnancy. Warfarin embryopathy risk is greatest at 6–12 weeks. What is the best next step?
options: Continue warfarin unchanged to protect the valve
Stop all anticoagulation until the second trimester
Switch to aspirin alone during the first trimester
Specialist-led switch to therapeutic LMWH with anti-Xa monitoring
notes: Continuing warfarin risks embryopathy in the sensitive window; if used, it needs specialist weighing of dose and risk.
Stopping all anticoagulation risks valve thrombosis and maternal death.
Aspirin alone gives inadequate protection against mechanical valve thrombosis.
questions.why: Warfarin is teratogenic at 6–12 weeks. In mechanical valves, urgent specialist planning is needed, usually switching to therapeutic LMWH with anti-Xa monitoring. DOACs are contraindicated.

questions.stem: In heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which mechanism explains the fall in platelets together with a paradoxical risk of thrombosis?
options: Antibodies to heparin-PF4 complexes activate platelets
Autoantibodies to GPIIb/IIIa cause splenic clearance
ADAMTS13 deficiency causes platelet-rich microthrombi
Marrow suppression from heparin reduces megakaryocytes
notes: This describes ITP, which causes bleeding rather than thrombosis.
This describes TTP, which does not follow heparin exposure.
Heparin does not suppress megakaryocytes; HIT is immune-mediated consumption.
questions.why: IgG against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes binds platelet FcγRIIa, causing activation, consumption and thrombin generation, so thrombosis occurs despite thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: Chlamydia trachomatis is a common cause of urethritis and cervicitis. Which property of the organism explains why it is detected by NAAT rather than routine culture on agar?
options: It is an obligate intracellular bacterium
It is a Gram-positive spore-former
It is an anaerobic spirochaete
It lacks nucleic acid
notes: It is not a Gram-positive spore-former.
Spirochaetes describe Treponema, not Chlamydia.
All bacteria contain nucleic acid; NAAT depends on this.
questions.why: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium that cannot grow on cell-free media, so NAAT is the standard diagnostic test.

questions.stem: A screening test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 90%. It is applied to 1000 people in a population where disease prevalence is 1%. About what proportion of positive results are true positives?
options: About 90%
About 50%
About 10%
About 1%
notes: 90% is the sensitivity, not the PPV; PPV depends on prevalence.
50% would need a much higher prevalence, about 10%.
1% is just the prevalence; the test still enriches for disease above this.
questions.why: 10 diseased: 9 true positives. 990 well: 99 false positives. PPV = 9/108, about 8–10%. PPV falls as prevalence falls.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old at 34 weeks presents with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding. She is stable and the uterus is soft and non-tender. What should be avoided until the placental site is known?
options: Cardiotocography
Digital vaginal examination
Intravenous access
Ultrasound
notes: CTG is needed to assess fetal wellbeing and is safe.
IV access and bloods are required in antepartum haemorrhage.
Ultrasound locates the placenta and is the investigation of choice.
questions.why: Painless bright bleeding suggests placenta praevia. A digital examination can provoke torrential haemorrhage, so avoid it until ultrasound has excluded praevia.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man on warfarin presents with a large intracerebral haemorrhage and GCS 10. INR is 5.2. What is the most appropriate immediate reversal?
options: Oral vitamin K alone
Fresh frozen plasma alone
Prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K
Tranexamic acid alone
notes: Oral vitamin K is too slow for life-threatening bleeding.
FFP needs large volumes and is slower; PCC is preferred.
Tranexamic acid does not reverse warfarin's coagulopathy.
questions.why: Life-threatening warfarin bleeding needs rapid PCC to replace factors II, VII, IX, X, plus IV vitamin K 5–10 mg for sustained effect.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes in Darwin has fever, cough and hypotension in March, with bilateral nodular infiltrates and Gram-negative bacilli in blood cultures. Melioidosis is suspected. Which intravenous therapy is most appropriate?
options: Meropenem
Ceftriaxone
Gentamicin
Flucloxacillin
notes: Ceftriaxone is not reliably active against B. pseudomallei.
Aminoglycosides are ineffective against it.
Flucloxacillin does not cover Gram-negative bacilli.
questions.why: Severe melioidosis needs intensive-phase IV meropenem (or ceftazidime) for at least 2 weeks, followed by eradication therapy with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for about 3 months or more.

questions.stem: Triptans relieve acute migraine mainly through agonism at which receptor?
options: 5-HT1B/1D receptors
5-HT3 receptors
Dopamine D2 receptors
Beta-2 adrenergic receptors
notes: 5-HT3 antagonism is the mechanism of ondansetron for nausea, not triptans.
D2 antagonism is how metoclopramide helps nausea and gastric stasis.
Beta-2 receptors are not the triptan target; propranolol, a beta blocker, is used for prophylaxis.
questions.why: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists: they cause cranial vasoconstriction and inhibit trigeminal release of CGRP. Hence they are contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman from a high-incidence country, now a new migrant, has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. She has no symptoms, a normal CXR and a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Active pulmonary tuberculosis
Latent tuberculosis infection
Prior BCG vaccination only
Non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease
notes: No symptoms or radiological features of active disease.
IGRA is not affected by BCG, unlike the tuberculin skin test.
IGRA is specific to M. tuberculosis complex antigens; this is unlikely.
questions.why: Positive IGRA with no symptoms and normal CXR indicates latent TB infection; offer treatment to reduce reactivation risk. IGRA cannot distinguish latent from active disease, so symptoms and imaging matter.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Her chest x-ray is normal and she has no leg symptoms. She has no asthma or lung disease. Which is the most appropriate imaging test?
options: V/Q scan
CTPA with no shielding
Pulmonary angiography
MRI chest
notes: CTPA delivers higher breast radiation dose; it is second-line when the chest x-ray is normal.
Invasive pulmonary angiography is rarely used and has higher risk.
MRI chest is not a validated first-line test for PE in pregnancy.
questions.why: With a normal chest x-ray in pregnancy, V/Q scanning is preferred: lower maternal breast radiation than CTPA and good diagnostic yield. CTPA is acceptable if the x-ray is abnormal or V/Q is unavailable.

questions.stem: A patient takes an ACE inhibitor, a thiazide diuretic and an NSAID, and becomes volume depleted. Which mechanism best explains the fall in glomerular filtration rate?
options: Afferent arteriole constriction with efferent arteriole dilatation
Afferent arteriole dilatation with efferent arteriole constriction
Direct tubular toxicity from the NSAID
Increased tubular reabsorption of sodium from the diuretic
notes: This is the normal compensatory pattern in hypovolaemia; the drugs abolish it by doing the reverse.
NSAIDs can cause interstitial nephritis, but the triple whammy is haemodynamic, not direct tubular injury.
Diuretics reduce sodium reabsorption, causing volume loss, not increased reabsorption.
